What People Are Saying About Nonviolent Communication™

人们对非暴力沟通™的评价

Relationships:

人际关系：

“Marshall Rosenberg’s dynamic communication techniques transform potential conflicts into peaceful dialogues. You’ll learn simple tools to defuse arguments and create compassionate connections with your family, friends, and other acquaintances.”

“马歇尔·卢森堡的动态沟通技巧能将潜在冲突转化为和平对话。你将学习到一些简单的工具，帮助你化解争论，并与家人、朋友和其他熟人建立充满关爱的联系。”

—JOHN GRAY, author, Men Are From Mars, Women Are From Venus

——约翰·格雷，《男人来自火星，女人来自金星》作者

“Nonviolent Communication can change the world. More importantly, it can change your life. I cannot recommend it highly enough.”

“非暴力沟通可以改变世界。更重要的是，它可以改变你的人生。我强烈推荐它。”

—JACK CANFIELD, author, Chicken Soup for the Soul Series

——杰克·坎菲尔德，《心灵鸡汤》系列丛书作者

“Marshall Rosenberg provides us with the most effective tools to foster health and relationships. Nonviolent Communication connects soul to soul, creating a lot of healing. It is the missing element in what we do.”

“马歇尔·卢森堡为我们提供了促进身心健康和良好人际关系的最有效工具。非暴力沟通能够连接人与人，带来诸多疗愈。它是我们工作中缺失的关键要素。”

—DEEPAK CHOPRA, author, How to Know God and Ageless Body and Timeless Mind

——迪帕克·乔普拉，《如何认识神》和《不老的身体与永恒的心智》的作者

“I have taken conversations that were headed for the dumps, starting using these techniques, and ended up with a very useful bonding experience.”

“我曾让一些原本陷入僵局的谈话变得毫无生气，但通过运用这些技巧，最终却获得了非常有益的增进彼此感情的机会。”

—An online reviewer

——一位网络评论员

“If you want to be heard, and to hear what your loved ones are truly saying behind what there saying, read this book! It will change your life.”

“如果你想被倾听，想听听你爱的人话语背后真正想表达的意思，那就读读这本书吧！它会改变你的人生。”

—An online reviewer

——一位网络评论员

“Rosenberg has developed a simple method of communicating that helps to avoid triggering a defensive reaction, and instead stimulate understanding and agreement. It is invaluable in all your relationships, and definitely should be required reading for everyone.”

“罗森伯格开发了一种简单的沟通方法，有助于避免引发对方的防御反应，反而能促进理解和共识。这种方法对你所有的人际关系都至关重要，绝对应该成为每个人的必读书目。”

—An online reviewer

——一位网络评论员

Conflict Transformation:

冲突转化：

“Nonviolent Communication is one of the most useful processes you will ever learn.”

“非暴力沟通是你所能学到的最有用的方法之一。”

—WILLIAM URY, coauthor, Getting to Yes

——威廉·尤里，《谈判力》合著者

“In this book, you will find an amazingly effective language for saying what’s on your mind and in your heart. Like so many essential and elegant systems, it’s simple on the surface, challenging to use in the heat of the moment and powerful in its results.”

“在这本书中，你会发现一种极其有效的语言，可以用来表达你的想法和内心感受。就像许多精妙而重要的系统一样，它表面上很简单，但在紧急情况下使用起来却很有挑战性，而且效果显著。”

—VICKI ROBIN, coauthor, Your Money or Your Life

——维姬·罗宾，《你的金钱还是你的生活》合著者

“As far as nonviolence and spiritual activism, Marshall Rosenberg is it! Applying the concepts within these books will guide the reader towards fostering more compassion in the world.”

“就非暴力和精神行动主义而言，马歇尔·卢森堡堪称典范！运用这些书中的理念将引导读者在世界上培养更多的同情心。”

—MARIANNE WILLIAMSON, author, Everyday Grace and honorary chairperson, Peace Alliance

——玛丽安·威廉姆森，《每日恩典》作者，和平联盟名誉主席

“Like Noam Chomsky, Rosenberg’s work is intrinsically radical, it subverts our whole status-quo system of power: between children and adults, the sane and the psychotic, the criminal and the law. Rosenberg’s distinction between punitive and protective force should be required reading for anyone making foreign policy or policing our streets.”

“和诺姆·乔姆斯基一样，罗森伯格的著作本质上是激进的，它颠覆了我们现有的整个权力体系：儿童与成人、理智者与精神病患者、罪犯与法律之间的权力关系。罗森伯格对惩罚性武力和保护性武力的区分，应该成为所有制定外交政策或负责街头治安的人员的必读之作。”

—D. KILLIAN, reporter, On The Front Line, Cleveland Free Times

——D·基利安，《克利夫兰自由时报》前线记者

“We have lived traumatic moments over and over again—moments of fear and panic, incomprehension, frustrations, disappointment, and injustice of all sorts, with no hope of escape—which made it even worse. Nonviolent Communication offers us a peaceful alternative for ending this interminable Rwandan conflict.”

“我们一次又一次地经历着创伤性的时刻——恐惧和恐慌、不理解、沮丧、失望以及各种各样的不公正，而且看不到任何逃脱的希望——这使得情况更加糟糕。非暴力沟通为我们提供了一种和平结束这场旷日持久的卢旺达冲突的替代方案。”

—THEODORE NYILIDANDI, Rwandan Department of Foreign Affairs; Kigali, Rwanda

—THEODORE NYILIDANDI，卢旺达外交部；卢旺达基加利

“In our present age of uncivil discourse and mean-spirited demagoguery, the principles and practices of Nonviolent Communication are as timely as they are necessary to the peaceful resolution of conflicts, personal or public, domestic or international.”

“在我们这个充斥着粗鲁言论和卑鄙煽动的时代，非暴力沟通的原则和实践对于和平解决个人或公共、国内或国际冲突而言，既及时又必要。”

—MIDWEST BOOK REVIEW, Taylor’s Shelf

——《中西部书评》，泰勒书架

“Rosenberg describes how, in numerous conflicts, once ‘enemies’ have been able to hear each other’s needs, they are able to connect compassionately and find new solutions to previously ‘impossible’ impasses. If you want to learn ways of more skillful speech I highly recommend this clear, easy-to-read book.”

罗森伯格描述了在许多冲突中，一旦“敌人”能够倾听彼此的需求，他们就能建立起同情心，并找到解决先前“不可能”僵局的新方案。如果您想学习更巧妙的沟通技巧，我强烈推荐这本清晰易懂的书。

—DIANA LION, Buddhist Peace Fellowship, Turning Wheel Magazine

——戴安娜·莱昂，佛教和平团契，《转轮》杂志

“A simple communication process that eliminates the competitive, adversarial, and violence provocative style of communication that has infected most of our lives. This is not about the meek inheriting the world or being nice docile cogs in our power-over, hierarchical system. It is about the ‘protective use of force,’ vulnerability, heart-to-heart dialogue, and getting our needs meet in a way we will less likely regret.”

“一种简单的沟通方式，可以消除充斥我们大多数人生活的竞争性、对抗性和暴力挑衅式的沟通风格。这并非关乎温顺的人继承世界，也不是关乎成为我们权力等级制度中顺从的齿轮。它关乎‘保护性地使用武力’、坦诚相待、敞开心扉的对话，以及以一种我们不太可能后悔的方式来满足我们的需求。”

—An online reviewer

——一位网络评论员

“As a professional in the field, I can say that this book practices what it preaches, and I found the step-by-step approach, exercises, and examples to be clear and easy to practice.”

“作为该领域的专业人士，我可以肯定地说，这本书言行一致，我发现它循序渐进的方法、练习和例子都清晰易懂，便于实践。”

—A reader in Maryland

——一位来自马里兰州的读者

“I have never read a clearer, more straightforward, insightful book on communication. Amazingly easy to read, great examples, and challenging to put into practice—this book is a true gift to all of us.”

“我从未读过比这本更清晰、更直白、更有见地的沟通书籍。它读起来非常轻松，例子精彩，而且实践起来也很有挑战性——这本书对我们所有人来说都是一份真正的礼物。”

—A reader in Washington

——一位华盛顿的读者

Personal Growth:

个人成长：

“Nonviolent Communication by Marshall Rosenberg is a great book teaching a compassionate way to talk to people—even if you (or they) are angry.”

“马歇尔·卢森堡的《非暴力沟通》是一本很棒的书，它教会我们如何用富有同情心的方式与人交谈——即使你（或他们）很生气。”

—JOE VITALE, author, Spiritual Marketing, The Power of Outrageous Marketing

——乔·维塔莱，《精神营销》、《惊世骇俗营销的力量》作者

“Changing the way the world has worked for 5,000 years sounds daunting, but Nonviolent Communication helps liberate us from ancient patterns of violence.”

“改变世界五千年来运转的方式听起来令人生畏，但非暴力沟通有助于我们从古老的暴力模式中解放出来。”

—FRANCIS LEFKOWITZ, reporter, Body & Soul

——弗朗西斯·莱夫科维茨，《身心》杂志记者

“A revolutionary way of looking at language. If enough people actually make use of the material in Nonviolent Communication we may soon live in a more peaceful and compassionate world.”

“一种革命性的语言观。如果足够多的人真正运用《非暴力沟通》中的内容，我们或许很快就能生活在一个更加和平、充满爱心的世界。”

—WES TAYLOR, Progressive Health

——韦斯·泰勒，《进步健康》

“The single toughest, most dangerous opponent I’d ever faced—the one that truly hurt me the most, causing me to spend 30 years of my life behind bars—was my own anger and fear. I write these words now, a gray-haired old man, hoping to God—before you suffer what I’ve suffered—that it will cause you to listen and learn Nonviolent Communication. It will teach you how to recognize anger before it becomes violence, and how to understand, deal with, and take control of the rage you may feel.”

迪帕克·乔普拉，医学博士

Founder of the Chopra Center for Wellbeing and author of more than eighty books translated in over forty-three languages, including twenty-two New York Times bestsellers

乔普拉健康中心创始人，著有八十余本书籍，已被翻译成四十三种语言，其中包括二十二本《纽约时报》畅销书。

N o one deserves our gratitude more than the late Marshall Rosenberg, who lived his life just as the title of one of his books states: Speak Peace in a World of Conflict. He was keenly aware of the maxim (or warning) that’s contained in the subtitle of that book: What You Say Next Will Change Your World. Personal reality always contains a story, and the story we live, beginning from infancy, is based on language. This became the foundation of Marshall’s approach to conflict resolution, getting people to exchange words in a way that excludes judgments, blame, and violence.

没有人比已故的马歇尔·卢森堡更值得我们感激，他的一生正如他的一本书的书名所言：《在冲突的世界中说和平》。他敏锐地意识到该书副标题中的格言（或警告）：你接下来说的话将改变你的世界。个人现实总是包含着一个故事，而我们从婴儿时期就开始经历的故事，正是建立在语言之上的。这成为了马歇尔解决冲突方法的基础，他致力于引导人们以一种排除评判、指责和暴力的方式进行沟通。

The contorted faces of protestors on the streets that make such disturbing images on the evening news are more than images. Each face, each shout, each gesture has a history. Everyone clings to their history with a vengeance, because it anchors their identity. So when Marshall advocated peaceful talk, he was advocating a new identity at the same time. He fully realized this fact. As he states about Nonviolent Communication and the role of the mediator in this new third edition, “We’re trying to live a different value system while we are asking for things to change.”

晚间新闻中那些令人不安的街头抗议者扭曲的面孔，不仅仅是画面。每一张脸、每一次呐喊、每一个手势都承载着一段历史。每个人都紧紧抓住自己的历史不放，因为它是他们身份认同的基石。因此，当马歇尔倡导和平对话时，他同时也在倡导一种新的身份认同。他对此有着深刻的认识。正如他在第三版《非暴力沟通》中谈到调解员的角色时所说：“我们试图在要求改变现状的同时，践行一种不同的价值观。”

In his vision of a new value system, conflicts are resolved without the usual frustrating compromises. Instead, the contending parties approach each other with respect. They ask about each other’s needs, and in an atmosphere free of passions and prejudices, they reach a connection. Gazing on a world rife with war and violence, where us-versus-them thinking is the norm, and where countries can break all bonds of civilized existence to commit unbearable atrocities, a new value system seems far away. At one European conference for mediators, a skeptic criticized Marshall’s approach as psychotherapy. In popular language, isn’t he asking us to simply forget the past and just be friends, a remote prospect not just in the war-torn areas but in any divorce case?

在他构想的新价值体系中，冲突无需以往令人沮丧的妥协即可解决。相反，冲突各方以尊重的态度彼此接触，询问对方的需求，并在一个没有激情和偏见的氛围中建立联系。放眼当今这个充斥着战争和暴力、非此即彼的思维模式盛行、国家可以为了犯下令人发指的暴行而背弃一切文明纽带的世界，新的价值体系似乎遥不可及。在一次欧洲调解员会议上，一位怀疑论者批评马歇尔的方法如同心理疗法。用通俗的话来说，他难道不是在要求我们忘记过去，做回朋友吗？这不仅在战乱地区遥不可及，在任何离婚案件中也同样如此。

Value systems are packed in the luggage of every worldview. Not only are they inescapable, but people are proud of them—there’s a long tradition around the world of prizing and fearing warriors at the same time. Jungians tell us that the archetype of Mars, the volatile god of war, is imbedded in everyone’s unconscious, making conflict and aggression inevitable, a kind of inherent vice.

每一种世界观都蕴含着价值体系。它们不仅无处不在，人们还以此为傲——世界各地都有着既崇敬又畏惧战士的悠久传统。荣格学派告诉我们，战神玛尔斯的原型，这位性情多变的战神，深深植根于每个人的潜意识中，使得冲突和侵略不可避免，成为一种与生俱来的恶习。

But there’s an alternative view of human nature, eloquently expressed in this book that must be considered, because it’s our only real hope. In this view, we are not our stories. These stories are self-created fictions that remain intact through habit, group coercion, old conditioning, and lack of self-awareness. Even the best stories collaborate in violence. If you want to use force to protect your family, guard yourself from attack, fight against wrongdoing, prevent crime, and engage in a so-called “good war,” you have been co-opted by the siren song of violence. If you decide to opt out, there’s a sizable chance that society will turn on you and exact retribution. In short, finding a way out isn’t easy.

但本书中对人性提出了另一种精辟的见解，我们必须认真考虑这种观点，因为它是我们唯一的真正希望。在这种观点看来，我们并非我们讲述的故事。这些故事是我们自我创造的虚构，它们因习惯、群体胁迫、旧有的制约以及缺乏自我意识而得以完整地存在。即使是最好的故事也会助长暴力。如果你想用武力保护家人、抵御攻击、打击不法行为、预防犯罪，并参与所谓的“正义之战”，那么你已经中了暴力的诱惑。如果你选择退出，社会很可能会反过来对付你，并对你进行报复。简而言之，找到出路并非易事。

In India there’s an ancient model for nonviolent living known as Ahimsa, which is central to the nonviolent life. Ahimsa is usually defined as nonviolence, although its meaning extends from Mahatma Gandhi’s peaceful protests to Albert Schweitzer’s reverence for life. “Do no harm” would be the first axiom of Ahimsa. What so impressed me about Marshall Rosenberg, who passed away at eighty, just six weeks before I write this, is that he grasped both levels of Ahimsa, action and consciousness.

在印度，有一种古老的非暴力生活模式，称为“阿希姆萨”（Ahimsa），它是非暴力生活的核心。阿希姆萨通常被定义为非暴力，但其含义涵盖了从圣雄甘地的和平抗议到阿尔伯特·史怀泽对生命的敬畏。“不伤害”是阿希姆萨的第一条准则。马歇尔·卢森堡（Marshall Rosenberg）令我印象深刻，他享年八十岁，就在我写下这篇文章前六周去世。他深刻理解阿希姆萨的两个层面：行动和意识。

The actions are well described in the following pages as principles of Nonviolent Communication, so I won’t repeat them here. To be in Ahimsa consciousness is much more powerful, and Marshall possessed that trait. In any conflict, he didn’t choose sides or even care primarily what their stories were. Recognizing that all stories lead to conflict, either overtly or covertly, he focused on connections as a psychological bridge. This is in keeping with another axiom of Ahimsa: It’s not what you do that counts, it’s the quality of your attention. As far as the legal system is concerned, a divorce is over once the two parties settle on how to split their assets. But this is far from the result that’s reached emotionally between the two divorced parties. Too much has been said, to use Marshall’s wording, that changed their world.

这些行动在接下来的篇章中作为非暴力沟通的原则已有详尽描述，因此我在此不再赘述。保持非暴力意识的力量远胜于此，而马歇尔恰恰具备这种特质。在任何冲突中，他都不选边站队，甚至不太在意对方的说辞。他意识到所有的故事最终都会导致冲突，无论公开还是隐蔽，因此他专注于建立人与人之间的联结，以此作为心理上的桥梁。这与非暴力的另一条准则相符：重要的不是你做了什么，而是你关注的质量。就法律体系而言，一旦双方就财产分割达成一致，离婚就结束了。但这与离婚双方在情感上达成的最终结果相去甚远。用马歇尔的话来说，太多的话语改变了他们的世界。

Aggression is built into the ego system, which totally focuses on “I, me, and mine” whenever conflict arises. Society pays lip service to saints and their vow to serve God instead of themselves, but there’s a huge gap between the values we espouse and the way we actually live. Ahimsa closes this gap only by expanding a person’s awareness. The only way to resolve all violence is to give up your story. No one can be enlightened who still has a personal stake in the world—that could be the third axiom of Ahimsa. But this seems like a teaching as radical as Jesus in the Sermon on the Mount when he promises that the meek shall inherit the earth.

攻击性根植于自我系统，一旦冲突发生，该系统便完全聚焦于“我、我、我的”。社会口头上推崇圣人及其侍奉上帝而非侍奉自己的誓言，但我们所宣扬的价值观与实际生活方式之间存在着巨大的鸿沟。非暴力（Ahimsa）唯有通过扩展人的觉知才能弥合这一鸿沟。解决一切暴力的唯一途径是放下你固有的执念。任何对世界仍抱有私利的人都无法获得觉悟——这或许可以称之为非暴力的第三条公理。但这似乎是一种如同耶稣在登山宝训中承诺“温柔的人必承受地土”般激进的教义。

In both cases, the point isn’t to change your actions but to change your consciousness. To do that, you must walk a path from A to B, where A is a life based on the incessant demands of the ego and B is selfless awareness. To be frank, nobody really desires selfless awareness; from the viewpoint of looking out for number one, it sounds at once scary and impossible. What’s the payoff if you depose the ego, which is all about payoffs? Once the ego is gone, do you sit around passively like a spiritual beanbag?

无论哪种情况，重点都不在于改变你的行为，而在于改变你的意识。要做到这一点，你必须走一条从A到B的道路，A代表基于自我永无止境的需求的生活，而B代表无私的觉知。坦白说，没有人真正渴望无私的觉知；从只顾自身利益的角度来看，这听起来既可怕又不可能。如果你摒弃了自我——而自我本身就是一切为了利益的——那么回报是什么呢？一旦自我消失，你就会像一个精神上的懒人一样被动地坐着吗？

The answer lies in those moments when the personal self falls away naturally and spontaneously. These occur in moments of meditation or simply deep contentment. Selfless awareness is the state we’re in when Nature or art or music creates a sense of wonder. The only difference between those moments—to which we can add all experiences of creativity, love, and play—and Ahimsa is that they flicker in and out while Ahimsa is a settled state. It reveals that stories and the egos that fuel them are illusions, self-created models for survival and selfishness. The payoff for Ahimsa isn’t that you upgrade the illusion, which is what the ego is always striving to do with more money, possessions, and power. The payoff is that you get to be who you really are.

答案就在于那些个人自我自然而然消融的时刻。这些时刻发生在冥想或深深的满足之中。当我们被自然、艺术或音乐所震撼时，我们便进入了无我的觉知状态。这些时刻——以及所有创造、爱和玩乐的体验——与非暴力（Ahimsa）的唯一区别在于，前者转瞬即逝，而非暴力则是一种稳定状态。它揭示了故事以及驱动故事的自我都是幻象，是为生存和自私而自我构建的模式。非暴力的回报并非在于提升幻象——而这正是自我总是试图用更多的金钱、财富和权力来实现的。非暴力的回报在于，你能够成为真正的自己。

Higher consciousness is too lofty as the term for Ahimsa. Normal consciousness is more accurate in a world where the norm is so abnormal that it amounts to psychopathology. It’s not normal to live in a world where thousands of nuclear warheads are aimed at the enemy and terrorism is an acceptable religious act—they are merely the norm.

“更高意识”作为“非暴力”（Ahimsa）的术语过于高深莫测。在一个常态如此反常以至于近乎病态的世界里，“正常意识”更为贴切。生活在一个成千上万枚核弹头瞄准敌人、恐怖主义被视为可接受的宗教行为的世界里，这并非正常——它们仅仅是常态而已。

For me, the legacy of Marshall’s lifelong work doesn’t lie in how he revolutionized the role of the mediator, valuable as that was. It lies in the new value system he lived by, which in truth is quite ancient. Ahimsa has to be revived in every generation, because human nature is torn between peace and violence. Marshall Rosenberg gave proof that entering this state of expanded awareness was real and, when it came to settling disputes, very practical. He leaves footprints that the rest of us can follow. If we have true self-interest at heart, we will follow. It’s the only alternative in a world desperately seeking wisdom and the end of strife.

对我而言，马歇尔毕生工作的遗产并非在于他如何革新了调解员的角色（尽管这本身也极具价值），而在于他所奉行的全新价值体系，而这体系实际上相当古老。非暴力（Ahimsa）需要在每个时代被重新唤醒，因为人性本身就游走于和平与暴力之间。马歇尔·罗森伯格用实际行动证明，进入这种更高层次的觉知状态是真实存在的，并且在解决争端方面非常实用。他留下的足迹值得我们效仿。如果我们真正以自身利益为重，我们就会追随他。在这个迫切渴望智慧和终结纷争的世界里，这或许是唯一的选择。

—Deepak Chopra

——迪帕克·乔普拉

Acknowledgments

致谢

I ’m grateful that I was able to study and work with Professor Carl Rogers at a time when he was researching the components of a helping relationship. The results of this research played a key role in the evolution of the process of communication that I will be describing in this book.

我很荣幸能在卡尔·罗杰斯教授研究助人关系构成要素的时期，与他一起学习和工作。这项研究的成果对我将在本书中描述的沟通过程的演变起到了关键作用。

I will be forever grateful that Professor Michael Hakeem helped me to see the scientific limitations and the social and political dangers of practicing psychology in the way that I had been trained: with a pathology-based understanding of human beings. Seeing the limitations of this model stimulated me to search for ways of practicing a different psychology, one based on a growing clarity about how we human beings were meant to live.

我将永远感激迈克尔·哈基姆教授，他帮助我认识到以病理学为基础的心理学方法在科学上的局限性，以及由此带来的社会和政治风险。认识到这种模式的局限性促使我去探索另一种心理学实践方式，一种基于对我们人类生存方式日益清晰的认识的心理学。

I’m grateful, too, for George Miller’s and George Albee’s efforts to alert psychologists to the need to find better ways for “giving psychology away.” They helped me see that the enormity of suffering on our planet requires more effective ways of distributing much-needed skills than can be offered by a clinical approach.

我也很感激乔治·米勒和乔治·阿尔比，他们努力提醒心理学家们需要找到更好的方法来“普及心理学”。他们让我明白，我们星球上巨大的苦难需要比临床方法更有效的方式来传播急需的技能。

I would like to thank Lucy Leu for editing this book and creating the final manuscript; Rita Herzog and Kathy Smith for their editing assistance; and, for their additional help, Darold Milligan, Sonia Nordenson, Melanie Sears, Bridget Belgrave, Marian Moore, Kittrell McCord, Virginia Hoyte, and Peter Weismiller.

我要感谢 Lucy Leu 对本书的编辑和最终稿的撰写；感谢 Rita Herzog 和 Kathy Smith 的编辑协助；以及 Darold Milligan、Sonia Nordenson、Melanie Sears、Bridget Belgrave、Marian Moore、Kittrell McCord、Virginia Hoyte 和 Peter Weismiller 的额外帮助。

Finally, I would like to express gratitude to my friend Annie Muller. Her encouragement to be clearer about the spiritual foundation of my work has strengthened that work and enriched my life.

最后，我要感谢我的朋友安妮·穆勒。她鼓励我更清晰地理解我作品的精神基础，这不仅增强了我的作品，也丰富了我的生活。

Words Are Windows
(or They’re Walls)

文字是窗户（或者它们是墙）

I feel so sentenced by your words,

你的话语让我感觉像是在判刑。

I feel so judged and sent away,

我感觉自己被评判和排斥了，

Before I go I’ve got to know,

在我走之前，我必须知道，

Is that what you mean to say?

你是这个意思吗？

Before I rise to my defense,

在我为自己辩护之前，

Before I speak in hurt or fear,

在我因伤痛或恐惧而开口之前，

Before I build that wall of words,

在我筑起那道文字之墙之前，

Tell me, did I really hear?

告诉我，我真的听到了吗？

Words are windows, or they’re walls,

文字要么是窗户，要么是墙。

They sentence us, or set us free.

他们要么判我们刑，要么释放我们。

When I speak and when I hear,

当我说话和倾听时，

Let the love light shine through me.

让爱的光芒照耀我。

There are things I need to say,

有些话我必须说，

Things that mean so much to me,

对我意义非凡的事物，

If my words don’t make me clear,

如果我的话语还不够清楚，

Will you help me to be free?

你会帮助我获得自由吗？

If I seemed to put you down,

如果我看起来让你觉得我贬低了你，

If you felt I didn’t care,

如果你觉得我不在乎，

Try to listen through my words,

请仔细聆听我的话语。

To the feelings that we share.

致我们共同的感受。

—Ruth Bebermeyer

——露丝·贝伯迈耶

# ↩

Introduction

介绍

B elieving that it is our nature to enjoy giving and receiving in a compassionate manner, I have been preoccupied most of my life with two questions: What happens to disconnect us from our compassionate nature, leading us to behave violently and exploitatively? And conversely, what allows some people to stay connected to their compassionate nature under even the most trying circumstances?

我相信，以慈悲之心给予和接受是我们的天性，因此我一生都在思考两个问题：是什么让我们与慈悲的天性脱节，导致我们做出暴力和剥削的行为？反过来，又是什么让一些人即使在最艰难的情况下也能保持慈悲的天性？

My preoccupation with these questions began in childhood, around the summer of 1943, when our family moved to Detroit, Michigan. The second week after we arrived, a race war erupted over an incident at a public park. More than forty people were killed in the next few days. Our neighborhood was situated in the center of the violence, and we spent three days locked in the house.

我对这些问题的思考始于童年时期，大约在1943年夏天，当时我们全家搬到了密歇根州的底特律。我们到达后的第二周，一场因公园事件引发的种族冲突爆发。接下来的几天里，四十多人丧生。我们居住的街区正处于冲突中心，我们被困在家中三天。

When the race riot ended and school began, I discovered that a name could be as dangerous as any skin color. When the teacher called my name during attendance, two boys glared at me and hissed, “Are you a kike?” I had never heard the word before and didn’t know some people used it in a derogatory way to refer to Jews. After school, the same two boys were waiting for me: they threw me to the ground and kicked and beat me.

种族骚乱结束后，学校重新开学，我发现名字的危险程度不亚于肤色。点名时，老师叫到我的名字，两个男孩怒视着我，嘶嘶地说：“你是犹太佬吗？”我以前从未听过这个词，也不知道有些人会用它来贬低犹太人。放学后，那两个男孩又在等着我：他们把我摔倒在地，拳打脚踢，拳打脚踢。

Since that summer in 1943, I have been examining the two questions I mentioned. What empowers us, for example, to stay connected to our compassionate nature even under the worst circumstances? I am thinking of people like Etty Hillesum, who remained compassionate even while subjected to the grotesque conditions of a German concentration camp. As she wrote in her journal at the time,

自1943年那个夏天以来，我一直在思考我提到的那两个问题。例如，是什么赋予我们力量，即使在最糟糕的情况下，也能保持我们慈悲的本性？我想到了像埃蒂·希勒苏姆这样的人，即使身处德国集中营的骇人听闻的环境中，她依然保持着慈悲之心。正如她当时在日记中所写的那样：

I am not easily frightened. Not because I am brave but because I know that I am dealing with human beings, and that I must try as hard as I can to understand everything that anyone ever does. And that was the real import of this morning: not that a disgruntled young Gestapo officer yelled at me, but that I felt no indignation, rather a real compassion, and would have liked to ask, ‘Did you have a very unhappy childhood, has your girlfriend let you down?’ Yes, he looked harassed and driven, sullen and weak. I should have liked to start treating him there and then, for I know that pitiful young men like that are dangerous as soon as they are let loose on mankind.

我并不容易被吓到。这并非因为我勇敢，而是因为我知道自己面对的是活生生的人，我必须尽我所能去理解每个人的一举一动。而这才是今天早上真正重要的：并非是一个心怀不满的年轻盖世太保军官对我大吼大叫，而是我没有感到愤怒，反而产生了一种真切的同情，我真想问问他：“你的童年很不幸吗？你的女朋友让你失望了吗？”是的，他看起来疲惫不堪，心烦意乱，阴郁而虚弱。我当时真想立刻开始治疗他，因为我知道，像他这样可怜的年轻人一旦被放逐到人群中，就会变得非常危险。

—Etty Hillesum in Etty: A Diary 1941–1943

——埃蒂·希勒森 (Etty Hillesum)，《埃蒂：日记 1941-1943》

While studying the factors that affect our ability to stay compassionate, I was struck by the crucial role of language and our use of words. I have since identified a specific approach to communicating—both speaking and listening—that leads us to give from the heart, connecting us with ourselves and with each other in a way that allows our natural compassion to flourish. I call this approach Nonviolent Communication, using the term nonviolence as Gandhi used it—to refer to our natural state of compassion when violence has subsided from the heart. While we may not consider the way we talk to be “violent,” words often lead to hurt and pain, whether for others or ourselves. In some communities, the process I am describing is known as Compassionate Communication; the abbreviation NVC is used throughout this book to refer to Nonviolent or Compassionate Communication.

在研究影响我们保持慈悲心的因素时，我深刻体会到语言及其运用方式的关键作用。此后，我发现了一种特定的沟通方式——包括说话和倾听——它能引导我们发自内心地付出，让我们与自身和他人建立连接，从而使我们与生俱来的慈悲心得以蓬勃发展。我将这种方法称为“非暴力沟通”，这里的“非暴力”一词源于甘地，指的是当内心不再充满暴力时，我们自然而然地流露出的慈悲之心。虽然我们可能并不认为自己的言谈举止是“暴力”的，但言语往往会造成伤害和痛苦，无论是对他人的伤害还是对我们自身的伤害。在一些社群中，我所描述的这种沟通方式被称为“慈悲沟通”；本书中，NVC 一词即指代非暴力沟通或慈悲沟通。

NVC: a way of communicating that leads us to give from the heart.

非暴力沟通：一种引导我们发自内心给予的沟通方式。

# ↩

A Way to Focus Attention

集中注意力的方法

NVC is founded on language and communication skills that strengthen our ability to remain human, even under trying conditions. It contains nothing new; all that has been integrated into NVC has been known for centuries. The intent is to remind us about what we already know—about how we humans were meant to relate to one another—and to assist us in living in a way that concretely manifests this knowledge.

非暴力沟通（NVC）建立在语言和沟通技巧之上，这些技巧能够增强我们在困境中保持人性的能力。它并不包含任何新内容；所有融入非暴力沟通的内容都已流传数百年。其目的是提醒我们那些我们早已知晓的道理——我们人类原本应该如何彼此相处——并帮助我们以一种切实体现这些知识的方式去生活。

NVC guides us in reframing how we express ourselves and hear others. Instead of habitual, automatic reactions, our words become conscious responses based firmly on awareness of what we are perceiving, feeling, and wanting. We are led to express ourselves with honesty and clarity, while simultaneously paying others a respectful and empathic attention. In any exchange, we come to hear our own deeper needs and those of others. NVC trains us to observe carefully, and to be able to specify behaviors and conditions that are affecting us. We learn to identify and clearly articulate what we are concretely wanting in any given situation. The form is simple, yet powerfully transformative.

非暴力沟通（NVC）引导我们重新构建表达自我和倾听他人的方式。我们的言语不再是习惯性的、自动的反应，而是基于对自身感知、感受和需求的清醒觉察而做出的有意识的回应。我们被引导以诚实和清晰的方式表达自己，同时给予他人尊重和同理心的关注。在任何交流中，我们都能听到自己和他人的深层需求。非暴力沟通训练我们仔细观察，并能够具体指出影响我们的行为和状况。我们学会识别并清晰地表达在任何特定情况下我们具体想要的是什么。这种沟通方式形式简单，却蕴含着强大的变革力量。

As NVC replaces our old patterns of defending, withdrawing, or attacking in the face of judgment and criticism, we come to perceive ourselves and others, as well as our intentions and relationships, in a new light. Resistance, defensiveness, and violent reactions are minimized. When we focus on clarifying what is being observed, felt, and needed rather than on diagnosing and judging, we discover the depth of our own compassion. Through its emphasis on deep listening—to ourselves as well as to others—NVC fosters respect, attentiveness, and empathy and engenders a mutual desire to give from the heart.

非暴力沟通（NVC）取代了我们面对评判和批评时惯用的防御、退缩或攻击模式，让我们得以用全新的视角看待自己、他人、以及我们的意图和人际关系。抗拒、防御和暴力反应都会被最小化。当我们专注于澄清所观察到的、感受到的和需要的，而不是诊断和评判时，我们便会发现自身慈悲的深度。非暴力沟通强调深度聆听——聆听自己和他人——从而培养尊重、专注和同理心，并激发彼此发自内心的付出意愿。

We perceive relationships in a new light when we use NVC to hear our own deeper needs and those of others.

当我们运用非暴力沟通来倾听自己和他人的深层需求时，我们会以全新的视角看待人际关系。

Although I refer to it as “a process of communication” or “a language of compassion,” NVC is more than a process or a language. On a deeper level, it is an ongoing reminder to keep our attention focused on a place where we are more likely to get what we are seeking.

虽然我称之为“沟通的过程”或“同理心的语言”，但非暴力沟通远不止于此。在更深层次上，它是一种持续的提醒，让我们将注意力集中在更有可能获得我们所寻求之物的地方。

There is a story of a man on all fours under a street lamp, searching for something. A policeman passing by asked what he was doing. “Looking for my car keys,” replied the man, who appeared slightly drunk. “Did you drop them here?” inquired the officer. “No,” answered the man, “I dropped them in the alley.” Seeing the policeman’s baffled expression, the man hastened to explain, “But the light is much better here.”

从前有个男人四肢着地趴在路灯下，似乎在找什么东西。一个路过的警察问他在干什么。“我在找车钥匙，”男人回答道，看起来有点醉醺醺的。“你把钥匙丢这儿了吗？”警察问。“没有，”男人回答，“我丢在巷子里了。”看到警察一脸疑惑，男人赶紧解释说：“可是这里的光线好多了。”

I find that my cultural conditioning leads me to focus attention on places where I am unlikely to get what I want. I developed NVC as a way to train my attention—to shine the light of consciousness—on places that have the potential to yield what I am seeking. What I want in my life is compassion, a flow between myself and others based on a mutual giving from the heart.

我发现，我的文化背景让我倾向于关注那些不太可能得到我想要的东西的地方。我发展出非暴力沟通（NVC）的方法，是为了训练我的注意力——让意识之光照亮那些有可能带来我所寻求的东西的地方。我渴望的是慈悲，是人与人之间基于彼此真诚付出而产生的和谐流动。

Let’s shine the light of consciousness on places where we can hope to find what we are seeking.

让我们用意识之光照亮那些我们有望找到我们所寻求之物的地方。

This quality of compassion, which I refer to as “giving from the heart,” is expressed in the following lyrics by my friend Ruth Bebermeyer:

这种同情心，我称之为“发自内心的给予”，在我的朋友露丝·贝伯迈尔的以下歌词中得到了体现：

I never feel more given to

我从未感到如此慷慨。

than when you take from me—

比你从我这里拿走的时候——

when you understand the joy I feel giving to you.

当你明白我给予你的快乐时。

And you know my giving isn’t done to put you in my debt,

你知道我这样做并不是为了让你欠我人情，

but because I want to live the love I feel for you.

但因为我想活出我对你的爱。

To receive with grace

以恩典领受

may be the greatest giving.

或许是最慷慨的奉献。

There’s no way I can separate the two.

我根本无法将这两者分开。

When you give to me,

当你给我的时候，

I give you my receiving.

我把我的接收情况告诉你。

When you take from me, I feel so given to.

当你从我这里拿走东西时，我感觉自己被给予了太多。

—“Given To” (1978) by Ruth Bebermeyer from the album Given To

—Ruth Bebermeyer 的歌曲“Given To”（1978 年），选自专辑《Given To》。

When we give from the heart, we do so out of the joy that springs forth whenever we willingly enrich another person’s life. This kind of giving benefits both the giver and the receiver. The receiver enjoys the gift without worrying about the consequences that accompany gifts given out of fear, guilt, shame, or desire for gain. The giver benefits from the enhanced self-esteem that results when we see our efforts contributing to someone’s well-being.

当我们发自内心地给予时，我们是因为乐于助人、丰富他人生活而产生的喜悦。这种给予方式对施予者和接受者都有益。接受者可以享受礼物，而无需担心因恐惧、内疚、羞耻或贪婪而赠送礼物所带来的后果。施予者则能从提升的自尊中受益，因为我们看到自己的努力为他人的福祉做出了贡献。

The use of NVC does not require that the persons with whom we are communicating be literate in NVC or even motivated to relate to us compassionately. If we stay with the principles of NVC, stay motivated solely to give and receive compassionately, and do everything we can to let others know this is our only motive, they will join us in the process, and eventually we will be able to respond compassionately to one another. I’m not saying that this always happens quickly. I do maintain, however, that compassion inevitably blossoms when we stay true to the principles and process of NVC.

运用非暴力沟通并不要求与我们沟通的人精通非暴力沟通，甚至也不要求他们有意愿以同理心对待我们。如果我们坚持非暴力沟通的原则，始终怀着同理心去给予和接受，并尽一切努力让对方明白这是我们唯一的动机，他们就会加入我们，最终我们也能彼此以同理心回应。我并不是说这总是会很快发生。但我相信，当我们忠于非暴力沟通的原则和方法时，同理心必然会萌芽。

# ↩

The NVC Process

非暴力沟通流程

To arrive at a mutual desire to give from the heart, we focus the light of consciousness on four areas—referred to as the four components of the NVC model.

为了达成发自内心的共同付出愿望，我们将意识之光聚焦于四个方面——这四个方面被称为非暴力沟通模式的四个组成部分。

First, we observe what is actually happening in a situation: what are we observing others saying or doing that is either enriching or not enriching our life? The trick is to be able to articulate this observation without introducing any judgment or evaluation—to simply say what people are doing that we either like or don’t like. Next, we state how we feel when we observe this action: are we hurt, scared, joyful, amused, irritated? And thirdly, we say what needs of ours are connected to the feelings we have identified. An awareness of these three components is present when we use NVC to clearly and honestly express how we are.

首先，我们要观察情境中实际发生的事情：我们观察到他人的言行举止是否丰富了我们的生活？关键在于，要能够清晰地表达这种观察，而不带任何评判或评价——只需简单地说出我们喜欢或不喜欢的行为即可。其次，我们要陈述观察到这种行为时的感受：我们感到受伤、害怕、喜悦、好笑还是恼怒？第三，我们要说明我们自身的哪些需求与这些感受相关联。当我们运用非暴力沟通（NVC）清晰、真诚地表达自己的感受时，就需要意识到这三个要素的存在。

Four components of NVC:

非暴力沟通的四个组成部分：

1. observations

1. 观察

2. feelings

2. 感觉

3. needs

3. 需求

4. requests

4. 请求

For example, a mother might express these three pieces to her teenage son by saying, “Felix, when I see two balls of soiled socks under the coffee table and another three next to the TV, I feel irritated because I am needing more order in the rooms that we share in common.”

例如，一位母亲可能会这样向她十几岁的儿子表达这三点：“费利克斯，当我看到咖啡桌下有两团脏袜子，电视机旁边还有三团脏袜子时，我会感到恼火，因为我需要我们共用的房间里更加整洁。”

She would follow immediately with the fourth component—a very specific request: “Would you be willing to put your socks in your room or in the washing machine?” This fourth component addresses what we are wanting from the other person that would enrich our lives or make life more wonderful for us.

她会紧接着提出第四个要素——一个非常具体的要求：“你愿意把袜子放在房间里或者洗衣机里吗？”这第四个要素关乎我们希望对方做什么，才能丰富我们的生活或让生活更美好。

Thus, part of NVC is to express these four pieces of information very clearly, whether verbally or by other means. The other part of this communication consists of receiving the same four pieces of information from others. We connect with them by first sensing what they are observing, feeling, and needing; then we discover what would enrich their lives by receiving the fourth piece—their request.

因此，非暴力沟通的一部分在于清晰地表达这四项信息，无论是口头表达还是其他方式。沟通的另一部分在于从他人那里接收这四项信息。我们首先通过感知他们的观察、感受和需求来与他们建立联系；然后，我们发现，如果接受他们的第四项信息——他们的请求——会如何丰富他们的生活。

As we keep our attention focused on the areas mentioned, and help others do likewise, we establish a flow of communication, back and forth, until compassion manifests naturally: what I am observing, feeling, and needing; what I am requesting to enrich my life; what you are observing, feeling, and needing; what you are requesting to enrich your life …

当我们持续关注上述领域，并帮助他人也这样做时，我们便能建立起双向的沟通，直至慈悲之心自然流露：我观察到的、感受到的和需要的；我请求什么来丰富我的生活；你观察到的、感受到的和需要的；你请求什么来丰富你的生活……

NVC Process

NVC流程

The concrete actions we observe that affect our well-being

我们观察到的、影响我们福祉的具体行为

How we feel in relation to what we observe

我们对所观察到的事物有何感受

The needs, values, desires, etc. that create our feelings

那些产生我们情感的需求、价值观、欲望等等

The concrete actions we request in order to enrich our lives

我们请求采取具体行动来丰富我们的生活

When we use this process, we may begin either by expressing ourselves or by empathically receiving these four pieces of information from others. Although we will learn to listen for and verbally express each of these components in Chapters 3 – 6 , it is important to keep in mind that NVC is not a set formula, but something that adapts to various situations as well as personal and cultural styles. While I conveniently refer to NVC as a “process” or “language,” it is possible to experience all four pieces of the process without uttering a single word. The essence of NVC is in our consciousness of the four components, not in the actual words that are exchanged.

当我们运用这种方法时，我们可以先表达自己，也可以先同理心地接收他人提供的这四条信息。虽然我们将在第三至第六章学习如何倾听并用语言表达这四条信息，但重要的是要记住，非暴力沟通并非一成不变的公式，而是可以根据不同的情境、个人风格和文化背景进行调整。虽然我方便地将非暴力沟通称为“过程”或“语言”，但即使不开口说话，我们也完全可以体验到这四个要素。非暴力沟通的精髓在于我们对这四个要素的觉察，而非实际交流的言语。

Two parts of NVC:

非暴力沟通的两个组成部分：

  1. expressing honestly through the four components
    通过四个组成部分真诚表达
  2. receiving empathically through the four components
    通过四个组成部分进行同理心接收
# ↩

Applying NVC in Our Lives and the World

在生活和世界中运用非暴力沟通

When we use NVC in our interactions—with ourselves, with another person, or in a group—we become grounded in our natural state of compassion. It is therefore an approach that can be effectively applied at all levels of communication and in diverse situations:

当我们运用非暴力沟通（NVC）进行人际互动——无论是与自己、与他人还是在群体中——我们都能回归到自身与生俱来的慈悲之心。因此，这种方法可以有效地应用于各个层次的沟通和各种不同的情境中：

  • intimate relationships
    亲密关系
  • families
    家庭
  • schools
    学校
  • organizations and institutions
    组织和机构
  • therapy and counseling relationships
    治疗和咨询关系
  • diplomatic and business negotiations
    外交和商务谈判
  • disputes and conflicts of any nature
    任何性质的争议和冲突

Some people use NVC to create greater depth and caring in their intimate relationships:

有些人运用非暴力沟通来增进亲密关系的深度和关爱：

W hen I learned how I can receive (hear), as well as give (express), through using NVC, I went beyond feeling attacked and ‘doormattish’ to really listening to words and extracting their underlying feelings. I discovered a very hurting man to whom I had been married for twenty-eight years. He had asked me for a divorce the weekend before the [NVC] workshop. To make a long story short, we are here today—together, and I appreciate the contribution [NVC has] made to our happy ending…. I learned to listen for feelings, to express my needs, to accept answers that I didn’t always want to hear. He is not here to make me happy, nor am I here to create happiness for him. We have both learned to grow, to accept, and to love, so that we can each be fulfilled.

当我学会如何运用非暴力沟通（NVC）来倾听（接受）和表达（给予）时，我不再感到被攻击和逆来顺受，而是真正倾听对方的话语，并理解其背后的情感。我发现，与我结婚二十八年的丈夫内心深处充满了伤痛。就在参加非暴力沟通工作坊的前一个周末，他向我提出了离婚。长话短说，我们今天能够在一起，我由衷地感谢非暴力沟通为我们带来幸福的结局……我学会了倾听彼此的感受，表达自己的需求，接受那些我并不总是想听到的答案。他来到这个世界不是为了让我快乐，我来到这个世界也不是为了让他快乐。我们都学会了成长、接纳和爱，这样我们才能各自获得满足。

—a workshop participant in San Diego, California

——一位在加利福尼亚州圣地亚哥参加研讨会的学员

Others use it to build more effective relationships at work:

其他人则利用它来建立更有效的工作关系：

I have been using NVC in my special education classroom for about one year. It can work even with children who have language delays, learning difficulties, and behavior problems. One student in our classroom spits, swears, screams, and stabs other students with pencils when they get near his desk. I cue him with, ‘Please say that another way. Use your giraffe talk.’ [Giraffe puppets are used in some workshops as a teaching aid to demonstrate NVC.] He immediately stands up straight, looks at the person toward whom his anger is directed, and says calmly, ‘Would you please move away from my desk? I feel angry when you stand so close to me.’ The other students might respond with something like, ‘Sorry! I forgot it bothers you.’

我在特殊教育课堂上使用非暴力沟通（NVC）大约一年了。它甚至对有语言发育迟缓、学习困难和行为问题的孩子也有效。我们班有个学生，当其他学生靠近他的桌子时，他会吐口水、骂脏话、尖叫，甚至用铅笔戳他们。我会引导他：“请换一种方式说。用你的‘长颈鹿语’（长颈鹿玩偶在一些工作坊中被用作非暴力沟通的教学辅助工具）。”他立刻站直，看着他发火的对象，平静地说：“请你离我的桌子远点好吗？你离我这么近，我感觉很生气。”其他学生可能会回应说：“对不起！我忘了这会让你不舒服。”

I began to think about my frustration with this child and to try to discover what I needed from him (besides harmony and order). I realized how much time I had put into lesson planning and how my needs for creativity and contribution were being short-circuited in order to manage behavior. Also, I felt I was not meeting the educational needs of the other students. When he was acting out in class, I began to say, ‘I need you to share my attention.’ It might take a hundred cues a day, but he got the message and would usually get involved in the lesson.

我开始反思自己对这个孩子的不满，并试图弄清楚除了和谐与秩序之外，我还需要他做什么。我意识到自己花了多少时间备课，为了管理他的行为，我自身的创造力和参与度都被牺牲了。同时，我也觉得我没有满足其他学生的学习需求。当他在课堂上表现不好时，我会说：“我需要你分担我的注意力。” 可能一天要提醒他一百次，但他最终明白了我的意思，通常也会积极参与到课堂中来。

—a teacher in Chicago, Illinois

——伊利诺伊州芝加哥的一位教师

A doctor writes:

一位医生写道：

I use NVC more and more in my medical practice. Some patients ask me whether I am a psychologist, saying that usually their doctors are not interested in the way they live their lives or deal with their diseases. NVC helps me understand what patients’ needs are and what they need to hear at a given moment. I find this particularly helpful in relating to patients with hemophilia and AIDS because there is so much anger and pain that the patient/health care-provider relationship is often seriously impaired. Recently a woman with AIDS, whom I have been treating for the past five years, told me that what has helped her the most have been my attempts to find ways for her to enjoy her daily life. My use of NVC helps me a lot in this respect. Often in the past, when I knew that a patient had a fatal disease, I myself would get caught in the prognosis, and it was hard for me to sincerely encourage them to live their lives. With NVC, I have developed a new consciousness as well as a new language. I am amazed to see how much it fits in with my medical practice. I feel more energy and joy in my work as I become increasingly engaged in the dance of NVC.

我在医疗实践中越来越多地运用非暴力沟通（NVC）。有些病人问我是不是心理学家，他们说通常医生对他们的生活方式或应对疾病的方式漠不关心。非暴力沟通帮助我理解病人的需求，以及他们在特定时刻需要听到什么。我发现这在与血友病和艾滋病患者沟通时尤其有效，因为这些患者内心充满愤怒和痛苦，医患关系往往严重受损。最近，一位我治疗了五年的艾滋病女性告诉我，对我帮助最大的是我努力帮她找到享受日常生活的方法。在这方面，非暴力沟通对我帮助很大。过去，当我知道病人患有绝症时，我常常会陷入对预后的担忧，很难真诚地鼓励他们好好生活。通过非暴力沟通，我不仅培养了一种新的意识，也掌握了一种新的沟通语言。我惊讶地发现它与我的医疗实践如此契合。随着我越来越投入到非暴力沟通中，我在工作中感到更有活力和快乐。

—a physician in Paris, France

——法国巴黎的一位医生

Still others use this process in the political arena. A French cabinet member visiting her sister remarked how differently the sister and her husband were communicating and responding to each other. Encouraged by their descriptions of NVC, she mentioned that she was scheduled the following week to negotiate some sensitive issues between France and Algeria regarding adoption procedures. Though time was limited, we dispatched a French-speaking trainer to Paris to work with the cabinet minister. The minister later attributed much of the success of her negotiations in Algeria to her newly acquired communication techniques.

还有一些人将这种方法运用到政治领域。一位法国内阁成员探望妹妹时，注意到妹妹和妹夫的沟通方式截然不同。受到他们关于非暴力沟通的描述启发，她提到自己下周要就法国和阿尔及利亚之间的一些敏感的收养程序问题进行谈判。尽管时间有限，我们还是派遣了一位法语培训师前往巴黎，协助这位内阁部长。这位部长后来将她在阿尔及利亚谈判中取得的成功很大程度上归功于她新近掌握的沟通技巧。

In Jerusalem, during a workshop attended by Israelis of varying political persuasions, participants used NVC to express themselves regarding the highly contested issue of the West Bank. Many of the Israeli settlers who have established themselves on the West Bank believe that they are fulfilling a religious mandate by doing so, and they are locked in conflict not only with Palestinians but also with other Israelis who recognize the Palestinian hope for national sovereignty in the region. During a session, one of my trainers and I modeled empathic hearing through NVC and then invited participants to take turns role-playing each other’s position. After twenty minutes, a settler announced that she would be willing to consider relinquishing her land claims and moving out of the West Bank into internationally recognized Israeli territory if her political opponents could listen to her in the way she had just been listened to.

在耶路撒冷，一场由不同政治倾向的以色列人参加的研讨会上，参与者运用非暴力沟通（NVC）就备受争议的西岸问题表达了自己的观点。许多在西岸定居的以色列定居者认为，他们这样做是在履行宗教使命，他们不仅与巴勒斯坦人发生冲突，也与那些承认巴勒斯坦人对该地区国家主权的愿望的其他以色列人发生冲突。在一次研讨会上，我和一位培训师示范了如何运用非暴力沟通进行共情倾听，然后邀请参与者轮流扮演彼此的立场。二十分钟后，一位定居者表示，如果她的政治对手能够像刚才那样倾听她，她愿意考虑放弃土地所有权，搬离西岸，迁往国际公认的以色列领土。

Worldwide, NVC now serves as a valuable resource for communities facing violent conflicts and severe ethnic, religious, or political tensions. The spread of NVC training and its use in mediation by people in conflict in Israel, the Palestinian Authority, Nigeria, Rwanda, Sierra Leone, and elsewhere have been a source of particular gratification for me. My associates and I were once in Belgrade for three highly charged days training citizens working for peace. When we first arrived, expressions of despair were visibly etched on the trainees’ faces, for their country was then enmeshed in a brutal war in Bosnia and Croatia. As the training progressed, we heard the ring of laughter in their voices as they shared their profound gratitude and joy for having found the empowerment they were seeking. Over the next two weeks, during trainings in Croatia, Israel, and Palestine, we again saw desperate citizens in war-torn countries regaining their spirits and confidence from the NVC training they received.

如今，非暴力沟通（NVC）已成为全球面临暴力冲突和严重种族、宗教或政治紧张局势的社区的宝贵资源。非暴力沟通培训的推广及其在以色列、巴勒斯坦权力机构、尼日利亚、卢旺达、塞拉利昂等地冲突各方调解中的应用，令我倍感欣慰。我和我的同事曾前往贝尔格莱德，为致力于和平的民众进行了三天充满激情的培训。我们初到时，学员们脸上写满了绝望，因为他们的国家当时正深陷波斯尼亚和克罗地亚的残酷战争之中。随着培训的进行，我们听到了他们声音中洋溢的笑声，他们分享着内心深处的感激和喜悦，因为他们找到了自己一直寻求的力量。在接下来的两周里，我们在克罗地亚、以色列和巴勒斯坦的培训中，再次看到饱受战争蹂躏的国家中那些绝望的民众，通过接受非暴力沟通培训，重拾了精神和信心。

I feel blessed to be able to travel throughout the world teaching people a process of communication that gives them power and joy. Now, with this book, I am pleased and excited to be able to share the richness of Nonviolent Communication with you.

我深感荣幸能够周游世界，向人们传授一种能赋予他们力量和快乐的沟通方法。现在，我很高兴也很激动能通过这本书与您分享非暴力沟通的精髓。

# ↩

Summary

概括

NVC helps us connect with each other and ourselves in a way that allows our natural compassion to flourish. It guides us to reframe the way we express ourselves and listen to others by focusing our consciousness on four areas: what we are observing, feeling, and needing, and what we are requesting to enrich our lives. NVC fosters deep listening, respect, and empathy and engenders a mutual desire to give from the heart. Some people use NVC to respond compassionately to themselves, some to create greater depth in their personal relationships, and still others to build effective relationships at work or in the political arena. Worldwide, NVC is used to mediate disputes and conflicts at all levels.

非暴力沟通（NVC）帮助我们以一种能够激发我们内在同情心的方式与他人和自己建立联系。它引导我们重新构建表达自我和倾听他人的方式，将意识集中在四个方面：我们正在观察的、感受到的、需要的以及我们为了丰富生活而提出的请求。非暴力沟通培养深度倾听、尊重和同理心，并激发彼此发自内心的付出意愿。有些人运用非暴力沟通来善待自己，有些人用它来加深人际关系，还有些人用它来在工作或政治领域建立有效的关系。在世界范围内，非暴力沟通被用于调解各层面的争端和冲突。

NVC in Action

非暴力沟通实践

Interspersed throughout the book are dialogues entitled NVC in Action. These dialogues intend to impart the flavor of an actual exchange in which a speaker is applying the principles of Nonviolent Communication. However, NVC is not simply a language or a set of techniques for using words; the consciousness and intent that it embraces may be expressed through silence, a quality of presence, as well as through facial expressions and body language. The NVC in Action dialogues you will be reading are necessarily distilled and abridged versions of real-life exchanges, where moments of silent empathy, stories, humor, gestures, and more would all contribute to a more natural flow of connection between the two parties than might be apparent when dialogues are condensed in print.

本书穿插着题为“非暴力沟通实践”的对话。这些对话旨在展现实际交流中，说话者如何运用非暴力沟通原则的精髓。然而，非暴力沟通并非仅仅是一种语言或一套语言技巧；它所蕴含的意识和意图可以通过沉默、临在感、面部表情和肢体语言来表达。您将读到的“非暴力沟通实践”对话必然是真实交流的精简版，其中蕴含的无声共情、故事、幽默、手势等等，都比文字浓缩的对话更能自然地促进双方的沟通。

“Murderer, Assassin, Child-Killer!”

“杀人犯、刺客、杀害儿童者！”

I was presenting Nonviolent Communication to about 170 Palestinian Muslim men in a mosque at Dheisheh Refugee Camp in Bethlehem. Attitudes toward Americans at that time were not favorable. As I was speaking, I suddenly noticed a wave of muffled commotion fluttering through the audience. “They’re whispering that you are American!” my translator alerted me, just as a gentleman in the audience leapt to his feet. Facing me squarely, he hollered at the top of his lungs, “Murderer!” Immediately a dozen other voices joined him in chorus: “Assassin!” “Child-killer!” “Murderer!”

我在伯利恒德黑舍难民营的一座清真寺里，向大约170名巴勒斯坦穆斯林男子讲授非暴力沟通。当时人们对美国人的态度并不友好。我讲着讲着，突然注意到听众席中传来一阵低低的骚动。“他们在窃窃私语说你是美国人！”我的翻译提醒我，话音刚落，一位男士就猛地站了起来。他直视着我，扯着嗓子喊道：“杀人犯！” 紧接着，十几个人也跟着他一起喊：“刺客！” “杀童犯！” “杀人犯！”

Fortunately, I was able to focus my attention on what the man was feeling and needing. In this case, I had some cues. On the way into the refugee camp, I had seen several empty tear gas canisters that had been shot into the camp the night before. Clearly marked on each canister were the words Made in U.S.A. I knew that the refugees harbored a lot of anger toward the United States for supplying tear gas and other weapons to Israel.

幸运的是，我能够将注意力集中在那个男人的感受和需求上。在这种情况下，我有一些线索。在进入难民营的路上，我看到了几个空的催泪瓦斯罐，那是前一天晚上射入营地的。每个罐子上都清晰地印着“美国制造”的字样。我知道难民们对美国向以色列提供催泪瓦斯和其他武器感到非常愤怒。

I addressed the man who had called me a murderer:

我向那个称我为杀人犯的人说道：

MBR: Are you angry because you would like my government to use its resources differently? (I didn’t know whether my guess was correct—what was critical was my sincere effort to connect with his feeling and need.)

MBR：你生气是因为你希望我的政府以不同的方式使用资源吗？（我不知道我的猜测是否正确——关键在于我真诚地努力去理解他的感受和需求。）

Man: Damn right I’m angry! You think we need tear gas? We need sewers, not your tear gas! We need housing! We need to have our own country!

男：我当然生气了！你以为我们需要催泪瓦斯？我们需要的是下水道，不是你的催泪瓦斯！我们需要住房！我们需要自己的国家！

MBR: So you’re furious and would appreciate some support in improving your living conditions and gaining political independence?

MBR：所以你很愤怒，希望得到一些支持，以改善你的生活条件并获得政治独立？

Man: Do you know what it’s like to live here for twenty-seven years the way I have with my family—children and all? Have you got the faintest idea what that’s been like for us?

男：你知道像我这样和家人——包括孩子——在这里生活了二十七年是什么感觉吗？你哪怕有一点点能体会我们这其中的滋味吗？

MBR: Sounds like you’re feeling very desperate and you’re wondering whether I or anybody else can really understand what it’s like to be living under these conditions. Am I hearing you right?

MBR：听起来你现在非常绝望，你想知道我或者其他人是否真的能理解在这种情况下生活的感受。我理解对吗？

Man: You want to understand? Tell me, do you have children? Do they go to school? Do they have playgrounds? My son is sick! He plays in open sewage! His classroom has no books! Have you seen a school that has no books?

男：你想了解吗？告诉我，你有孩子吗？他们上学吗？学校有操场吗？我儿子生病了！他只能在露天污水沟里玩耍！他的教室里连本书都没有！你见过哪所学校没有书吗？

MBR: I hear how painful it is for you to raise your children here; you’d like me to know that what you want is what all parents want for their children—a good education, opportunity to play and grow in a healthy environment …

MBR：我听说在这里养育孩子对您来说很艰难；您想让我知道，您想要的也是所有父母都希望孩子拥有的——良好的教育，在健康的环境中玩耍和成长的机会……

Man: That’s right, the basics! Human rights—isn’t that what you Americans call it? Why don’t more of you come here and see what kind of human rights you’re bringing here!

男：没错，这才是基本原则！人权——你们美国人不就是这么叫的吗？为什么你们美国人不多来这里看看，你们把什么样的人权带到这里来了！

MBR: You’d like more Americans to be aware of the enormity of the suffering here and to look more deeply at the consequences of our political actions?

MBR：您是否希望更多美国人意识到这里苦难的巨大程度，并更深入地思考我们政治行为的后果？

Our dialogue continued, with him expressing his pain for nearly twenty more minutes, and me listening for the feeling and need behind each statement. I didn’t agree or disagree. I received his words, not as attacks, but as gifts from a fellow human willing to share his soul and deep vulnerabilities with me.

我们的对话继续进行，他又倾诉了近二十分钟的痛苦，而我则倾听着每句话背后的感受和需求。我没有赞同也没有反对。我接受他的话语，不是将其视为攻击，而是视为一位愿意与我分享他灵魂深处脆弱一面的同胞所赠予的礼物。

Once the gentleman felt understood, he was able to hear me explain my purpose for being at the camp. An hour later, the same man who had called me a murderer was inviting me to his home for a Ramadan dinner.

那位先生感到被理解后，便听我解释了我来营地的目的。一个小时后，那位之前还骂我是杀人犯的人，竟然邀请我去他家吃斋月晚餐。
