5

Taking Responsibility for Our Feelings

为自己的情绪负责

People are disturbed not by things, but by the view they take of them.

真正困扰人们的不是事物本身，而是他们看待事物的方式。

—Epictetus

——爱比克泰德

# ↩

Hearing a Negative Message: Four Options

听到负面信息：四种选择

T he third component of NVC entails the acknowledgment of the root of our feelings. NVC heightens our awareness that what others say and do may be the stimulus, but never the cause, of our feelings. We see that our feelings result from how we choose to receive what others say and do, as well as from our particular needs and expectations in that moment. With this third component, we are led to accept responsibility for what we do to generate our own feelings.

非暴力沟通的第三个要素是承认我们感受的根源。非暴力沟通提升了我们的觉察力，让我们意识到他人的言行可能只是我们感受的刺激，而非根源。我们明白，我们的感受源于我们如何选择接受他人的言行，以及我们当下的特定需求和期望。通过这第三个要素，我们被引导去承担起自身行为的责任，而正是这些行为产生了我们的感受。

What others do may be the stimulus of our feelings, but not the cause.

他人的行为可能会刺激我们的情绪，但并非情绪的起因。

When someone gives us a negative message, whether verbally or nonverbally, we have four options as to how to receive it. One option is to take it personally by hearing blame and criticism. For example, someone is angry and says, “You’re the most self-centered person I’ve ever met!” If choosing to take it personally, we might react: “Oh, I should’ve been more sensitive!” We accept the other person’s judgment and blame ourselves. We choose this option at great cost to our self-esteem, for it inclines us toward feelings of guilt, shame, and depression.

当有人以言语或非言语的方式向我们传递负面信息时，我们有四种应对方式。其中一种是将其视为针对个人的指责和批评。例如，有人生气地说：“你是我见过最自私的人！”如果我们选择这样做，可能会回应：“哦，我应该更体贴一些！”我们接受了对方的评判，并责怪自己。选择这种方式会严重损害我们的自尊，因为它会让我们更容易产生内疚、羞耻和抑郁的情绪。

Four options for receiving negative messages: 1. blame ourselves.

收到负面信息后的四种选择：1.责怪自己。

A second option is to fault the speaker. For example, in response to “You’re the most self-centered person I’ve ever met,” we might protest: “You have no right to say that! I am always considering your needs. You’re the one who is really self-centered.” When we receive messages this way, and blame the speaker, we are likely to feel anger.

第二种选择是指责说话者。例如，如果有人说“你是我见过最自私的人”，我们可能会反驳道：“你没资格这么说！我一直都在为你着想。真正自私的是你。” 当我们收到这样的信息并指责说话者时，我们很可能会感到愤怒。

2. blame others.

2. 把责任推卸给别人。

When receiving negative messages, our third option would be to shine the light of consciousness on our own feelings and needs. Thus, we might reply, “When I hear you say that I am the most self-centered person you’ve ever met, I feel hurt, because I need some recognition of my efforts to be considerate of your preferences.” By focusing attention on our own feelings and needs, we become conscious that our current feeling of hurt derives from a need for our efforts to be recognized.

收到负面信息时，我们的第三种选择是关注自身的感受和需求。例如，我们可以这样回应：“听到你说我是你见过的最以自我为中心的人，我感到很受伤，因为我需要别人认可我为体贴你的喜好所做的努力。” 通过关注自身的感受和需求，我们就能意识到，我们此刻的受伤感源于渴望自己的努力得到认可。

3. sense our own feelings and needs.

3. 感知我们自己的感受和需求。

Finally, a fourth option on receiving a negative message is to shine the light of consciousness on the other person’s feelings and needs as they are currently expressed. We might for example ask, “Are you feeling hurt because you need more consideration for your preferences?”

最后，收到负面信息后的第四种方法是，关注对方当前表达的感受和需求。例如，我们可以问：“你感到受伤是因为你的喜好需要更多考虑吗？”

4. sense others’ feelings and needs.

4. 感知他人的感受和需求。

We accept responsibility for our feelings, rather than blame other people, by acknowledging our own needs, desires, expectations, values, or thoughts. Note the difference between the following expressions of disappointment:

我们承认自己的需求、欲望、期望、价值观或想法，从而为自己的感受负责，而不是责怪他人。请注意以下几种表达失望的方式之间的区别：

Example 1

例 1

A: “You disappointed me by not coming over last evening.”

A：“你昨晚没来，我真失望。”

B: “I was disappointed when you didn’t come over, because I wanted to talk over some things that were bothering me.”

B：“你没来让我很失望，因为我想和你谈谈一些困扰我的事情。”

Speaker A attributes responsibility for his disappointment solely to another person’s action. Speaker B traces his feeling of disappointment to his own unfulfilled desire.

发言者A将自己的失望完全归咎于他人的行为。发言者B则将自己的失望感追溯到自己未实现的愿望。

Example 2

例 2

A: “Their cancelling the contract really irritated me!”

A：“他们取消合同真的让我很生气！”

B: “When they cancelled the contract, I felt really irritated because I was thinking to myself that it was an awfully irresponsible thing to do.”

B：“当他们取消合同时，我感到非常生气，因为我觉得这是非常不负责任的做法。”

Speaker A attributes her irritation solely to the behavior of the other party, whereas Speaker B accepts responsibility for her feeling by acknowledging the thought behind it. She recognizes that her blaming way of thinking has generated her irritation. In NVC, however, we would urge this speaker to go a step further by identifying what she is wanting: what need, desire, expectation, hope, or value of hers has not been fulfilled? As we shall see, the more we are able to connect our feelings to our own needs, the easier it is for others to respond compassionately. To relate her feelings to what she is wanting, Speaker B might have said: “When they cancelled the contract, I felt really irritated because I was hoping for an opportunity to rehire the workers we laid off last year.”

发言者A将她的恼怒完全归咎于对方的行为，而发言者B则承认自己感受背后的原因，并承担起责任。她意识到，正是这种指责式的思维方式导致了她的恼怒。然而，在非暴力沟通中，我们会鼓励发言者B更进一步，明确自己的需求：她有哪些需求、愿望、期望、希望或价值观没有得到满足？正如我们将看到的，我们越能将自己的感受与自身需求联系起来，他人就越容易以同理心回应。为了将自己的感受与需求联系起来，发言者B可能会这样说：“当他们取消合同时，我感到非常恼火，因为我原本希望有机会重新雇用我们去年解雇的员工。”

It is helpful to recognize a number of common speech patterns that tend to mask accountability for our own feelings:

认识到一些常见的言语模式会帮助我们掩盖对自身感受的责任：

  1. Use of impersonal pronouns such as it and that:
    “It really infuriates me when spelling mistakes appear in our public brochures.” “That bugs me a lot.”
    使用诸如 it 和 that 之类的非人称代词：
    “当我们的宣传册上出现拼写错误时，我真的很生气。”“这让我很恼火。”
  2. The use of the expression “I feel (an emotion) because … ” followed by a person or personal pronoun other than I :
    “I feel hurt because you said you don’t love me.” “I feel angry because the supervisor broke her promise.”
    使用“我感到（某种情绪）是因为……”这样的表达方式，后面跟除“我”以外的人称或人称代词：
    “我感到受伤，因为你说你不爱我。”“我感到生气，因为主管违背了她的承诺。”
  3. Statements that mention only the actions of others:
    “When you don’t call me on my birthday, I feel hurt.” “Mommy is disappointed when you don’t finish your food.”
    仅提及他人行为的陈述：
    “你生日那天不给我打电话，我会很难过。”“你不吃完饭，妈妈会很失望。”

In each of these instances, we can deepen our awareness of our own responsibility by substituting the phrase, “I feel … because I … ” For example:

在上述每种情况下，我们可以通过替换为“我感到……因为我……”这样的表达方式来加深对自身责任的认识。例如：

Connect your feeling with your need: “I feel … because I need …”

将你的感受与你的需求联系起来：“我感到……是因为我需要……”

  1. “I feel really infuriated when spelling mistakes like that appear in our public brochures, because I want our company to project a professional image.”
    “当我的宣传册上出现这样的拼写错误时，我感到非常愤怒，因为我希望我们公司展现出专业的形象。”
  2. “I feel angry that the supervisor broke her promise, because I was counting on getting that long weekend to visit my brother.”
    “我很生气，因为主管违背了承诺，而我原本指望着利用那个长周末去看望我的哥哥。”
  3. “Mommy feels disappointed when you don’t finish your food, because I want you to grow up strong and healthy.”
    “妈妈看到你不吃完饭会很失望，因为我希望你健康强壮地长大。”

The basic mechanism of motivating by guilt is to attribute the responsibility for one’s own feelings to others. When parents say, “It hurts Mommy and Daddy when you get poor grades at school,” they are implying that the child’s actions are the cause of the parents’ happiness or unhappiness. On the surface, taking responsibility for the feelings of others can easily be mistaken for positive caring. It may appear that the child cares for the parent and feels bad because the parent is suffering. However, if children who assume this kind of responsibility change their behavior in accordance with parental wishes, they are not acting from the heart, but acting to avoid guilt.

利用内疚感激励孩子的基本机制是将自身感受的责任归咎于他人。当父母说“你在学校成绩不好，爸爸妈妈会难过的”，他们实际上是在暗示孩子的行为是父母快乐或不快乐的原因。表面上看，承担他人的感受很容易被误认为是积极的关爱。孩子似乎在关心父母，因为父母的痛苦而感到难过。然而，如果承担了这种责任的孩子按照父母的意愿改变自己的行为，那么他们并非出于真心，而是为了逃避内疚。

Distinguish between giving from the heart and being motivated by guilt.

区分发自内心的捐赠和出于愧疚的捐赠。

# ↩

The Needs at the Roots of Feelings

情感根源的需求

Judgments, criticisms, diagnoses, and interpretations of others are all alienated expressions of our needs. If someone says, “You never understand me,” they are really telling us that their need to be understood is not being fulfilled. If a wife says, “You’ve been working late every night this week; you love your work more than you love me,” she is saying that her need for intimacy is not being met.

对他人做出评判、批评、诊断和解读，其实都是我们自身需求的疏离表达。如果有人说：“你从来不理解我”，他们实际上是在告诉我们，他们被理解的需求没有得到满足。如果妻子说：“你这周每天晚上都工作到很晚；你爱工作胜过爱我”，她是在说，她对亲密关系的需求没有得到满足。

Judgments of others are alienated expressions of our own unmet needs.

对别人的评判，其实是我们自身未被满足的需求的一种疏离表达。

When we express our needs indirectly through the use of evaluations, interpretations, and images, others are likely to hear criticism. And when people hear anything that sounds like criticism, they tend to invest their energy in self-defense or counterattack. If we wish for a compassionate response from others, it is self-defeating to express our needs by interpreting or diagnosing their behavior. Instead, the more directly we can connect our feelings to our own needs, the easier it is for others to respond to us compassionately.

当我们通过评价、解读和比喻等间接方式表达需求时，他人很可能听出是批评。而当人们听到任何听起来像是批评的话语时，他们往往会把精力投入到自我防御或反击中。如果我们渴望得到他人的同情回应，那么通过解读或诊断他人的行为来表达需求，只会适得其反。相反，我们越能直接将自己的感受与需求联系起来，他人就越容易以同情的眼光看待我们。

If we express our needs, we have a better chance of getting them met.

如果我们表达自己的需求，就更有可能得到满足。

Unfortunately, most of us have never been taught to think in terms of needs. We are accustomed to thinking about what’s wrong with other people when our needs aren’t being fulfilled. Thus, if we want coats to be hung up in the closet, we may characterize our children as lazy for leaving them on the couch. Or we may interpret our co-workers as irresponsible when they don’t go about their tasks the way we would prefer them to.

不幸的是，我们大多数人从未被教导要从需求的角度思考问题。当我们的需求得不到满足时，我们习惯于去想别人哪里做得不对。因此，如果我们希望外套挂进衣橱，我们可能会因为孩子把外套扔在沙发上而指责他们懒惰。或者，当同事的工作方式不符合我们的期望时，我们可能会认为他们不负责任。

I was once invited to Southern California to mediate between some landowners and migrant farm workers whose conflicts had grown increasingly hostile and violent. I began the meeting by asking these two questions: “What is it that you are each needing? And what would you like to request of the other in relation to these needs?”

我曾受邀前往南加州，调解一些土地所有者和外来务农工人之间的冲突，他们的冲突日益激烈，甚至演变成暴力事件。会议伊始，我提出了这两个问题：“你们各自需要什么？你们又希望对方在满足这些需求方面做出什么贡献？”

“The problem is that these people are racist!” shouted a farm worker. “The problem is that these people don’t respect law and order!” shouted a landowner even more loudly. As is often the case, these groups were more skilled in analyzing the perceived wrongness of others than in clearly expressing their own needs.

“问题在于这些人是种族主义者！”一名农场工人喊道。“问题在于这些人不尊重法律和秩序！”一名地主喊得更大声。通常情况下，这些群体更擅长分析他们认为他人的错误行为，而不是清晰地表达自己的需求。

In a comparable situation, I once met with a group of Israelis and Palestinians who wanted to establish the mutual trust necessary to bring peace to their homelands. I opened the session with the same questions, “What is it you are needing and what would you like to request from one another in relation to those needs?” Instead of directly stating his needs, a Palestinian mukhtar (who is like a village mayor) answered, “You people are acting like a bunch of Nazis.” A statement like that is not likely to get the cooperation of a group of Israelis! Almost immediately, an Israeli woman jumped up and countered, “Mukhtar, that was a totally insensitive thing for you to say!”

在类似的情况下，我曾与一群以色列人和巴勒斯坦人会面，他们希望建立互信，为各自的家园带来和平。会议伊始，我提出了同样的问题：“你们需要什么？为了满足这些需求，你们希望彼此提出哪些要求？”一位巴勒斯坦村长（相当于村长）没有直接说明自己的需求，而是回答说：“你们这些人简直像一群纳粹。”这样的话，很难赢得以色列人的合作！几乎立刻，一位以色列妇女站起来反驳道：“村长，你刚才那句话太不体贴了！”

Here were people who had come together to build trust and harmony, but after only one interchange, matters were worse than before they began. This happens often when people are used to analyzing and blaming one another rather than clearly expressing what they need. In this case, the woman could have responded to the mukhtar in terms of her own needs and requests by saying, for example, “I am needing more respect in our dialogue. Instead of telling us how you think we are acting, would you tell us what it is we are doing that you find disturbing?”

这些人原本聚在一起是为了建立信任与和谐，但仅仅一次交流之后，情况却比之前更糟。这种情况经常发生在人们习惯于互相分析和指责，而不是清晰地表达自己的需求时。在这种情况下，这位女士本可以根据自己的需求和要求回应村长，例如说：“我希望在我们的对话中得到更多的尊重。与其告诉我们您认为我们的行为如何，不如告诉我们您觉得我们哪里做得不对？”

It has been my experience over and over again that from the moment people begin talking about what they need rather than what’s wrong with one another, the possibility of finding ways to meet everybody’s needs is greatly increased. The following are some of the basic human needs we all share:

我的经验一次又一次地证明，当人们开始谈论自己的需求而不是彼此的缺点时，找到满足所有人需求的方法的可能性就会大大增加。以下是我们共同拥有的一些基本人类需求：

Autonomy

自治

  • to choose one’s dreams, goals, values
    选择自己的梦想、目标和价值观
  • to choose one’s plan for fulfilling one’s dreams, goals, values
    选择实现梦想、目标和价值观的计划

Celebration

庆典

  • to celebrate the creation of life and dreams fulfilled
    庆祝生命的诞生和梦想的实现
  • to celebrate losses: loved ones, dreams, etc. (mourning)
    庆祝逝去的亲人、梦想等等（哀悼）

Integrity

正直

  • authenticity
    真实性
  • creativity
    创造力
  • meaning
    意义
  • self-worth
    自我价值

Interdependence

相互依存

  • acceptance
    验收
  • appreciation
    欣赏
  • closeness
    亲近
  • community
    社区
  • consideration
    考虑
  • contribution to the enrichment of life (to exercise one’s power by giving that which contributes to life)
    为丰富生活做出贡献（通过给予有益于生活的事物来发挥自身的力量）
  • emotional safety
    情绪安全
  • empathy
    共情
  • honesty (the empowering honesty that enables us to learn from our limitations)
    诚实（那种赋予我们力量的诚实，使我们能够从自身的局限性中学习）
  • love
    爱
  • reassurance
    放心
  • respect
    尊重
  • support
    支持
  • trust
    相信
  • understanding
    理解
  • warmth
    温暖

Play

玩

  • fun
    乐趣
  • laughter
    笑声

Spiritual Communion

灵性交流

  • beauty
    美丽
  • harmony
    和谐
  • inspiration
    灵感
  • order
    命令
  • peace
    和平

Physical Nurturance

身体滋养

  • air
    空气
  • food
    食物
  • movement, exercise
    运动、锻炼
  • protection from life-threatening forms of life: viruses, bacteria, insects, predatory animals
    保护自己免受致命生物的侵害：病毒、细菌、昆虫、捕食性动物
  • rest
    休息
  • sexual expression
    性表达
  • shelter
    庇护所
  • touch
    触碰
  • water
    水
# ↩

The Pain of Expressing Our Needs versus the Pain of Not Expressing Our Needs

表达需求的痛苦与不表达需求的痛苦

In a world where we’re often judged harshly for identifying and revealing our needs, doing so can be very frightening. Women, in particular, are susceptible to criticism. For centuries, the image of the loving woman has been associated with sacrifice and the denial of one’s own needs to take care of others. Because women are socialized to view the caretaking of others as their highest duty, they often learn to ignore their own needs.

在一个我们常常因为表达自身需求而遭受严厉评判的世界里，这样做可能会令人非常恐惧。女性尤其容易受到批评。几个世纪以来，慈爱的女性形象一直与牺牲奉献、压抑自身需求以照顾他人联系在一起。由于女性从小就被灌输照顾他人是她们最重要的责任，她们往往学会了忽视自己的需求。

At one workshop, we discussed what happens to women who internalize such beliefs. These women, if they ask for what they want, will often do so in a way that both reflects and reinforces the beliefs that they have no genuine right to their needs and that their needs are unimportant. For example, because she is fearful of asking for what she needs, a woman may fail to simply say that she’s had a busy day, is feeling tired, and wants some time in the evening to herself; instead, her words come out sounding like a legal case: “You know I haven’t had a moment to myself all day. I ironed all the shirts, did the whole week’s laundry, took the dog to the vet, made dinner, packed the lunches, and called all the neighbors about the block meeting, so [imploringly] … so how about if you … ?”

在一次研讨会上，我们讨论了女性如果内化了这类信念会发生什么。这些女性如果提出自己的需求，往往会以一种既反映又强化她们“自己没有权利拥有自己的需求，而且自己的需求无关紧要”这种信念的方式进行表达。例如，因为害怕开口求助，一位女性可能不会简单地说自己忙碌了一天，感到疲惫，想要晚上独处一会儿；相反，她会用一种像是在陈述法律问题的方式说出来：“你知道我今天一整天都没休息过。我熨了所有的衬衫，洗了一周的衣服，带狗去看兽医，做了晚饭，打包了午餐，还给所有邻居打电话通知街区会议，所以（恳求地）……你能不能……？”

“No!” comes the swift response. Her plaintive request elicits resistance rather than compassion from her listeners. They have difficulty hearing and valuing the needs behind her pleas, and furthermore react negatively to her weak attempt to argue from a position of what she “should” get or “deserves” to get from them. In the end the speaker is again persuaded that her needs don’t matter, not realizing that they were expressed in a way unlikely to draw a positive response.

“不！”对方迅速回应。她哀求的请求非但没有博得同情，反而激起了听者的抵触情绪。他们难以理解和重视她恳求背后的需求，更对她试图从“她应该”或“应得”得到什么的角度出发的辩解嗤之以鼻。最终，说话者再次确信自己的需求无关紧要，却丝毫没有意识到自己表达需求的方式根本无法获得积极的回应。

My mother was once at a workshop where other women were discussing how frightening it was to be expressing their needs. Suddenly she got up and left the room, and didn’t return for a long time. She finally reappeared, looking very pale. In the presence of the group, I asked, “Mother, are you all right?”

我母亲曾参加一个研讨会，会上其他女性正在讨论表达自身需求是多么令人恐惧。突然，她起身离开了房间，过了很久才回来。最后她回来时，脸色苍白。在大家面前，我问她：“妈妈，您还好吗？”

If we don’t value our needs, others may not either.

如果我们不重视自己的需求，别人也未必会重视。

“Yes,” she answered, “but I just had a sudden realization that’s very hard for me to take in.”

“是的，”她回答说，“但我突然意识到一件事，我很难接受。”

“What’s that?”

“那是什么？”

“I’ve just become aware that for thirty-six years, I was angry with your father for not meeting my needs, and now I realize that I never once clearly told him what I needed.”

“我刚刚意识到，三十六年来，我一直因为你父亲没有满足我的需求而生气，而现在我意识到，我从来没有清楚地告诉他我需要什么。”

My mother’s revelation was accurate. Not one time, that I can remember, did she clearly express her needs to my father. She’d hint around and go through all kinds of convolutions, but never would she ask directly for what she needed.

我母亲的描述很准确。据我所知，她从未直接向父亲表达过自己的需求。她总是拐弯抹角，拐弯抹角，但从不直接开口要。

We tried to understand why it was so hard for her to have done so. My mother grew up in an economically impoverished family. She recalled asking for things as a child and being admonished by her brothers and sisters, “You shouldn’t ask for that! You know we’re poor. Do you think you are the only person in the family?” Eventually she grew to fear that asking for what she needed would only lead to disapproval and judgment.

我们试图理解为什么她这样做如此艰难。我的母亲在一个经济拮据的家庭长大。她回忆起小时候向兄弟姐妹要东西时，总是遭到他们的责备：“你不应该要那个！你知道我们家很穷。你以为家里只有你一个人吗？” 最终，她开始害怕，如果开口要东西，只会招致责备和评判。

She related a childhood anecdote about one of her sisters who had had an appendix operation and afterwards had been given a beautiful little purse by another sister. My mother was fourteen at the time. Oh, how she yearned to have an exquisitely beaded purse like her sister’s, but she dared not open her mouth. So guess what? She feigned a pain in her side and went the whole way with her story. Her family took her to several doctors. They were unable to produce a diagnosis and so opted for exploratory surgery. It had been a bold gamble on my mother’s part, but it worked—she was given an identical little purse! When she received the coveted purse, my mother was elated despite being in physical agony from the surgery. Two nurses came in and one stuck a thermometer in her mouth. My mother said, “Ummm, ummm,” to show the purse to the second nurse, who answered, “Oh, for me? Why, thank you!” and took the purse! My mother was at a loss, and never figured out how to say, “I didn’t mean to give it to you. Please return it to me.” Her story poignantly reveals how painful it can be when people don’t openly acknowledge their needs.

她讲了一个小时候的故事：她有个姐姐做了阑尾手术，术后另一个姐姐送给她一个漂亮的小钱包。那时我母亲十四岁。哦，她多么渴望拥有一个像姐姐那样精致的串珠钱包啊，但她不敢开口。所以你猜怎么着？她假装腰侧疼痛，把故事讲得天衣无缝。家人带她看了好几个医生。医生们都无法确诊，于是决定做探查手术。这对母亲来说是个大胆的尝试，但成功了——她得到了一个一模一样的小钱包！拿到梦寐以求的钱包时，尽管手术后身体疼痛难忍，母亲还是欣喜若狂。两个护士走了进来，其中一个把体温计放进她嘴里。母亲“嗯嗯”地把钱包递给第二个护士，护士回答说：“哦，是给我的吗？谢谢！”然后接过钱包！我母亲不知所措，始终没能说出那句“我不是故意给你的，请还给我”。她的故事令人心酸地揭示了，当人们不愿坦诚表达自己的需求时，会造成多么大的痛苦。

# ↩

From Emotional Slavery to Emotional Liberation

从情感奴役到情感解放

In our development toward a state of emotional liberation, most of us experience three stages in the way we relate to others.

在迈向情感解放的过程中，我们大多数人在与他人相处时都会经历三个阶段。

Stage 1: In this stage, which I refer to as emotional slavery, we believe ourselves responsible for the feelings of others. We think we must constantly strive to keep everyone happy. If they don’t appear happy, we feel responsible and compelled to do something about it. This can easily lead us to see the very people who are closest to us as burdens.

第一阶段：在这个阶段，我称之为“情感奴役”。我们认为自己要为他人的感受负责。我们觉得必须不断努力让每个人都开心。如果他们看起来不开心，我们就会感到有责任，并且有义务做些什么。这很容易让我们把最亲近的人视为负担。

Taking responsibility for the feelings of others can be very detrimental to intimate relationships. I routinely hear variations on the following theme: “I’m really scared to be in a relationshi p. Every time I see my partner in pain or needing something, I feel overwhelmed. I feel like I’m in prison, that I’m being smothered—and I just have to get out of the relationship as fast as possible.” This response is common among those who experience love as denial of one’s own needs in order to attend to the needs of the beloved. In the early days of a relationship, partners typically relate joyfully and compassionately to each other out of a sense of freedom. The relationship is exhilarating, spontaneous, wonderful. Eventually, however, as the relationship becomes “serious,” partners may begin to assume responsibility for each other’s feelings.

承担他人的感受可能会对亲密关系造成极大的损害。我经常听到类似这样的说法：“我真的很害怕谈恋爱。每次看到伴侣痛苦或需要什么，我都感到不知所措。感觉就像身处牢笼，窒息难耐——我只想尽快结束这段关系。”这种反应在那些将爱理解为为了满足爱人的需求而压抑自身需求的人身上很常见。在恋爱初期，伴侣通常会因为自由自在而愉快地、充满同情地相处。这段关系令人兴奋、充满活力、美好无比。然而，随着关系逐渐“认真”，伴侣们最终可能会开始承担起彼此感受的责任。

First stage: Emotional slavery. We see ourselves responsible for others’ feelings.

第一阶段：情感奴役。我们认为自己要为他人的感受负责。

If I were a partner who is conscious of doing this, I might acknowledge the situation by explaining, “I can’t bear it when I lose myself in relationships. When I see my partner’s pain, I lose me, and then I just have to break free.” However, if I have not reached this level of awareness, I am likely to blame my partner for the deterioration of the relationship. Thus I might say, “My partner is so needy and dependent it’s really stressing out our relationship.”

如果我是一个有这种意识的伴侣，我可能会这样解释：“我无法忍受在感情中迷失自我。当我看到伴侣痛苦时，我也会迷失自我，这时我只能选择离开。” 然而，如果我还没有达到这种意识，我可能会把感情的恶化归咎于伴侣。因此，我可能会说：“我的伴侣太需要我、太依赖我了，这真的让我们的关系压力很大。”

In such a case, my partner would do well to reject the notion that there is anything wrong with her needs. It would only make a bad situation worse to accept that blame. Instead, she could offer an empathic response to the pain of my emotional slavery: “So you find yourself in panic. It’s very hard for you to hold on to the deep caring and love we’ve had without turning it into a responsibility, duty, obligation…. You sense your freedom closing down because you think you constantly have to take care of me.” If, however, instead of an empathic response, she says, “Are you feeling tense because I have been making too many demands on you?” then both of us are likely to stay enmeshed in emotional slavery, making it that much more difficult for the relationship to survive.

在这种情况下，我的伴侣最好不要认为自己的需求有什么问题。接受这种指责只会让糟糕的情况雪上加霜。相反，她可以对我的情感奴役之痛给予同理心的回应：“所以你感到恐慌。你很难在不把我们之间深厚的关爱和感情变成责任、义务和责任的情况下，继续保持下去……你感觉自己的自由正在被剥夺，因为你觉得你必须不断地照顾我。” 然而，如果她没有给予同理心的回应，而是说：“你是不是因为我对你的要求太多而感到紧张？” 那么我们双方都可能继续深陷情感奴役的泥潭，让这段关系更加难以维系。

Stage 2: In this stage, we become aware of the high costs of assuming responsibility for others’ feelings and trying to accommodate them at our own expense. When we notice how much of our lives we’ve missed and how little we have responded to the call of our own soul, we may get angry. I refer jokingly to this stage as the obnoxious stage because we tend toward obnoxious comments like, “That’s your problem! I’m not responsible for your feelings!” when presented with another person’s pain. We are clear what we are not responsible for, but have yet to learn how to be responsible to others in a way that is not emotionally enslaving.

第二阶段：在这个阶段，我们开始意识到承担他人感受的责任并试图牺牲自身利益来迁就他人的代价有多高昂。当我们注意到自己错过了多少人生，以及自己对内心呼唤的回应有多么少时，我们可能会感到愤怒。我戏称这个阶段为“令人讨厌的阶段”，因为当面对他人的痛苦时，我们往往会说出一些令人讨厌的话，比如“那是你的问题！我才不会为你的感受负责！”。我们清楚地知道自己不该为哪些事情负责，但却还没有学会如何以一种不让自己陷入情感奴役的方式来对他人负责。

Second stage: The obnoxious stage. We feel angry; we no longer want to be responsible for others’ feelings.

第二阶段：令人厌恶的阶段。我们感到愤怒；我们不再想为他人的感受负责。

As we emerge from the stage of emotional slavery, we may continue to carry remnants of fear and guilt around having our own needs. Thus it is not surprising that we end up expressing our needs in ways that sound rigid and unyielding to the ears of others. For example, during a break in one of my workshops, a young woman expressed appreciation for the insights she’d gained into her own state of emotional enslavement. When the workshop resumed, I suggested an activity to the group. The same young woman then declared assertively, “I’d rather do something else.” I sensed she was exercising her newfound right to express her needs—even if they ran counter to those of others.

当我们从情感奴役的阶段走出来时，我们可能仍然会因为拥有自身需求而感到恐惧和内疚。因此，我们最终表达需求的方式在他人听来显得生硬固执也就不足为奇了。例如，在我的一次工作坊休息期间，一位年轻女性表达了她对自身情感奴役状态的深刻理解的感激之情。工作坊重新开始后，我向大家提议了一项活动。这时，这位年轻女性却坚定地说：“我更想做点别的。” 我意识到，她是在行使她新获得的权利——表达自己的需求，即使这些需求与他人的需求相悖。

To encourage her to sort out what she wanted, I asked, “Do you want to do something else even if it conflicts with my needs?” She thought for a moment, and then stammered, “Yes…. er … I mean, no.” Her confusion reflects how, in the obnoxious stage, we have yet to grasp that emotional liberation entails more than simply asserting our own needs.

为了鼓励她理清自己的需求，我问：“即使和我的需求相冲突，你也想做点别的吗？”她想了一会儿，然后结结巴巴地说：“嗯……呃……我是说，不。”她的困惑反映出，在叛逆阶段，我们尚未理解，情感解放不仅仅意味着表达自己的需求。

I recall an incident during my daughter Marla’s passage toward emotional liberation. She had always been the “perfect little girl” who denied her own needs to comply with the wishes of others. When I became aware of how frequently she suppressed her own desires in order to please others, I talked to her about how I’d enjoy hearing her express her needs more often. When we first broached the subject, Marla cried. “But, Daddy, I don’t want to disappoint anybody!” she protested helplessly. I tried to show Marla how her honesty would be a gift more precious to others than accommodating them to prevent their upset. I also clarified ways she could empathize with people when they were upset without taking responsibility for their feelings.

我记得女儿玛拉在走向情感解放的过程中发生的一件事。她一直是个“完美小女孩”，为了迎合别人的愿望而压抑自己的需求。当我意识到她为了取悦他人而频繁地压抑自己的欲望时，我跟她谈了谈，告诉她我很希望听到她更频繁地表达自己的需求。我们第一次提起这个话题时，玛拉哭了。“可是，爸爸，我不想让任何人失望！”她无助地抗议道。我试图向玛拉解释，坦诚相待对别人来说比为了避免别人不高兴而迁就他们更珍贵。我还向她阐明了如何在不承担他人感受责任的情况下，理解他人的难过。

A short time later, I saw evidence that my daughter was beginning to express her needs more openly. A call came from her school principal, apparently disturbed by a communication he’d had with Marla, who had arrived at school wearing overalls. “Marla,” he’d said, “young women do not dress this way.” To which Marla had responded, “Bug off!”

不久之后，我发现女儿开始更坦率地表达自己的需求。她学校的校长打来电话，显然是被他和玛拉的谈话内容所困扰。玛拉穿着背带裤来上学，校长说：“玛拉，年轻女孩不应该这样穿。”玛拉回答说：“滚开！”

Hearing this was cause for celebration: Marla had graduated from emotional slavery to obnoxiousness! She was learning to express her needs and risk dealing with the displeasure of others. Surely she had yet to assert her needs comfortably and in a way that respected the needs of others, but I trusted this would occur in time.

听到这话真是令人欣喜：玛拉终于从情感奴役中脱身，蜕变为一个令人讨厌的家伙！她正在学习如何表达自己的需求，并承担得起惹恼他人的风险。当然，她现在还无法自如地、既表达自己的需求又尊重他人的需求，但我相信她终会做到。

Stage 3: At the third stage, emotional liberation, we respond to the needs of others out of compassion, never out of fear, guilt, or shame. Our actions are therefore fulfilling to us, as well as to those who receive our efforts. We accept full responsibility for our own intentions and actions, but not for the feelings of others. At this stage, we are aware that we can never meet our own needs at the expense of others. Emotional liberation involves stating clearly what we need in a way that communicates we are equally concerned that the needs of others be fulfilled. NVC is designed to support us in relating at this level.

第三阶段：在第三阶段，即情绪解放阶段，我们出于同情而非恐惧、内疚或羞耻来回应他人的需求。因此，我们的行为不仅让我们自己感到满足，也让接受我们帮助的人感到满足。我们对自己的意图和行为负全部责任，但无需为他人的感受负责。在这个阶段，我们意识到，我们永远不能以牺牲他人为代价来满足自己的需求。情绪解放意味着清晰地表达自己的需求，同时传达出我们同样关心他人需求的满足。非暴力沟通（NVC）旨在帮助我们达到这个层面的沟通。

Third stage: Emotional liberation. We take responsibility for our intentions and actions.

第三阶段：情感解放。我们开始为自己的意图和行为负责。

# ↩

Summary

概括

The third component of NVC is the acknowledgment of the needs behind our feelings. What others say and do may be the stimulus for, but never the cause of, our feelings. When someone communicates negatively, we have four options as to how to receive the message: (1) blame ourselves, (2) blame others, (3) sense our own feelings and needs, (4) sense the feelings and needs hidden in the other person’s negative message.

非暴力沟通的第三个要素是承认我们感受背后的需求。他人的言行可能刺激我们的情绪，但绝非情绪的根源。当有人传递负面信息时，我们有四种不同的解读方式：（1）责怪自己；（2）责怪他人；（3）觉察自身的感受和需求；（4）觉察隐藏在对方负面信息中的感受和需求。

Judgments, criticisms, diagnoses, and interpretations of others are all alienated expressions of our own needs and values. When others hear criticism, they tend to invest their energy in self-defense or counterattack. The more directly we can connect our feelings to our needs, the easier it is for others to respond compassionately.

对他人做出的评判、批评、诊断和解读，都是我们自身需求和价值观的一种疏离表达。当别人听到批评时，往往会把精力投入到自我辩护或反击中。我们越能将自己的感受与需求直接联系起来，别人就越容易以同理心回应我们。

In a world where we are often harshly judged for identifying and revealing our needs, doing so can be very frightening, especially for women who are socialized to ignore their own needs while caring for others.

在一个我们常常因为发现和表达自己的需求而受到严厉评判的世界里，这样做可能会非常可怕，尤其是对于那些从小就被教导要忽略自身需求而照顾他人的女性而言。

In the course of developing emotional responsibility, most of us experience three stages: (1) “emotional slavery”—believing ourselves responsible for the feelings of others, (2) “the obnoxious stage”—in which we refuse to admit to caring what anyone else feels or needs, and (3) “emotional liberation”—in which we accept full responsibility for our own feelings but not the feelings of others, while being aware that we can never meet our own needs at the expense of others.

在培养情感责任感的过程中，我们大多数人都会经历三个阶段：（1）“情感奴役”——认为自己要对别人的感受负责；（2）“令人讨厌的阶段”——拒绝承认自己关心他人的感受或需求；（3）“情感解放”——接受对自己感受的全部责任，但不对别人的感受负责，同时意识到我们永远不能以牺牲他人为代价来满足自己的需求。

NVC in Action

非暴力沟通实践

“Bring Back the Stigma of Illegitimacy!”

“恢复对非婚生子女的歧视！”

A student of Nonviolent Communication volunteering at a food bank was shocked when an elderly co-worker burst out from behind a newspaper, “What we need to do in this country is bring back the stigma of illegitimacy!”

一名学习非暴力沟通的学生在食品银行做义工时，一位年长的同事突然从报纸后面跳出来，震惊地说：“我们这个国家需要做的就是恢复对非婚生子女的歧视！”

The student’s habitual reaction to this kind of statement would have been to say nothing, to judge the other severely but silently, and eventually to process her own feelings safely away from the scene. This time, she remembered she had the option of listening for the feelings and needs behind the words that had shocked her.

这位学生以往面对这类言论的惯常反应是保持沉默，默默地严厉评判对方，最终独自离开现场，独自消化自己的感受。但这一次，她想起自己可以选择倾听那些令她震惊的话语背后隐藏的情感和需求。

Student:
学生： 		(first checking out her guess as to what the coworker was observing) Are you reading something about teenage pregnancies in the paper?
（首先确认她对同事所观察到的情况的猜测）你是不是在报纸上看到关于青少年怀孕的新闻？
Co-worker:
同事： 		Yes, it’s unbelievable how many of them are doing it!
是的，难以置信竟然有这么多人这样做！
Student:
学生： 		(now listening for the co-worker’s feeling, and what unmet need might be giving rise to this feeling) Are you feeling alarmed because you’d like kids to have stable families?
（现在倾听同事的感受，以及可能引起这种感受的未被满足的需求）你感到担忧是因为你想让孩子拥有稳定的家庭吗？
Co-worker:
同事： 		Of course! Do you know, my father would have killed me if I had done anything like that!
当然！你知道吗，如果我做了那种事，我父亲会杀了我的！
Student:
学生： 		So you’re remembering how it was for the girls in your generation who got pregnant?
所以你还记得你那一代女孩怀孕时的感受吗？
Co-worker:
同事： 		Sure thing! We knew what would happen to us if we got pregnant. We were scared about it all the time, not like these girls nowadays.
当然！我们知道如果怀孕会发生什么。我们一直都很害怕，不像现在的女孩子那样。
Student:
学生： 		Are you annoyed that there is no fear of punishment for the girls who get pregnant these days?
你是否对如今女孩怀孕却无需担心受到惩罚感到不满？
Co-worker:
同事： 		Well, at least fear and punishment worked! It says here that there are girls sleeping around with different men just so they can get pregnant! That’s right! They have babies and the rest of us in society pay for it!
好吧，至少恐惧和惩罚奏效了！这里说有些女孩为了怀孕，和不同的男人乱搞！没错！她们生孩子，而我们其他人却要为此买单！

The student of NVC heard two different feelings in this statement: astonishment that girls would deliberately get pregnant, and annoyance that taxpayers end up paying for children born in this way. She chose which feeling to empathize with.

非暴力沟通（NVC）专业的学生从这句话中听出了两种不同的感受：一是震惊于女孩竟然会故意怀孕，二是恼怒于纳税人最终要为这样出生的孩子买单。她选择认同哪一种感受。

Student:
学生： 		Are you astonished to realize that people are getting pregnant these days without any consideration for reputation, consequences, financial stability … all the things you used to consider?
你是否惊讶地发现，如今人们怀孕时完全不考虑名誉、后果、经济稳定……所有这些你过去都会考虑的事情？
Co-worker:
同事： 		Yeah, and guess who ends up paying for it?
是啊，猜猜最后是谁来买单？

The co-worker, probably feeling heard around her astonishment, moved on to her other feeling: that of annoyance. As often happens when there is a mixture of feelings present, the speaker will return to those that have not received empathic attention. It is not necessary for the listener to reflect back a complex mixture of feelings all at once; the flow of compassion will continue as each feeling comes up again in its turn.

这位同事或许感到自己的惊讶得到了理解，于是转而谈起了另一种感受：恼怒。当多种情绪交织在一起时，说话者往往会再次关注那些尚未得到同理心回应的情绪。倾听者无需一次性复述所有复杂的情绪；随着每一种情绪的再次出现，同情之流会持续流淌。

Student:
学生： 		Sounds like you’re exasperated because you’d like your tax money to be used for other purposes. Is that so?
听起来你很恼火，因为你希望你的税款用于其他用途。是这样吗？
Co-worker:
同事： 		Certainly is! Do you know that my son and his wife want a second child and they can’t have one—even though they have two jobs—because it costs so much?
当然！你知道吗？我儿子和儿媳想要第二个孩子，但他们却负担不起——即使他们有两份工作——因为养育孩子的费用太高了！
Student:
学生： 		I guess you’re sad about that? You’d probably love to have a second grandchild …
我猜你为此感到难过吧？你大概很想再抱一个孙子/孙女吧……
Co-worker:
同事： 		Yes, and it’s not just for me that it would make a difference.
是的，而且这不仅仅对我个人有意义。
Student:
学生： 		… and for your son to have the family he wants … (Even though the student guessed only partially correctly, she did not interrupt the flow of empathy, instead allowing the co-worker to continue and realize another concern.)
……也希望你的儿子能拥有他想要的家庭……（尽管这位学生只猜对了一部分，但她并没有打断同事的同理心，而是让她继续说下去，并意识到另一个问题。）
Co-worker:
同事： 		Yes, I think it’s sad to be a single child too.
是的，我觉得做独生子女也很可悲。
Student:
学生： 		Oh, I see; you’d like for Katie to have a little brother?
哦，我明白了；你想让凯蒂有个弟弟？
Co-worker:
同事： 		That would be nice.
那太好了。

At this point, the student sensed a release in her co-worker. A moment of silence elapsed. She felt surprised to discover that, while she still wanted to express her own views, her urgency and tension had dissipated because she no longer felt “adversarial.” She understood the feelings and needs behind her co-worker’s statements and no longer felt that the two of them were “worlds apart.”

这时，学生察觉到同事如释重负。一阵沉默过后，她惊讶地发现，虽然自己仍然想表达观点，但那种急迫和紧张感却消散了，因为她不再感到“敌对”。她理解了同事话语背后的感受和需求，也不再觉得两人之间“天壤之别”。

Student:
学生： 		(expressing herself in NVC, and using all four parts of the process: observation [O], feeling [F], need [N], request [R]) You know, when you first said that we should bring back the stigma of illegitimacy (O), I got really scared (F), because it really matters to me that all of us here share a deep caring for people needing help (N). Some of the people coming here for food are teenage parents (O), and I want to make sure they feel welcome (N). Would you mind telling me how you feel when you see Dashal, or Amy and her boyfriend, walking in? (R)
（她用非暴力沟通的方式表达自己，并运用了沟通的四个步骤：观察[O]、感受[F]、需求[N]、请求[R]）你知道吗，你第一次说我们应该恢复对非婚生子女的歧视时（O），我真的很害怕（F），因为我们所有人对需要帮助的人都怀有深深的关怀，这对我来说非常重要（N）。来这里领取食物的人中，有些是十几岁的父母（O），我想确保他们感到受欢迎（N）。你介意告诉我，当你看到达沙尔，或者艾米和她的男朋友走进来时，你的感受是什么吗？（R）

The dialogue continued with several more exchanges until the woman got the reassurance she needed that her co-worker did indeed offer caring and respectful help to unmarried teen clients. Even more importantly, what the woman gained was a new experience in expressing disagreement in a way that met her needs for honesty and mutual respect.

双方又进行了几次对话，直到这位女士确信她的同事确实会以关怀和尊重的态度帮助未婚青少年客户。更重要的是，这位女士从中获得了新的体验，学会了如何以一种既能表达不同意见又能满足她对诚实和相互尊重的需求的方式来表达异议。

In the meantime, the co-worker left satisfied that her concerns around teen pregnancy had been fully heard. Both parties felt understood, and their relationship benefited from their having shared their understanding and differences without hostility. In the absence of NVC, their relationship might have begun to deteriorate from this moment, and the work they both wanted to do in common—helping people—might have suffered.

与此同时，这位同事带着欣慰离开，因为她对青少年怀孕问题的担忧得到了充分的倾听。双方都感到被理解，并且由于彼此坦诚地分享了理解和分歧，他们的关系也因此受益。如果没有非暴力沟通，他们的关系可能从那时起就开始恶化，而他们共同想要从事的工作——帮助他人——也可能受到影响。

练习3

ACKNOWLEDGING NEEDS

承认需求

To practice identifying needs, please circle the number in front of each statement where the speaker is acknowledging responsibility for his or her feelings.

为了练习识别需求，请圈出说话者承认对自己感受负责的每句话前面的数字。

  1. “You irritate me when you leave company documents on the conference room floor.”
    “你把公司文件乱扔在会议室地板上，真让我恼火。”

Here are my responses for Exercise 3:

以下是我对练习3的回答：

  1. If you circled this number, we’re not in agreement. To me, the statement implies that the other person’s behavior is solely responsible for the speaker’s feelings. It doesn’t reveal the needs or thoughts that are contributing to the speaker’s feelings. To do so, the speaker might have said, “I’m irritated when you leave company documents on the conference room floor, because I want our documents to be safely stored and accessible.”
    如果你圈出了这个数字，说明我们意见不一致。在我看来，这句话暗示说话者的感受完全是由对方的行为造成的，而没有揭示导致说话者感受的真正需求或想法。为了更好地表达，说话者可能会说：“你把公司文件乱扔在会议室地板上让我很恼火，因为我希望我们的文件能够安全存放，并且方便取用。”
  2. If you circled this number, we’re in agreement that the speaker is acknowledging responsibility for his or her feelings.
    如果你圈出了这个数字，我们就一致认为说话者承认自己要为自己的感受负责。
  3. If you circled this number, we’re not in agreement. To express the needs or thoughts underlying his or her feelings, the speaker might have said, “I feel frustrated when you come late because I was hoping we’d be able to get some front-row seats.”
    如果你圈出了这个数字，说明我们意见不一致。为了表达自己内心深处的需求或想法，说话者可能会说：“你来晚了，我感到很沮丧，因为我本来希望我们能买到前排的座位。”
  4. If you circled this number, we’re in agreement that the speaker is acknowledging responsibility for his or her feelings.
    如果你圈出了这个数字，我们就一致认为说话者承认自己要为自己的感受负责。
  5. If you circled this number, we’re not in agreement. To express the needs and thoughts underlying his or her feelings, the speaker might have said, “When you said you’d do it and then didn’t, I felt disappointed because I want to be able to rely upon your words.”
    如果你圈出了这个数字，说明我们意见不一致。为了表达自己内心深处的需求和想法，说话者可能会说：“你答应了却没做到，我感到很失望，因为我希望你能信守承诺。”
  6. If you circled this number, we’re in agreement that the speaker is acknowledging responsibility for his or her feelings.
    如果你圈出了这个数字，我们就一致认为说话者承认自己要为自己的感受负责。
  7. If you circled this number, we’re not in agreement. To express the needs and thoughts underlying his or her feelings, the speaker might have said, “Sometimes when people say little things, I feel hurt because I want to be appreciated, not criticized.”
    如果你圈出了这个数字，说明我们意见不一致。为了表达自己内心深处的需求和想法，说话者可能会说：“有时候别人说些无关紧要的话，我会感到受伤，因为我想要的是赞赏，而不是批评。”
  8. If you circled this number, we’re not in agreement. To express the needs and thoughts underlying his or her feelings, the speaker might have said, “When you received that award, I felt happy because I was hoping you’d be recognized for all the work you’d put into the project.”
    如果你圈出了这个数字，说明我们意见不一致。为了表达自己内心深处的想法和需求，说话者可能会说：“当你获得那个奖项时，我感到很高兴，因为我一直希望你为这个项目付出的所有努力都能得到认可。”
