However, it’s that kind of thinking on your part that makes you feel very angry. Focus your attention on your needs: what are your needs in this situation?
我并不是说你这样想有什么错。请注意，如果我说你这样想有问题，那我也同样会这么想你。我并不是说评判别人、称他们为冷冰冰的官僚，或者说他们的行为不体贴、自私是错的。然而，正是你这种想法让你感到非常愤怒。请把注意力集中在你的需求上：在这种情况下，你的需求是什么？
John:
约翰： 		(after a long silence) Marshall, I need the training I was requesting. If I don’t get that training, as sure as I’m sitting here, I’m gonna end up back in this prison when I get out.
（一阵长时间的沉默后）马歇尔，我需要我之前申请的训练。如果我得不到训练，我敢肯定，我出狱后肯定还会回到这所监狱。
MBR:
MBR： 		Now that your attention is on your needs, how do you feel? John: Scared.
现在你的注意力都集中在自己的需求上了，你感觉如何？约翰：害怕。
MBR:
MBR： 		Now put yourself in the shoes of a prison official. If I’m an inmate, am I more likely to get my needs met if I come to you saying, “Hey, I really need that training and I’m scared of what’s going to happen if I don’t get it,” or if I approach while seeing you as a faceless bureaucrat? Even if I don’t say those words out loud, my eyes will reveal that kind of thinking. Which way am I more likely to get my needs met? (John stares at the floor and remains silent.)
现在，请你设身处地地站在监狱官员的角度思考。如果我是一名囚犯，我更有可能得到满足的是我坦诚地告诉你：“嘿，我真的需要接受培训，我很害怕如果得不到培训会发生什么”，还是仅仅把你当成一个冷冰冰的官僚来对待？即使我不把这些话说出口，我的眼神也会泄露我的想法。哪种方式更有可能满足我的需求？（约翰盯着地板，沉默不语。）
MBR:
MBR： 		Hey, buddy, what’s going on?
嘿，哥们儿，出什么事了？
John:
约翰： 		Can’t talk about it.
没法谈论这件事。

When we become aware of our needs, anger gives way to life-serving feelings.

当我们意识到自己的需求时，愤怒就会让位于有益于生活的情感。

Three hours later, John approached me and said, “Marshall, I wish you had taught me two years ago what you taught me this morning. I wouldn’t have had to kill my best friend.”

三个小时后，约翰走过来对我说：“马歇尔，我真希望你两年前就教我今天早上教我的东西。那样我就不用杀死我最好的朋友了。”

Violence comes from the belief that other people cause our pain and therefore deserve punishment.

暴力源于这样一种信念：他人造成了我们的痛苦，因此理应受到惩罚。

All violence is the result of people tricking themselves, as did this young man, into believing that their pain derives from other people and that consequently those people deserve to be punished.

一切暴力都是人们欺骗自己（就像这个年轻人一样）的结果，让他们相信自己的痛苦源于他人，因此这些人应该受到惩罚。

One time I saw my younger son take a fifty-cent piece from his sister’s room. I said, “Brett, did you ask your sister whether you could have that?” “I didn’t take it from her,” he answered. Now I faced my four options. I could have called him a liar, which would, however, have worked against my getting my needs met since any judgment of another person diminishes the likelihood of our needs being met. Where I focused my attention at that moment was critical. If I were to judge him a liar, it would point me in one direction. If I were to think that he didn’t respect me enough to tell me the truth, I would be pointed in another direction. If, however, I were either to empathize with him at that moment, or express nakedly what I was feeling and needing, I would greatly increase the possibility of getting my needs met.

有一次，我看到小儿子从他姐姐房间里拿了一枚五毛钱的硬币。我问他：“布雷特，你问过你姐姐能不能拿吗？”他回答说：“我没拿。”这时，我面临四个选择。我可以指责他撒谎，但这会阻碍我的需求得到满足，因为任何对他人的评判都会降低我们自身需求得到满足的可能性。那一刻，我的注意力集中在哪里至关重要。如果我认定他是骗子，我的判断会指向一个方向。如果我认为他不够尊重我，所以才不跟我说实话，我的判断又会指向另一个方向。然而，如果我当时能够理解他，或者坦诚地表达自己的感受和需求，我的需求得到满足的可能性就会大大增加。

We recall four options when hearing a difficult message:

听到令人沮丧的消息时，我们通常会想到以下四种选择：

1. Blame ourselves

1. 责怪自己

2. Blame others

2. 把责任推卸给别人

3. Sense our own feelings and needs

3. 感知我们自身的感受和需求

4. Sense others’ feelings and needs

4. 感知他人的感受和需求

The way I expressed my choice—which in this situation turned out to be helpful—was not so much through what I said, but through what I did. Instead of judging him as lying, I tried to hear his feeling: he was scared, and his need was to protect himself from being punished. By empathizing with him, I had a chance of making an emotional connection out of which we could both get our needs met. However, if I had approached him with the view that he was lying—even if I hadn’t expressed it out loud—he would have been less likely to feel safe expressing truthfully what had happened. I would have then become part of the process: by the very act of judging another person as a liar, I would contribute to a self-fulfilling prophecy. Why would people want to tell the truth, knowing they will be judged and punished for doing so?

我表达选择的方式——在这种情况下，事实证明这种方式很有帮助——与其说是通过我说了什么，不如说是通过我的行动。我没有评判他是否在撒谎，而是努力倾听他的感受：他很害怕，他需要保护自己免受惩罚。通过与他共情，我有机会建立一种情感联系，从而满足我们双方的需求。然而，如果我一开始就认定他在撒谎——即使我没有说出口——他也会更难感到安全，从而不敢如实讲述事情经过。那样一来，我反而成了这个过程的一部分：仅仅通过评判他人是否在撒谎，我就助长了一种自我实现的预言。人们既然知道说真话会被评判和惩罚，又何必愿意说真话呢？

Judgments of others contribute to self-fulfilling prophecies.

他人的评判会促成自我实现的预言。

I would like to suggest that when our heads are filled with judgments and analyses that others are bad, greedy, irresponsible, lying, cheating, polluting the environment, valuing profit more than life, or behaving in other ways they shouldn’t, very few of them will be interested in our needs. If we want to protect the environment, and we go to a corporate executive with the attitude, “You know, you are really a killer of the planet, you have no right to abuse the land in this way,” we have severely impaired our chances of getting our needs met. It is a rare human being who can maintain focus on our needs when we are expressing them through images of their wrongness. Of course, we may be successful in using such judgments to intimidate people into meeting our needs. If they feel so frightened, guilty, or ashamed that they change their behavior, we may come to believe that it is possible to “win” by telling people what’s wrong with them.

我想指出的是，当我们满脑子都是评判和分析，认为他人是坏人、贪婪的人、不负责任的人、说谎的人、欺骗的人、污染环境的人、唯利是图的人，或者行为不端的人时，很少有人会关心我们的需求。如果我们想要保护环境，却带着“你知道吗，你简直是地球的杀手，你没有权利这样糟蹋土地”的态度去找企业高管，那么我们满足自身需求的可能性就大大降低了。当我们用指责他人错误的方式来表达需求时，很少有人能真正关注到我们的需求。当然，我们或许可以成功地利用这种评判来恐吓他人，迫使他们满足我们的需求。如果他们感到恐惧、内疚或羞愧，从而改变了自己的行为，我们或许会误以为，只要指出别人的错误，就能“赢”他们。

With a broader perspective, however, we realize that each time our needs are met in this way, we not only lose, but we have contributed very tangibly to violence on the planet. We may have solved an immediate problem, but we will have created another one. The more people hear blame and judgment, the more defensive and aggressive they become and the less they will care about our needs in the future. So even if our present need is met in the sense that people do what we want, we will pay for it later.

然而，从更广阔的视角来看，我们意识到，每次以这种方式满足自身需求时，我们不仅会蒙受损失，还会切实地助长地球上的暴力。我们或许解决了眼前的难题，却又制造了新的问题。人们听到的指责和评判越多，就越会变得防卫和咄咄逼人，也就越不会在未来关心我们的需求。因此，即便我们眼前的需求得到了满足——人们按照我们的意愿行事——我们终将为此付出代价。

# ↩

Four Steps to Expressing Anger

表达愤怒的四个步骤

Let’s look at what the process of fully expressing our anger actually requires in concrete form. The first step is to stop and do nothing except to breathe. We refrain from making any move to blame or punish the other person. We simply stay quiet. Then we identify the thoughts that are making us angry. For example, we overhear a statement that leads us to believe that we’ve been excluded from a conversation because of race. We sense anger, stop, and recognize the thoughts stirring in our head: “It’s unfair to act like that. She’s being racist.” We know that all judgments like these are tragic expressions of unmet needs, so we take the next step and connect to the needs behind those thoughts. If we judge someone to be racist, the need may be for inclusion, equality, respect, or connection.

让我们具体看看充分表达愤怒的过程究竟需要哪些步骤。第一步是停下来，什么也不做，只是深呼吸。我们克制住想要指责或惩罚对方的冲动，保持沉默。然后，我们找出那些让我们愤怒的想法。例如，我们无意中听到一句话，让我们觉得因为种族原因而被排除在谈话之外。我们感到愤怒，停下来，意识到脑海中涌现的想法：“这样做不公平。她是在搞种族歧视。” 我们知道，所有这些评判都是未被满足的需求的悲剧性表达，所以我们继续下一步，去探究这些想法背后的需求。如果我们评判某人是种族主义者，那么他/她的需求可能是被接纳、平等、尊重或联结。

Steps to expressing anger:

表达愤怒的步骤：

1. Stop. Breathe.

1. 停下来。深呼吸。

2. Identify our judgmental thoughts.

2. 识别我们的评判性想法。

3. Connect with our needs.

3. 满足我们的需求。

4. Express our feelings and unmet needs.

4.表达我们的感受和未被满足的需求。

To fully express ourselves, we now open our mouth and speak the anger—but the anger has been transformed into needs and need-connected feelings. To articulate these feelings may require a lot of courage. For me it’s easy to get angry and tell people, “That was a racist thing to do!” In fact, I may even enjoy saying such things, but to get down to the deeper feelings and needs behind such a statement may be very frightening. To fully express our anger, we may say to the other person, “When you entered the room and started talking to the others and didn’t say anything to me, and then made the comment about white people, I felt really sick to my stomach, and got so scared; it triggered off all kinds of needs on my part to be treated equally. I’d like you to tell me how you feel when I tell you this.”

为了充分表达自我，我们现在会开口说出愤怒——但愤怒已经转化为需求以及与需求相关的感受。要清晰地表达这些感受可能需要很大的勇气。对我来说，生气并告诉别人“你那样做是种族歧视！”很容易。事实上，我甚至可能乐于说出这样的话，但要深入探究这句话背后更深层次的感受和需求却可能非常可怕。为了充分表达我们的愤怒，我们可能会对对方说：“当你走进房间，开始和其他人说话，却不跟我说话，然后又发表了关于白人的言论时，我感到非常恶心，也很害怕；这触发了我内心深处渴望被平等对待的各种需求。我想听听你听到这些话时的感受。”

# ↩

Offering Empathy First

首先展现同理心

In most cases, however, another step needs to take place before we can expect the other party to connect with what is going on in us. Because it will often be difficult for others to receive our feelings and needs in such situations, if we want them to hear us we would need first to empathize with them. The more we empathize with what leads them to behave in the ways that are not meeting our needs, the more likely it is that they will be able to reciprocate afterwards.

然而，在大多数情况下，我们需要先采取另一个步骤，才能期望对方理解我们的内心感受。因为在这种情况下，他人往往难以察觉我们的感受和需求，所以如果我们想让他们倾听，首先需要对他们产生共情。我们越能理解他们行为背后的原因，越能体会到他们为何会做出无法满足我们需求的行为，他们就越有可能在之后给予我们相应的回应。

Over the last thirty years I’ve had a wealth of experience speaking NVC with people who harbor strong beliefs about specific races and ethnic groups. Early one morning I was picked up by a cab at an airport to take me into town. A message from the dispatcher came over the loudspeaker for the cabbie: “Pick up Mr. Fishman at the synagogue on Main Street.” The man next to me in the cab muttered, “These kikes get up early in the morning so they can screw everybody out of their money.”

过去三十年里，我积累了丰富的经验，运用非暴力沟通（NVC）与那些对特定种族和族裔群体抱有强烈偏见的人交流。一天清晨，我在机场搭乘出租车进城。调度员通过广播通知司机：“在主街的犹太教堂接菲什曼先生。”坐在我旁边的司机嘟囔道：“这些犹太佬一大早就起来，就是为了骗走大家的钱。”

The more we hear them, the more they’ll hear us.

我们越是倾听他们的声音，他们就越会倾听我们的声音。

For twenty seconds, there was smoke coming out of my ears. In earlier years, my first reaction would have been to want to physically hurt such a person. Instead I took a few deep breaths and then gave myself some empathy for the hurt, fear, and rage that were stirring inside me. I attended to my feelings. I stayed conscious that my anger wasn’t coming from my fellow passenger nor the statement he had just made. His comment had triggered off a volcano inside of me, but I knew that my anger and profound fear came from a far deeper source than those words he had just uttered. I sat back and simply allowed the violent thoughts to play themselves out. I even enjoyed the image of actually grabbing his head and smashing it.

整整二十秒，我的耳朵仿佛都冒出了烟。放在以前，我第一反应肯定是想狠狠揍他一顿。但现在，我深吸了几口气，然后开始体谅自己内心翻腾的伤痛、恐惧和愤怒。我正视自己的感受。我清楚地意识到，我的愤怒并非源于那位乘客，也并非源于他刚才说的话。他的话确实在我心中引爆了一座火山，但我知道，我的愤怒和深深的恐惧源自比他刚才说的那些话更深层的根源。我靠在椅背上，任由那些暴力的念头肆意蔓延。我甚至幻想着抓住他的脑袋，狠狠地砸碎它。

Giving myself this empathy enabled me to then focus my attention on the humanness behind his message, after which the first words out of my mouth were, “Are you feeling … ?” I tried to empathize with him, to hear his pain. Why? Because I wanted to see the beauty in him, and I wanted for him to fully apprehend what I had experienced when he made his remark. I knew I wouldn’t receive that kind of understanding if there were a storm brewing inside of him. My intention was to connect with him and show a respectful empathy for the life energy in him that was behind the comment. My experience told me that if I were able to empathize, then he would be able to hear me in return. It would not be easy, but he would be able to.

给予自己这种同理心，使我能够将注意力集中在他话语背后的人性层面，随后我脱口而出的第一句话是：“你感觉……？”我试图与他共情，倾听他的痛苦。为什么？因为我想看到他身上美好的一面，也想让他充分理解我听到他那句话时的感受。我知道，如果他内心正经历着风暴，我是无法获得这种理解的。我的目的是与他建立联系，并对他话语背后蕴藏的生命能量表达尊重和同理心。我的经验告诉我，如果我能够感同身受，他也能听到我的回应。这并不容易，但他一定能做到。

Stay conscious of the violent thoughts that arise in our minds, without judging them.

时刻觉察脑海中出现的暴力念头，不要评判它们。

“Are you feeling frustrated?” I asked. “It appears that you might have had some bad experiences with Jewish people.”

“你感到沮丧吗？”我问。“看来你可能和犹太人有过一些不愉快的经历。”

He eyed me for a moment. “Yeah! These people are disgusting. They’ll do anything for money.”

他打量了我一会儿。“是啊！这些人真恶心。为了钱什么都做得出来。”

“You feel distrust and the need to protect yourself when you’re involved in financial affairs with them?”

“当你和他们有财务往来时，你会感到不信任，并需要保护自己吗？”

“That’s right!” he exclaimed, continuing to release more judgments, as I listened for the feeling and need behind each one. When we settle our attention on other people’s feelings and needs, we experience our common humanity. When I hear that he’s scared and wants to protect himself, I recognize how I also have a need to protect myself and I too know what it’s like to be scared. When my consciousness is focused on another human being’s feelings and needs, I see the universality of our experience. I had a major conflict with what went on in his head, but I’ve learned that I enjoy human beings more if I don’t hear what they think. Especially with folks who have his kind of thoughts. I’ve learned to savor life much more by only hearing what’s going on in their hearts and not getting caught up with the stuff in their heads.

“没错！”他大声说道，一边继续发表着各种评判，而我则仔细聆听着每条评判背后的感受和需求。当我们把注意力集中在他人的感受和需求上时，我们便能体验到人性的共通之处。当我听到他感到害怕，想要保护自己时，我意识到自己也有保护自己的需求，我也知道害怕是什么滋味。当我的意识专注于另一个人的感受和需求时，我看到了我们经历的普遍性。我曾对他的想法感到很困扰，但后来我明白，如果我不去在意别人的想法，我会更享受与人相处的时光。尤其是像他这样想法的人。我学会了只倾听他们内心的想法，而不去纠结于他们的想法，这样才能更好地品味生活。

When we hear another person’s feelings and needs, we recognize our common humanity.

当我们倾听他人的感受和需求时，我们便意识到我们共同的人性。

This man kept on pouring out his sadness and frustration. Before I knew it, he’d finished with Jews and moved on to blacks. He was charged with pain around a number of subjects. After nearly ten minutes of my just listening, he stopped: he had felt understood.

这个人不停地倾诉他的悲伤和沮丧。我还没反应过来，他已经说完了犹太人，又开始谈论黑人。他对很多事情都感到痛苦。我静静地听了将近十分钟后，他停了下来：他觉得自己被理解了。

Then I let him know what was going on in me:

然后我告诉他我内心的感受：

MBR:
MBR： 		You know, when you first started to talk, I felt a lot of anger, a lot of frustration, sadness, and discouragement, because I’ve had very different experiences with Jews than you’ve had, and I was wanting you to have much more the kind of experiences I’ve had. Can you tell me what you heard me say?
你知道，你刚开始说话的时候，我感到非常愤怒、沮丧、悲伤和失望，因为我和犹太人的经历与你截然不同，我原本希望你能有更多像我一样的经历。你能告诉我你听到我说了些什么吗？
Man:
男人： 		Oh, I’m not saying they’re all …
哦，我不是说他们都是……
MBR:
MBR： 		Excuse me, hold on, hold it. Can you tell me what you heard me say?
不好意思，等一下，等一下。你能告诉我你刚才听到我说了什么吗？
Man:
男人： 		What are you talking about?
你在说什么？
MBR:
MBR： 		Let me repeat what I’m trying to say. I really want you to just hear the pain I felt when I heard your words. It’s really important to me that you hear that. I was saying I felt a real sense of sadness because my experiences with Jewish people have been very different. I was just wishing that you had had some experiences that were different from the ones you were describing. Can you tell me what you heard me say?
让我再说一遍。我真的希望你能感受到我听到你的话时所感受到的痛苦。对我来说，让你听到这一点非常重要。我刚才说的是，我感到非常难过，因为我与犹太人的经历截然不同。我只是希望你的经历能和你描述的有所不同。你能告诉我你听到了什么吗？
Man:
男人： 		You’re saying I have no right to talk the way I did.
你的意思是说我没有权利那样说话吗？
MBR:
MBR： 		No, I would like you to hear me differently. I really don’t want to blame you. I have no desire to blame you.
不，我希望你能换个角度理解我的意思。我真的不想责怪你。我根本不想责怪你。

Our need is for the other person to truly hear our pain.

我们需要的是对方真正理解我们的痛苦。

I intended to slow down the conversation, because in my experience, to whatever degree people hear blame, they have failed to hear our pain. If this man said, “Those were terrible things for me to say; those were racist remarks I made,” he would not have heard my pain. As soon as people think that they have done something wrong, they will not be fully apprehending our pain.

我本想放慢谈话节奏，因为根据我的经验，人们越是关注指责，就越是忽略了我们的痛苦。如果这个人说：“我不应该说那些话；我的确发表了种族歧视言论”，他就无法真正理解我的痛苦。一旦人们觉得自己做错了事，就很难完全体会到我们的痛苦。

People do not hear our pain when they believe they are at fault.

当人们认为错在自己身上时，他们是听不到我们的痛苦的。

I didn’t want him to hear blame, because I wanted him to know what had gone on in my heart when he uttered his remark. Blaming is easy. People are used to hearing blame; sometimes they agree with it and hate themselves—which doesn’t stop them from behaving the same way—and sometimes they hate us for calling them racists or whatever—which also doesn’t stop their behavior. If we sense blame entering their mind, as I did in the cab, we may need to slow down, go back, and hear their pain for a while more.

我不想责备他，因为我想让他知道，当他说出那句话时，我内心究竟在想些什么。责备很容易。人们习惯了被责备；有时他们认同这种指责，并因此憎恨自己——但这并不能阻止他们继续以同样的方式行事——有时他们恨我们指责他们是种族主义者或其他什么——但这同样无法阻止他们的行为。如果我们察觉到责备的念头正在他们心中滋生，就像我在出租车里感觉到的那样，我们或许需要放慢脚步，回到他们身边，再多倾听一会儿他们的痛苦。

# ↩

Taking Our Time

慢慢来

Probably the most important part of learning how to live the process we have been discussing is to take our time. We may feel awkward deviating from the habitual behaviors that our conditioning has rendered automatic, but if our intention is to consciously live life in harmony with our values, then we’ll want to take our time.

学习如何践行我们一直在讨论的生活方式，最重要的或许就是放慢脚步。我们可能会因为要打破那些由后天环境塑造而成的习惯性行为而感到不自在，但如果我们真心想要有意识地按照自己的价值观生活，那么我们就需要放慢脚步。

A friend of mine, Sam Williams, jotted down the basic components of the NVC process on a three-by-five card, which he would use as a cheat sheet at work. When his boss would confront him, Sam would stop, refer to the card in his hand, and take time to remember how to respond. When I asked whether his colleagues were finding him a little strange, constantly staring into his hand and taking so much time to form his sentences, Sam replied, “It doesn’t actually take that much more time, but even if it did, it’s still worth it to me. It’s important for me to know that I am responding to people the way I really want to.” At home he was more overt, explaining to his wife and children why he was taking the time and trouble to consult the card. Whenever there was an argument in the family, he would pull out the card and take his time. After about a month, he felt comfortable enough to put it away. Then one evening, he and Scottie, age four, were having a conflict over television and it wasn’t going well. “Daddy,” Scottie said urgently, “get the card!”

我的朋友萨姆·威廉姆斯把非暴力沟通的基本要素写在一张三乘五英寸的卡片上，作为工作时的“小抄”。每当老板质问他时，萨姆都会停下来，看看手里的卡片，然后花时间回忆该如何回应。我问他同事们是否觉得他有点奇怪，总是盯着卡片看，说话也总是慢吞吞的，萨姆回答说：“其实并没有多花多少时间，但即使真的多花了很多，对我来说也值得。对我来说，重要的是确保我能以自己真正想要的方式回应别人。” 在家，他更坦诚地向妻子和孩子解释自己为什么会花时间和精力去查阅卡片。每当家里发生争吵时，他都会拿出卡片，仔细思考。大约一个月后，他觉得可以把卡片收起来了。然后有一天晚上，他和四岁的儿子斯科蒂因为看电视发生了争执，情况不太妙。 “爸爸，”斯科蒂急切地说，“把卡拿来！”

For those of you wishing to apply NVC, especially in challenging situations of anger, I would suggest the following exercise. As we have seen, our anger comes from judgments, labels, and thoughts of blame, of what people “should” do and what they “deserve.” List the judgments that float most frequently in your head by using the cue, “I don’t like people who are … ” Collect all such negative judgments in your head and then ask yourself, “When I make that judgment of a person, what am I needing and not getting?” In this way, you train yourself to frame your thinking in terms of unmet needs rather than in terms of judgments of other people.

对于那些希望运用非暴力沟通（NVC）的人，尤其是在充满愤怒的棘手情境中，我建议你们尝试以下练习。正如我们所见，我们的愤怒源于评判、贴标签和责备的想法，源于对他人“应该”做什么以及他们“应得”什么的执念。你可以用“我不喜欢这样的人……”作为提示，列出你脑海中最常浮现的评判。将所有这些负面评判都收集起来，然后问问自己：“当我做出这样的评判时，我需要什么而又没有得到什么？” 通过这种方式，你可以训练自己将思维模式从对他人的评判转移到未被满足的需求上。

Practice translating each judgment into an unmet need.

练习将每项判断转化为未被满足的需求。

Take your time.

慢慢来。

Practice is essential, because most of us were raised, if not on the streets of Detroit, then somewhere only slightly less violent. Judging and blaming have become second nature to us. To practice NVC, we need to proceed slowly, think carefully before we speak, and often just take a deep breath and not speak at all. Learning the process and applying it both take time.

练习至关重要，因为我们大多数人即便不是在底特律的街头长大，也是在暴力程度稍低的地方长大。评判和指责已经成了我们的第二天性。要练习非暴力沟通，我们需要放慢节奏，三思而后行，很多时候，我们只需深呼吸，保持沉默。学习和运用非暴力沟通都需要时间。

# ↩

Summary

概括

Blaming and punishing others are superficial expressions of anger. If we wish to fully express anger, the first step is to divorce the other person from any responsibility for our anger. Instead we shine the light of consciousness on our own feelings and needs. By expressing our needs, we are far more likely to get them met than by judging, blaming, or punishing others.

责备和惩罚他人只是肤浅的愤怒表达。如果我们想要充分表达愤怒，第一步是撇清对方与我们愤怒的任何关系。相反，我们应该将意识的光芒照耀在自身的感受和需求上。通过表达自身需求，我们更有可能获得满足，而不是通过评判、责备或惩罚他人。

The four steps to expressing anger are (1) stop and breathe, (2) identify our judgmental thoughts, (3) connect with our needs, and (4) express our feelings and unmet needs. Sometimes, in between steps 3 and 4, we may choose to empathize with the other person so that he or she will be better able to hear us when we express ourselves in step 4.

表达愤怒的四个步骤是：(1) 停下来深呼吸；(2) 识别我们带有评判性的想法；(3) 与自身需求建立联系；(4) 表达我们的感受和未被满足的需求。有时，在步骤 3 和步骤 4 之间，我们可以选择与对方共情，这样对方在在步骤 4 中我们表达自己时，就能更好地理解我们。

We need to take our time both in learning and in applying the process of NVC.

我们需要花时间去学习和应用非暴力沟通的过程。

NVC in Action

非暴力沟通实践

Parent and Teen Dialogue: A Life-Threatening Issue

父母与青少年对话：一个关乎生死的问题

In this situation, fifteen-year-old Bill took a car, without permission, from Jorge, a family friend. He went on a joy ride with two friends and returned the car undamaged to the garage, where its absence had not been detected. Since then, however, Jorge’s fourteen-year-old daughter, Eva, who had gone along for the ride, told her father what had happened. Jorge informed Bill’s father, who is now approaching his son. The father has just recently been practicing NVC.

在这种情况下，15岁的比尔未经允许就从朋友豪尔赫那里开走了一辆车。他和两个朋友兜风，之后把车完好无损地还回了车库，车库里的人也没有发现车不见了。然而，豪尔赫14岁的女儿伊娃当时也和比尔一起兜风，她把这件事告诉了父亲。豪尔赫随后通知了比尔的父亲，比尔的父亲现在正在和儿子谈话。比尔的父亲最近才开始练习非暴力沟通（NVC）。

Father:
父亲： 		So I hear you, Eva, and Dave took Jorge’s car without asking.
我明白了，伊娃，戴夫未经允许就开走了豪尔赫的车。
Bill:
账单： 		No, we didn’t!
不，我们没有！
Father:
父亲： 		(in a loud voice) Don’t lie to me; it’ll only make it worse!
（大声）别骗我，只会让情况更糟！

Then he remembered to first connect to his own feelings and needs in order to stay in connection with his son.

然后他想起，要先关注自己的感受和需求，才能与儿子保持联系。

Father:
父亲： 		You just sit there for a moment; I need to think.
你先在那儿坐一会儿；我需要思考一下。

Going inside himself, he saw how angry and scared he was. Angry when telling himself, “Bill should have known better!” and “What a liar he’s become!” Scared when he thinks of all the potential consequences of not only Bill’s action, but his own misjudgment of what his son might do.

他审视内心，发现自己既愤怒又恐惧。愤怒的是，他对自己说：“比尔本该更懂事些！”“他竟然变成了一个骗子！”恐惧的是，他想到比尔的行为以及自己对儿子可能做出的举动的误判所带来的所有潜在后果。

Father:
父亲： 		(silently to himself) That was stupid of me to assume he knows better. Someone could have gotten killed in this! (then catching himself) Oops, I need to translate the labels “stupid” and “liar” into feelings and needs. For “stupid,” I guess the feeling is disappointment in myself: I would have liked to think that I knew him better. And as for “liar,” I’m feeling pretty scared because I want to be able to count on getting accurate information to deal with this situation.
（默默地对自己说）我真是太蠢了，居然以为他比我更懂。这事儿差点儿害死人！（然后意识到自己说错了）哎呀，我得把“蠢”和“骗子”这两个词转化成具体的感受和需求。“蠢”的感觉，大概是对自己失望吧：我本来以为自己更了解他。至于“骗子”，我其实挺害怕的，因为我需要能够获得准确的信息来应对这种情况。
Father:
父亲： 		(out loud, after silence while he mulls over how to begin talking) Bill, are you worried that you’d be punished if you gave me accurate information?
（沉默片刻后，他思考着如何开口，然后大声说道）比尔，你担心如果你告诉我准确的信息，你会受到惩罚吗？
Bill:
账单： 		Yeah, you’re always so mean whenever I do anything you don’t like.
是啊，每次我做了你不喜欢的事，你总是那么刻薄。
Father:
父亲： 		Are you saying you’d like more understanding and fairer treatment for what you do?
你是说你希望自己的工作能得到更多理解和更公平的对待吗？
Bill:
账单： 		Oh, sure, like I’m really gonna get fair treatment and understanding from you!
哦，当然了，好像我真的会从你那里得到公平对待和理解似的！
Father:
父亲： 		(silently to himself) Boy, do I get angry when he says that! Can’t he see how hard I’m trying? I really need a little respect for how hard this is, and I guess also a little caring for how scared I’m feeling.
（默默地自言自语）他这么说真是让我火冒三丈！难道他看不出我有多努力吗？我真的需要他尊重一下这件事的艰难，也需要他关心一下我有多害怕。
Father:
父亲： 		(out loud to Bill) Sounds to me like you’re worried that no matter what you say, you won’t be treated fairly?
（大声对比尔说）听起来你好像担心无论你说什么，都不会得到公平对待？
Bill:
账单： 		What do you care about treating me fairly? When something happens, you just want someone to punish. Besides, what’s the big deal? Even if we did take the car, no one got hurt and it’s back where it was. I mean, this is no major crime wave.
你才不在乎公平对待我吗？出了事，你只想找个人来惩罚。再说，这又有什么大不了的？就算我们把车开走了，也没人受伤，车现在也还回去了。我的意思是，这又不是什么重大犯罪事件。
Father:
父亲： 		Are you scared there’ll be harsh consequences if you admit to taking the car, and you want to trust that you’ll be treated justly?
你是否害怕承认偷车后会面临严重的后果，并且希望相信自己会受到公正的对待？
Bill:
账单： 		Yeah.
是的。
Father:
父亲： 		(allowing time for silence and the connection to go deeper) What could I do to give you that reassurance?
（留出时间让彼此沉默，加深联系）我该怎么做才能让你安心呢？
Bill:
账单： 		Promise to never punish me again.
答应我以后永远不要再惩罚我了。
Father:
父亲： 		(Aware that punishment will not help Bill develop consciousness around potential consequences of his behavior, but will only contribute to greater disconnection and resistance, Bill’s father expresses willingness to agree to Bill’s request.) I’d be open to that agreement if you agree to stay in dialogue with me. That is, we talk until I’m satisfied you’re aware of all the possible consequences of your having taken that car. However, in the future, if it happens that I’m not confident that you see the potential danger of what you’re in for, I might still use force—but only in order to protect you.
（比尔的父亲意识到惩罚并不能帮助比尔意识到自己行为的潜在后果，反而会加剧他的疏离感和抵触情绪，因此他表示愿意同意比尔的请求。）“如果你同意继续和我对话，我愿意接受这个协议。也就是说，我们会一直谈下去，直到我确信你已经意识到你偷车可能带来的所有后果。但是，将来如果我不能确定你是否意识到自己行为的潜在危险，我可能仍然会使用武力——但那只是为了保护你。”
Bill:
账单： 		Wow, great! It really feels good knowing I’m so stupid you have to use force to protect me from myself!
哇，太好了！知道我蠢到需要你动用武力来保护我，这种感觉真好！
Father:
父亲： 		(losing touch with his own needs, but silently) Man, there are times when I could just kill the little … I’m so furious when he says things like that! It really doesn’t seem like he cares…. Damn, what am I needing here? I’m needing to know, when I’m working this hard, that at least he cares.)
（他似乎忽略了自己的需求，但默默地）唉，有时候我真想杀了那个小家伙……他说这种话的时候我真是气疯了！他好像根本不在乎……该死，我到底需要什么？我这么努力工作，只是需要知道他至少在乎我。
Father:
父亲： 		(out loud, angrily) You know, Bill, when you say things like that, I get really pissed off. I’m trying so hard to stay with you on this, and when I hear things like that … Look, I need to know if you even want to keep talking with me.
（大声，生气地）比尔，你知道吗，你说这种话的时候，我真的非常生气。我这么努力地想在这件事上和你保持一致，可当我听到这种话的时候……听着，我需要知道你是否还想继续和我谈下去。
Bill:
账单： 		I don’t care.
我不在乎。
Father:
父亲： 		Bill, I really want to listen to you rather than fall into my old habits of blaming and threatening you whenever something comes up that I’m upset about. But when I hear you say things like, “It feels good to know I’m so stupid,” in the tone of voice you just used, I find it hard to control myself. I could use your help on this. That is, if you would rather me listen to you than blame or threaten. Or if not, then, I suppose my other option is to just handle this the way I’m used to handling things.
比尔，我真的很想听你说话，而不是像以前那样，一遇到不顺心的事就责怪你、威胁你。可是，你刚才用那种语气说“知道自己这么蠢真好”，我就很难控制自己。我需要你的帮助。如果你希望我听你的话，而不是责怪你或威胁我，那就太好了。如果你不愿意，那我只能像以前那样处理这件事了。
Bill:
账单： 		And what would that be?
那会是什么呢？
Father:
父亲： 		Well, by now, I’d probably be saying, “Hey, you’re grounded for two years: no TV, no car, no money, no dates, no nothing! ”
嗯，现在我大概会说：“嘿，你被禁足两年：不准看电视，不准开车，不准花钱，不准约会，什么都不准！”
Bill:
账单： 		Well, I guess I’d want you to do it the new way then.
那我想你应该用新方法试试。
Father:
父亲： 		(with humor) I’m glad to see that your sense of self-preservation is still intact. Now I need you to tell me whether you’re willing to share some honesty and vulnerability.
（带着幽默）很高兴看到你的自我保护意识依然完好无损。现在我需要你告诉我，你是否愿意坦诚相待，展现一些脆弱的一面。
Bill:
账单： 		What do you mean by “vulnerability”?
你说的“脆弱性”是什么意思？
Father:
父亲： 		It means that you tell me what you are really feeling about the things we’re talking about, and I tell you the same from my end. (in a firm voice) Are you willing?
这意味着你要告诉我你对我们正在谈论的事情的真实感受，我也要告诉你我的真实感受。（语气坚定）你愿意吗？
Bill:
账单： 		Okay, I’ll try.
好的，我试试。
Father:
父亲： 		(with sigh of relief) Thank you. I’m grateful for your willingness to try. Did I tell you—Jorge grounded Eva for three months—she won’t be allowed to do anything. How do you feel about that?
（如释重负地叹了口气）谢谢你。我很感激你愿意尝试。我有没有跟你说过——豪尔赫把伊娃禁足了三个月——她什么都不许做。你对此有什么看法？
Bill:
账单： 		Oh man, what a bummer; that’s so unfair!
哎呀，真倒霉；太不公平了！
Father:
父亲： 		I’d like to hear how you really feel about it.
我想听听你对此事的真实感受。
Bill:
账单： 		I told you—it’s totally unfair!
我跟你说过——这太不公平了！
Father:
父亲： 		(realizing Bill isn’t in touch with what he’s feeling, decides to guess) Are you sad that she’s having to pay so much for her mistake?
（意识到比尔没有意识到自己的感受，决定猜测）你是不是很伤心，因为她要为自己的错误付出如此沉重的代价？
Bill:
账单： 		No, it’s not that. I mean, it wasn’t her mistake really.
不，不是那样的。我的意思是，那真的不是她的错。
Father:
父亲： 		Oh, so are you upset she’s paying for something that was your idea to start with?
哦，所以你生气是因为她要为当初是你提出的想法买单吗？
Bill:
账单： 		Well, yeah, she just went along with what I told her to do.
是的，她只是按照我的指示做了。
Father:
父亲： 		Sounds to me like you’re kind of hurting inside seeing the kind of effect your decision had on Eva.
听起来你好像内心很痛苦，因为你看到了你的决定对伊娃造成的影响。
Bill:
账单： 		Sorta.
算是吧。
Father:
父亲： 		Billy, I really need to know that you are able to see how your actions have consequences.
比利，我真的需要知道你是否能够意识到你的行为会带来怎样的后果。
Bill:
账单： 		Well, I wasn’t thinking about what could’ve gone wrong. Yeah, I guess I did really screw up bad.
我当时根本没想过可能会出什么问题。唉，看来我真的搞砸了。
Father:
父亲： 		I’d rather you see it as something you did that didn’t turn out the way you wanted. And I still need reassurance about your being aware of the consequences. Would you tell me what you’re feeling right now about what you did?
我希望你把这件事看作是你做的事情，只是结果不如你所愿。我仍然需要你确认你是否意识到后果。你现在对自己的所作所为有何感受？
Bill:
账单： 		I feel really stupid, Dad…. I didn’t mean to hurt anyone.
爸爸，我觉得自己好蠢……我不是故意要伤害任何人的。
Father:
父亲： 		(translating Bill’s self-judgments into feelings and needs) So you’re sad, and regret what you did because you’d like to be trusted not to do harm?
（将比尔的自我评判转化为感受和需求）所以你感到难过，后悔自己所做的事，因为你想被信任，不会伤害别人？
Bill:
账单： 		Yeah, I didn’t mean to cause so much trouble. I just didn’t think about it.
是啊，我不是故意要惹出这么多麻烦的。我只是没考虑到这一点。
Father:
父亲： 		Are you saying you wish you had thought about it more and gotten clearer before you acted?
你是说你希望自己在行动之前能多考虑考虑，把事情想得更清楚一些吗？
Bill:
账单： 		(reflecting) Yeah …
（沉思）是啊……
Father:
父亲： 		Well, it’s reassuring for me to hear that, and for there to be some real healing with Jorge, I would like you to go to him and tell him what you just told me. Would you be willing to do that?
听到这些我感到很欣慰。为了让豪尔赫真正走出困境，我希望你能去告诉他你刚才跟我说的话。你愿意这样做吗？
Bill:
账单： 		Oh man, that’s so scary; he’ll be really mad!
天哪，太可怕了；他肯定会非常生气！
Father:
父亲： 		Yeah, it’s likely he will be. That’s one of the consequences. Are you willing to be responsible for your actions? I like Jorge and I want to keep him for a friend, and I’m guessing that you would like to keep your connection with Eva. Is that the case?
是的，他很可能会那样做。这是后果之一。你愿意为自己的行为负责吗？我喜欢豪尔赫，我想和他保持朋友关系，我猜你也想和伊娃继续保持联系，对吗？
Bill:
账单： 		She’s one of my best friends.
她是我最好的朋友之一。
Father:
父亲： 		So shall we go see them?
那我们去看看他们吧？
Bill:
账单： 		(fearfully and reluctantly) Well … okay. Yeah, I guess so.
（战战兢兢、不情愿地）好吧……好吧。嗯，我想是的。
Father:
父亲： 		Are you scared and needing to know that you will be safe if you go there?
你是不是很害怕，想知道如果去那里是否安全？
Bill:
账单： 		Yeah.
是的。
Father:
父亲： 		We’ll go together: I’ll be there for you and with you. I’m really proud that you are willing.
我们会一起去：我会陪在你身边，支持你。你愿意这样做，我真的为你感到骄傲。
# ↩

11

Conflict Resolution and Mediation

冲突解决与调解

N ow that you are familiar with the steps involved in Nonviolent Communication, I want to address how to apply them in resolving conflicts. These could be conflicts between yourself and someone else, or you may be asked to—or choose to—involve yourself in a conflict between others: family members, partners, co-workers, or even strangers in conflict. Whatever the situation may be, resolving conflicts involves all the principles I outlined previously in this book: observing, identifying and expressing feelings, connecting feelings with needs, and making doable requests of another person using clear, concrete, positive action language.

既然您已经熟悉了非暴力沟通的步骤，接下来我想谈谈如何运用这些步骤来解决冲突。这些冲突可能发生在您与他人之间，也可能是您被要求或主动介入他人之间的冲突：例如家庭成员、伴侣、同事，甚至是陌生人之间的冲突。无论情况如何，解决冲突都离不开我在本书前面提到的所有原则：观察、识别和表达感受，将感受与需求联系起来，并使用清晰、具体、积极的行动语言向对方提出切实可行的要求。

Over the course of several decades, I’ve used Nonviolent Communication to resolve conflicts around the world. I’ve met with unhappy couples, families, workers and their employers, and ethnic groups at war with each other. My experience has taught me that it’s possible to resolve just about any conflict to everybody’s satisfaction. All it takes is a lot of patience, the willingness to establish a human connection, the intention to follow NVC principles until you reach a resolution, and trust that the process will work.

几十年来，我一直运用非暴力沟通来解决世界各地的冲突。我曾与不幸福的伴侣、家庭、员工及其雇主，以及交战的族群会面。我的经验告诉我，几乎任何冲突都有可能得到圆满解决。关键在于要有足够的耐心，愿意建立人与人之间的联结，决心遵循非暴力沟通的原则直至达成解决方案，并相信这个过程终将奏效。

# ↩

Human Connection

人际联系

In NVC-style conflict resolution, creating a connection between the people who are in conflict is the most important thing. This is what enables all the other steps of NVC to work, because it’s not until you have forged that connection that each side will seek to know exactly what the other side is feeling and needing. The parties also need to know from the start that the objective is not to get the other side to do what they want them to do. And once the two sides understand that, it becomes possible—sometimes even easy—to have a conversation about how to meet their needs.

在非暴力沟通（NVC）的冲突解决方式中，建立冲突双方之间的联结至关重要。这是NVC其他步骤得以奏效的基础，因为只有在建立起这种联结之后，双方才会真正了解对方的感受和需求。此外，双方从一开始就需要明白，NVC的目标并非强迫对方按照自己的意愿行事。一旦双方理解了这一点，就有可能——有时甚至很容易——就如何满足彼此的需求展开对话。

Creating a connection between people is the most important thing.

建立人与人之间的联系是最重要的。

With NVC, we’re trying to live a different value system while we are asking for things to change. What’s most important is that every connection along the line mirrors the kind of world we’re trying to create. Each step needs to reflect energetically what we’re after, which is a holographic image of the quality of relationships we’re trying to create. In short, how we ask for change reflects the value system we’re trying to support. When we see the difference between these two objectives, we consciously refrain from trying to get a person to do what we want. Instead we work to create that quality of mutual concern and respect where each party thinks their own needs matter and they are conscious that their needs and the other person’s well-being are interdependent. When that happens, it’s amazing how conflicts that otherwise seem irresolvable are easily resolved.

在非暴力沟通中，我们试图践行一种不同的价值体系，同时又要求改变现状。最重要的是，沟通中的每一次互动都应反映出我们努力创造的世界。每一步都需要在能量层面上体现我们所追求的目标，即构建我们所希望的高质量人际关系的全息图景。简而言之，我们要求改变的方式反映了我们试图维护的价值体系。当我们意识到这两个目标之间的区别时，我们会自觉地避免强迫他人按照我们的意愿行事。相反，我们会努力营造一种相互关心和尊重的氛围，让双方都觉得自己的需求很重要，并且意识到自身需求与对方的福祉是相互依存的。当这种情况发生时，那些看似无法解决的冲突也会迎刃而解，令人惊叹。

When I’m asked to resolve a conflict, I work to lead the two sides to this caring and respectful connection. This is often the tough part. Once that is accomplished, I help both sides create strategies that will resolve the conflict to both sides’ satisfaction.

当被要求解决冲突时，我会努力引导双方建立起关爱和尊重的关系。这往往是最难的部分。一旦做到这一点，我会帮助双方制定策略，以期最终达成双方都满意的解决方案。

Notice that I use the word satisfaction instead of compromise! Most attempts at resolution search for compromise, which means everybody gives something up and neither side is satisfied. NVC is different; our objective is to meet everyone’s needs fully.

请注意，我用的是“满足”而不是“妥协”！大多数解决问题的尝试都追求妥协，这意味着每个人都要做出让步，最终谁也不满意。非暴力沟通则不同；我们的目标是充分满足每个人的需求。

# ↩

NVC Conflict Resolution versus Traditional Mediation

非暴力沟通冲突解决方式与传统调解方式的比较

Let’s consider the human connection aspect of NVC again, this time looking at third-party mediation—a person stepping in to resolve a conflict between two other parties. When I’m working with two people, or two groups, that have a conflict they haven’t been able to resolve, I approach this very differently from the way professional mediators often approach a conflict.

让我们再次探讨非暴力沟通中的人际联结层面，这次着眼于第三方调解——即由第三方介入解决两方之间的冲突。当我与两个无法自行解决冲突的个人或团体合作时，我的方法与专业调解员处理冲突的方式截然不同。

For example, once I was in Austria meeting with a group of professional mediators who work on many kinds of international conflicts, including those between unions and management. I described several conflicts I had mediated, such as one in California between landowners and migrant workers where there had been considerable physical violence. And I talked about mediating between two African tribes (which I discuss fully in my book Speak Peace in a World of Conflict) and a few other extremely entrenched, dangerous conflicts.

例如，有一次我在奥地利会见了一群专业调解员，他们处理各种国际冲突，包括工会与管理层之间的冲突。我描述了我调解过的几起冲突，比如加利福尼亚州的一起土地所有者与移民工人之间的冲突，那次冲突中发生了相当严重的肢体暴力。我还谈到了我调解过的两个非洲部落之间的冲突（我在我的著作《在冲突的世界中倡导和平》中对此有详细论述），以及其他一些根深蒂固、极其危险的冲突。

I was asked how much time I give myself to study a situation I was to mediate. He was referring to the process most mediators use: educating themselves about the issues involved in the conflict and then mediating with those issues as the focus instead of focusing on creating a human connection. In fact, in typical third-party mediation, the conflicting parties may not even be in the same room. Once, as a participant in mediation, our party was in one room and the other party was in another room, with the mediator traveling back and forth between rooms. He’d ask us, “What do you want them to do?” and he’d take that back to the other side and see if they were willing to do it. Then he would come back and say, “They’re unwilling to do that, but how about this?”

有人问我，在调解案件时，我会给自己多少时间来研究情况。他指的是大多数调解员的做法：先了解冲突涉及的问题，然后以这些问题为中心进行调解，而不是专注于建立人际关系。事实上，在典型的第三方调解中，冲突双方甚至可能不在同一个房间里。有一次，我作为调解员参与了一次调解，我们一方在一个房间，对方在另一个房间，调解员则在两个房间之间来回走动。他会问我们：“你们希望他们怎么做？”然后他会把这个问题带回给对方，看看他们是否愿意这样做。之后他会回来问：“他们不愿意这样做，那这样呢？”

Many mediators define their role as a “third head” trying to think of a way to get everybody to come to an agreement. They are not at all concerned with creating a quality of connection, thus overlooking the only conflict resolution tool I have ever known to work. When I described the NVC method and the role of human connection, one of the participants at the Austria meeting raised the objection that I was talking about psychotherapy, and that mediators were not psychotherapists.

许多调解员将自己的角色定义为“第三人称”，试图找到让各方达成一致的办法。他们完全不关心建立高质量的沟通，因此忽略了我所知的唯一有效的冲突解决工具。当我向奥地利会议的与会者介绍非暴力沟通（NVC）方法以及人际沟通的作用时，有人提出异议，认为我是在谈论心理治疗，而调解员并非心理治疗师。

In my experience, connecting people at this level isn’t psychotherapy; it’s actually the core of mediation because when you make the connection, the problem solves itself most of the time. Instead of a third head asking, “What can we agree to here?,” if we had a clear statement of each person’s needs—what those parties need right now from each other—we will then discover what can be done to get everybody’s needs met. These become the strategies the parties agree to implement after the mediation session concludes and the parties leave the room.

以我的经验来看，建立这种程度的沟通并非心理治疗；它实际上是调解的核心，因为一旦建立了这种沟通，问题往往就能迎刃而解。与其让第三方来问“我们能达成什么共识？”，不如让我们清楚地了解每个人的需求——他们此刻需要彼此提供什么——这样我们就能找到满足所有人需求的方法。这些需求将成为各方在调解结束后离开房间时共同商定的行动策略。

When you make the connection, the problem usually solves itself.

当你把两者联系起来，问题通常就会迎刃而解。

# ↩

NVC Conflict Resolution Steps—A Quick Overview

非暴力沟通冲突解决步骤——快速概述

Before we get deeper into a discussion of some of the other key elements of conflict resolution, let me give you a thumbnail sketch of the steps involved in resolving a conflict between ourselves and somebody else. There are five steps in this process. Either side may express their needs first, but for the sake of simplicity in this overview, let’s assume we begin with our needs.

在深入探讨冲突解决的其他关键要素之前，让我先简要概述一下我们与他人之间解决冲突的步骤。这个过程分为五个步骤。双方都可以先表达自己的需求，但为了便于概述，我们假设先从我们自己的需求开始。

  • First, we express our own needs.
    首先，我们表达自己的需求。
  • Second, we search for the real needs of the other person, no matter how they are expressing themselves. If they are not expressing a need, but instead an opinion, judgment, or analysis, we recognize that, and continue to seek the need behind their words, the need underneath what they are saying.
    其次，无论对方如何表达，我们都要探寻其真正的需求。如果他们表达的并非需求，而是观点、判断或分析，我们也要意识到这一点，并继续探寻他们话语背后的需求，探寻他们话语之下隐藏的需求。
  • Third, we verify that we both accurately recognize the other person’s needs, and if not, continue to seek the need behind their words.
    第三，我们要确认我们双方是否准确地理解了对方的需求，如果没有，就要继续探寻他们话语背后的需求。
  • Fourth, we provide as much empathy as is required for us to mutually hear each other’s needs accurately.
    第四，我们给予彼此足够的同理心，以便准确地倾听对方的需求。
  • And fifth, having clarified both parties’ needs in the situation, we propose strategies for resolving the conflict, framing them in positive action language.
    第五，在明确了双方在当前情况下的需求之后，我们提出了解决冲突的策略，并以积极的行动语言来表述这些策略。

Throughout, we’re listening to each other with utmost care, avoiding the use of language that implies wrongness on either side.

我们始终认真倾听对方的意见，避免使用任何一方有错的语言。

Avoid the use of language that implies wrongness.

避免使用带有错误暗示的语言。

# ↩

On Needs, Strategies, and Analysis

关于需求、策略和分析

Since the understanding and expression of needs are essential to resolving conflicts through NVC, let us review this vital concept which has been emphasized throughout this book, and particularly in Chapter 5 .

由于理解和表达需求对于通过非暴力沟通解决冲突至关重要，让我们回顾一下本书中，特别是第 5 章中强调的这一重要概念。

Fundamentally, needs are the resources life requires to sustain itself. We all have physical needs: air, water, food, rest. And we have psychological needs such as understanding, support, honesty, and meaning. I believe that all people basically have the same needs regardless of nationality, religion, gender, income, education, etc.

从根本上讲，需求是生命维持自身运转所需的资源。我们都有生理需求：空气、水、食物、休息。我们也有心理需求，例如理解、支持、诚实和意义感。我相信，无论国籍、宗教、性别、收入、教育程度等如何，所有人的基本需求都是相同的。

Next, let’s consider the difference between a person’s needs and his or her strategy for fulfilling them. It is important, when resolving conflicts, that we can clearly recognize the difference between needs and strategies.

接下来，我们来探讨一下一个人的需求和他/她满足这些需求的策略之间的区别。在解决冲突时，能够清楚地认识到需求和策略之间的区别至关重要。

Many of us have great difficulty expressing our needs: we have been taught by society to criticize, insult, and otherwise (mis)communicate in ways that keep us apart. In a conflict, both parties usually spend too much time intent on proving themselves right, and the other party wrong, rather than paying attention to their own and the other’s needs. And such verbal conflicts can far too easily escalate into violence—and even war.

我们很多人都难以表达自己的需求：社会教导我们批评、侮辱，以及用其他方式（错误地）沟通，从而造成彼此疏远。在冲突中，双方通常花费太多时间试图证明自己正确、对方错误，而不是关注彼此的需求。而这种言语冲突很容易升级为暴力，甚至战争。

In order not to confuse needs and strategies, it is important to recall that needs contain no reference to anybody taking any particular action. On the other hand, strategies, which may appear in the form of requests, desires, wants, and “solutions,” refer to specific actions that specific people may take.

为了避免混淆需求和策略，需要记住的是，需求本身并不涉及任何人采取任何具体行动。而策略，例如请求、愿望、需求和“解决方案”，则指的是特定人员可能采取的具体行动。

For example, I once met with a couple who had just about given up on their marriage. I asked the husband what needs of his weren’t being fulfilled in the marriage. He said, “I need to get out of this marriage.” What he was describing was a specific person (himself) taking a specific action (leaving the marriage). He wasn’t expressing a need; he was identifying a strategy.

例如，我曾经遇到一对几乎对婚姻彻底绝望的夫妇。我问丈夫，他在婚姻中哪些需求没有得到满足。他说：“我需要离开这段婚姻。”他描述的是一个具体的人（他自己）采取的具体行动（离开婚姻）。他表达的并非需求，而是策略。

I pointed this out to the husband and suggested that he first clarify his and his wife’s needs before undertaking the strategy of “getting out of this marriage.” After both of them had connected with their own and each other’s needs, they discovered that these needs could be met with strategies other than ending the marriage. The husband acknowledged his needs for appreciation and understanding for the stress generated by his rather demanding job; the wife recognized her needs for closeness and connection in a situation where she experienced her husband’s job occupying much of his time.

我向丈夫指出了这一点，并建议他先弄清楚自己和妻子的需求，然后再考虑“结束这段婚姻”的策略。在他们各自了解了彼此的需求之后，他们发现除了结束婚姻之外，还有其他方法可以满足这些需求。丈夫意识到，他需要妻子理解和体谅他繁忙的工作带来的压力；妻子也意识到，在丈夫工作占据了她大部分时间的情况下，她需要亲密感和情感联结。

Once they truly understood their mutual needs, this husband and wife were able to arrive at a set of agreements that satisfied both their needs while working around the demands of the husband’s job.

这对夫妻真正了解了彼此的需求后，便达成了一系列协议，既满足了双方的需求，又兼顾了丈夫的工作要求。

In the case of another couple, the lack of “needs literacy” took the form of confusion between the expression of needs and the expression of analysis, and ultimately led to their inflicting physical violence on each other. I was invited to mediate in this situation at the end of a workplace training when a man tearfully described his situation and asked if he and his wife could speak with me in private.

另一对夫妇由于缺乏“需求认知”，导致他们混淆了需求表达和分析表达，最终演变成肢体暴力。在一次职场培训结束后，我受邀介入调解此事。当时，一位男士声泪俱下地讲述了自己的遭遇，并请求我和妻子私下谈谈。

I agreed to meet them at their home, and opened the evening by saying: “I’m aware that you’re both in a lot of pain. Let’s begin with each of you expressing whatever needs of yours aren’t being fulfilled in your relationship. Once you understand each other’s needs, I’m confident we can work on strategies to meet those needs.”

我同意去他们家见面，并在当晚开场白中说道：“我知道你们俩都很痛苦。我们先从你们各自表达一下在这段关系中哪些需求没有得到满足开始。一旦你们了解了彼此的需求，我相信我们就能找到满足这些需求的策略。”

Not being “needs literate,” the husband started off by telling his wife, “The problem with you is that you’re totally insensitive to my needs.” She answered in the same manner, “That’s typical of you to say unfair things like that!”

由于不了解对方的需求，丈夫一开始就对妻子说：“你的问题在于你完全不顾及我的需求。”妻子也以同样的方式回应道：“你总是说这种不公平的话，这很符合你的性格！”

Instead of expressing needs, they were doing analysis, which is easily heard as criticism by a listener. As mentioned earlier in this book, analyses that imply wrongness are essentially tragic expressions of unmet needs. In the case of this couple, the husband had a need for support and understanding but expressed it in terms of the wife’s “insensitivity.” The wife also had a need for being accurately understood, but she expressed it in terms of the husband’s “unfairness.” It took a while to move through the layers of needs on the part of both husband and wife, but only through truly acknowledging and appreciating each other’s needs were they finally able to begin the process of exploring strategies to address their long-standing conflicts.

他们没有表达需求，而是进行分析，这很容易被听者解读为批评。正如本书前面提到的，带有错误意味的分析本质上是未被满足的需求的一种悲剧性表达。就这对夫妻而言，丈夫需要支持和理解，但他却用妻子的“冷漠”来表达。妻子也需要被准确理解，但她却用丈夫的“不公平”来表达。夫妻双方花了很长时间才理清彼此的需求，但只有真正承认并欣赏对方的需求，他们才能最终开始探索解决长期冲突的策略。

I once worked with a company where both morale and productivity took a dive due to a very disturbing conflict. Two factions in the same department were fighting over which software to use, generating strong emotions on both sides. One faction had worked especially hard to develop the software that was presently in use, and wanted to see its continued use. The other faction had strong emotions tied up in creating new software.

我曾经在一家公司工作，由于一场令人不安的冲突，公司士气和生产力都大幅下降。同一部门的两个派系为了使用哪款软件而争执不休，双方都情绪激动。其中一方曾为开发目前使用的软件付出了巨大的努力，希望继续使用它。而另一方则对开发新软件抱有强烈的热情。

I started by asking each side to tell me what needs of theirs would be better fulfilled by the software they advocated. Their response was to offer an intellectual analysis that the other side received as criticism. A member on the side that favored new software said: “We can continue to be overly conservative, but if we do that, I think we could be out of work in the future. Progress means that we take some risks, and dare to show that we are beyond old-fashioned ways of doing things.” A member of the opposing faction responded, “But I think that impulsively grabbing for every new thing that comes along is not in our best interest.” They acknowledged that they had been repeating these same analyses for months and were getting nowhere other than increasing tension for themselves.

我首先询问双方，他们各自支持的软件能更好地满足哪些需求。他们的回应是提出一些理性的分析，而对方则将这些分析视为批评。一位支持新软件的一方成员说：“我们可以继续过于保守，但如果这样做，我认为我们将来可能会失业。进步意味着我们要承担一些风险，并且敢于证明我们已经超越了老旧的做事方式。”一位反对者回应道：“但我认为，盲目地接受每一个新事物并不符合我们的最佳利益。”他们承认，几个月来他们一直在重复这些分析，但除了加剧彼此间的紧张关系之外，没有任何进展。

Intellectual analysis is often received as criticism.

理性的分析常常被视为批评。

When we don’t know how to directly and clearly express what we need, but can only make analyses of others that sound like criticism to them, wars are never far away—whether verbal, psychological, or physical.

当我们不知道如何直接、清晰地表达自己的需求，而只能对别人进行分析，而这些分析在别人看来就像是在批评别人一样时，战争——无论是言语上的、心理上的还是身体上的——都永远不会远离。

# ↩

Sensing Others’ Needs, No Matter What They’re Saying

无论别人说什么，都能感知到他们的需求

To resolve conflicts using NVC, we need to train ourselves to hear people expressing needs regardless of how they do the expressing. If we really want to be of assistance to others, the first thing to learn is to translate any message into an expression of a need. The message might take the form of silence, denial, a judgmental remark, a gesture—or, hopefully, a request. We hone our skills to hear the need within every message, even if at first we have to rely on guesses.

要运用非暴力沟通解决冲突，我们需要训练自己倾听他人表达的需求，无论他们以何种方式表达。如果我们真心想帮助他人，首先要学会的是将任何信息解读为一种需求的表达。这种需求可能以沉默、否认、评判性言论、手势——或者，我们希望看到的，一个请求——的形式出现。我们需要不断磨练自己的技能，才能听出每条信息中隐藏的需求，即使一开始我们只能依靠猜测。

For example, in the middle of a conversation, if I ask the other person something about what they’ve just said, and I am met with “That’s a stupid question,” I hear them expressing a need in the form of a judgment of me. I proceed to guess what that need might be—maybe the question I asked did not fulfill their need to be understood. Or if I ask my partner to talk about the stress in our relationship and they answer, “I don’t want to talk about it,” I may sense that their need is for protection from what they imagine could happen if we were to communicate about our relationship. So this is our work: learning to recognize the need in statements that don’t overtly express any need. It takes practice, and it always involves some guessing. Once we sense what the other person needs, we can check in with them, and then help them put their need into words. If we are able to truly hear their need, a new level of connection is forged—a critical piece that moves the conflict toward successful resolution.

例如，在谈话中，如果我问对方一些关于他们刚才所说的话的问题，而对方回答“这是个愚蠢的问题”，我就会意识到他们其实是在用一种评判的方式表达某种需求。我会尝试猜测他们的需求是什么——也许我问的问题没有满足他们被理解的需求。或者，如果我请伴侣谈谈我们关系中的压力，而他们回答“我不想谈”，我可能会感觉到他们需要的是保护，因为他们想象如果我们谈论彼此的关系，可能会发生一些不好的事情。所以，我们需要做的就是：学会识别那些表面上没有明确表达需求的话语背后隐藏的需求。这需要练习，而且总是需要一些猜测。一旦我们感知到对方的需求，就可以询问他们的想法，然后帮助他们把需求表达出来。如果我们能够真正理解他们的需求，就能建立起一种新的联结——这是推动冲突走向成功解决的关键一步。

Learn to hear needs regardless of how people express them.

学会倾听人们的需求，无论他们以何种方式表达。

In workshops for married couples, I often look for the couple with the longest unresolved conflict to demonstrate my prediction that, once each side can state the other side’s needs, it would take no more than twenty minutes for the conflict to come to a resolution. Once there was a couple whose marriage suffered thirty-nine years of conflict about money. Six months into the marriage, the wife had twice overdrawn their checking account whereupon the husband took control of the finances and would no longer let her write checks. The two of them had never stopped arguing about it since.

在为已婚夫妇举办的研讨会上，我经常会寻找那些冲突持续时间最长的夫妻，以此来验证我的预测：一旦双方都能表达出对方的需求，冲突最多只需二十分钟就能得到解决。曾经有一对夫妻，他们的婚姻因为金钱问题而持续了三十九年。结婚六个月后，妻子两次透支了银行账户，丈夫便接管了财务，不再让她开支票。从那以后，两人就一直为此争吵不休。

The wife challenged my prediction, saying that even though they had a good marriage and can communicate well, it wouldn’t be possible for their historically entrenched conflict to resolve so quickly.

妻子对我的预测提出质疑，她说，即使他们的婚姻美满，沟通良好，他们之间根深蒂固的冲突也不可能这么快得到解决。

I invited her to begin by telling me if she knew what her husband’s needs were in this conflict.

我请她先告诉我，她是否知道她丈夫在这场冲突中的需求是什么。

She replied, “He obviously doesn’t want me to spend any money.”

她回答说：“他显然不想让我花钱。”

To which her husband exclaimed: “That’s ridiculous!”

她的丈夫惊呼：“这太荒谬了！”

In stating that her husband didn’t want her to spend any money, the wife was identifying what I call a strategy. Even if she had been accurate in guessing her husband’s strategy, she had nowhere identified his need. Here again is the key distinction. By my definition, a need doesn’t refer to a specific action, such as spending or not spending money. I told the wife that all people share the same needs, and if she could only understand her husband’s needs, the issue would be resolved. When encouraged again to state her husband’s needs, she replied, “He is just like his father,” describing how his father had been reluctant to spend money. At this point, she was making an analysis.

妻子说她丈夫不想让她花钱，这其实是在指出一种我称之为“策略”的东西。即便她猜对了丈夫的策略，她也从未真正理解他的需求。关键的区别就在这里。按照我的定义，“需求”并非指具体的行动，比如花钱或不花钱。我告诉妻子，所有人都有相同的需求，如果她能理解丈夫的需求，问题就能迎刃而解。当我再次鼓励她说明丈夫的需求时，她回答说：“他跟他父亲一样”，并描述了她父亲不愿花钱的习惯。此时，她其实是在进行分析。

I stopped her to ask again, “What was his need?”

我拦住她，再次问道：“他有什么需要？”

It became clear that, even after thirty-nine years of “communicating well,” she still had no idea what his needs were.

很明显，即使经过三十九年的“良好沟通”，她仍然不知道他的需求是什么。

I then turned to the husband. “Since your wife isn’t in touch with what your needs are, why don’t you tell her? What needs are you meeting by keeping the checkbook from her?”

然后我转向丈夫说：“既然你妻子不了解你的需求，为什么不告诉她呢？你瞒着她管钱，到底满足了你什么需求呢？”

Criticism and diagnosis get in the way of peaceful resolution of conflicts.

批评和诊断会阻碍冲突的和平解决。

To which he responded, “Marshall, she’s a wonderful wife, a wonderful mother. But when it comes to money, she’s totally irresponsible.” His use of diagnosis (“She is irresponsible.”) is reflective of language that gets in the way of peaceful resolution of conflicts. When either side hears itself criticized, diagnosed, or interpreted, the energy of the situation will likely turn toward self-defense and counter-accusations rather than toward resolution.

他回应道：“马歇尔，她是个好妻子，好母亲。但说到钱，她就完全不负责任。”他使用诊断式的措辞（“她不负责任。”）反映了这种阻碍和平解决冲突的语言。当任何一方听到自己被批评、被诊断或被解读时，事态的焦点很可能会转向自我辩护和反驳，而不是寻求解决之道。

I tried to hear the feeling and need behind him stating that his wife was irresponsible: “Are you feeling scared because you have a need to protect your family economically?” He agreed that this was indeed the case. Admittedly, I had merely guessed correctly, but I didn’t have to get it right the first time because even if I had guessed wrong, I would still have been focusing on his needs—and that’s the heart of the matter. In fact, when we reflect back incorrect guesses to others, it may help them get in touch with their true needs. It takes them out of analysis toward greater connection to life.

我试图理解他指责妻子不负责任背后的感受和需求：“你是不是因为需要保护家人的经济利益而感到害怕？”他承认确实如此。诚然，我只是猜对了，但我并不需要第一次就猜对，因为即使我猜错了，我仍然关注着他的需求——而这才是问题的关键。事实上，当我们把错误的猜测反馈给别人时，或许能帮助他们更好地了解自己的真正需求。这能让他们摆脱分析的束缚，与生活建立更深层次的联系。

# ↩

Have the Needs Been Heard?

需求是否已被听到？

The husband had finally acknowledged his need: to keep his family safe. The next step is to ascertain that the wife heard that need. This is a crucial stage in conflict resolution. We must not assume that when one party expresses a need clearly, that the other party hears it accurately. I asked the wife, “Can you tell me back what you heard to be your husband’s needs in this situation?”

丈夫终于承认了自己的需求：保护家人的安全。下一步是确认妻子是否听到了这个需求。这是解决冲突的关键一步。我们不能想当然地认为，当一方清楚地表达需求时，另一方就能准确理解。我问妻子：“你能复述一下，你觉得你丈夫在这种情况下有哪些需求吗？”

“Well, just because I overdrew the bank account a couple of times, it doesn’t mean I’m going to continue doing it.”

“嗯，虽然我之前几次透支了银行账户，但这并不意味着我会继续这样做。”

Her response was not unusual. When we have pain built up over many years, it can get in the way of our ability to hear clearly, even when what is being expressed is clear to others. To continue, I said to the wife: “I’d like to tell you what I heard your husband say, and I’d like you to repeat it back. I heard that your husband says he has a need to protect the family, and he’s scared because he wants to be sure that the family is protected.”

她的反应并不奇怪。多年积压的痛苦会妨碍我们清晰地聆听，即使对方表达的意思对别人来说很清楚。于是，我继续对妻子说：“我想告诉你我听到你丈夫说的话，请你复述一遍。我听到你丈夫说他需要保护家人，他很害怕，因为他想确保家人的安全。”

# ↩

Empathy to Ease the Pain That Prevents Hearing

同理心可以减轻阻碍听力的痛苦

But she was still in too much pain to hear me. This brings up another skill that is needed if we are to effectively engage the NVC process of conflict resolution. When people are upset, they often need empathy before they can hear what is being said to them. In this instance, I changed course: instead of trying to have her repeat what her husband had said, I tried to understand the pain she was in—the pain that kept her from hearing him. Especially if there is a long history of pain, it is important to offer enough empathy so that the parties feel reassured that their pain is being recognized and understood.

但她当时仍然痛苦不堪，听不见我说话。这引出了另一个技巧，如果我们想要有效地运用非暴力沟通（NVC）来解决冲突，就必须掌握这个技巧。当人们情绪激动时，他们往往需要先获得共情，才能听清别人对他们说的话。在这种情况下，我改变了策略：我没有试图让她重复她丈夫说过的话，而是努力理解她内心的痛苦——正是这种痛苦让她无法听清丈夫的话。尤其是在长期存在痛苦的情况下，给予足够的共情至关重要，这样双方才能感到安心，确信他们的痛苦被理解和认可。

People often need empathy before they are able to hear what is being said.

人们往往需要先有同理心，才能听懂别人在说什么。

When I addressed the wife with empathy, “I sense that you’re feeling really hurt and you need to be trusted that you can learn from past experience,” the expression in her eyes showed me how much she needed that understanding. “Yes, exactly,” she replied, but when asked to repeat back what her husband had said, she answered, “He thinks I spend too much money.”

当我带着同理心对妻子说：“我感觉你真的很受伤，你需要被信任，相信你能从过去的经历中吸取教训。”她眼中的神情让我明白她多么需要这种理解。“是的，没错，”她回答道。但当被要求复述她丈夫说过的话时，她回答说：“他觉得我花钱太多了。”

Just as we are not trained to express our own needs, most of us have not been trained in hearing the needs of others. All this wife could hear was criticism or diagnosis on part of her husband. I encouraged her to try to simply hear his needs. After I repeated his need—for safety for his family—two more times, she finally was able to hear it. Then, after a few more rounds, they were both able to hear each other’s needs. And just as I had predicted, once they understood—for the first time in thirty-nine years—each other’s needs concerning the checkbook, it took less than twenty minutes to find practical ways to meet both their needs.

正如我们没有接受过如何表达自身需求的训练一样，我们大多数人也没有接受过如何倾听他人需求的训练。这位妻子只能听到丈夫的批评或指责。我鼓励她试着去倾听他的需求。在我重复了他两遍的需求——保障家人安全——之后，她终于听进去了。然后，经过几轮沟通，他们终于能够倾听彼此的需求了。正如我预料的那样，一旦他们——三十九年来第一次——理解了彼此在财务方面的需求，不到二十分钟，他们就找到了满足双方需求的切实可行的方法。

The more experience I have gained in mediating conflicts over the years and the more I’ve seen what leads families to argue and nations to go to war, the more convinced I am that most schoolchildren could solve these conflicts. If we could just say, “Here are the needs of both sides. Here are the resources. What can be done to meet these needs?,” conflicts would be easily resolved. But instead, our thinking is focused on dehumanizing one another with labels and judgments until even the simplest of conflicts becomes very difficult to solve. NVC helps us avoid that trap, thereby enhancing the chances of reaching a satisfying resolution.

多年来，我在调解冲突方面积累了越来越多的经验，也越发了解导致家庭争吵和国家开战的原因，我就越发确信，大多数小学生都能解决这些冲突。如果我们能简单地说：“这是双方的需求。这是双方拥有的资源。我们可以做些什么来满足这些需求？”，冲突就能迎刃而解。然而，我们的思维却往往局限于用标签和评判来贬低彼此，以至于即使是最简单的冲突也变得难以解决。非暴力沟通（NVC）能帮助我们避免落入这个陷阱，从而提高达成令人满意的解决方案的可能性。

# ↩

Using Present and Positive Action Language to Resolve Conflict

运用当下和积极行动语言解决冲突

Although I addressed the use of present, positive action language in Chapter 6 , I’d like to present a few more examples to demonstrate its importance in resolving conflicts. Once both parties have connected with each other’s needs, the next step is to arrive at strategies that meet those needs. It’s important to avoid moving hastily into strategies, as this may result in a compromise that lacks the deep quality of authentic resolution that is possible. By fully hearing each other’s needs before addressing solutions, parties in conflict are much more likely to adhere to the agreements they make to each other. The process of resolving conflict has to end with actions that meet everybody’s needs. It is the presentation of strategies in clear, present, positive action language that moves conflicts toward resolution.

虽然我在第六章已经探讨过使用清晰、积极的行动语言，但我还想再举几个例子来说明它在解决冲突中的重要性。一旦双方都了解了彼此的需求，下一步就是制定满足这些需求的策略。重要的是避免仓促地制定策略，因为这可能会导致最终达成的妥协缺乏真正意义上的深度解决。在讨论解决方案之前，充分倾听彼此的需求，冲突各方更有可能遵守他们达成的协议。解决冲突的过程必须以满足所有人需求的行动告终。正是用清晰、积极、积极的行动语言来呈现策略，才能推动冲突走向解决。

A present language statement refers to what is wanted at this moment. For example, one party might say, “I’d like you to tell me if you would be willing to—” and describe the action they’d like the other party to take. The use of a present language request that begins with “Would you be willing to …” helps foster a respectful discussion. If the other side answers that they are not willing, it invites the next step of understanding what prevents their willingness.

现在时态的表达方式指的是当下想要表达的意思。例如，一方可能会说：“我想请你告诉我你是否愿意——”，并描述他们希望对方采取的行动。使用以“你是否愿意……”开头的现在时态请求有助于营造尊重彼此的讨论氛围。如果对方回答不愿意，那么下一步就是了解他们不愿意的原因。

On the other hand, in the absence of present language, a request such as “I’d like you to go to the show with me Saturday night” fails to convey what’s being asked of the listener at that moment. The use of present language to hone such a request, for example, “Would you be willing to tell me whether you will go to the show with me Saturday night?,” supports clarity and ongoing connection in the exchange. We can further clarify the request by indicating what we may want from the other person in the present moment, “Would you be willing to tell me how you feel about going to the show with me Saturday night?” The clearer we are regarding the response we want right now from the other party, the more effectively we move the conflict toward resolution.

另一方面，如果缺乏当下语境，像“我想让你周六晚上和我一起去看演出”这样的请求就无法清晰地传达我们此刻想要表达的意思。使用当下语境来完善这样的请求，例如“你愿意告诉我你周六晚上是否愿意和我一起去看演出吗？”，有助于保持沟通的清晰度和持续的联系。我们还可以通过指出我们此刻想要从对方那里得到的答案来进一步明确请求，例如“你愿意告诉我你对周六晚上和我一起去看演出有什么想法吗？”我们越清楚地表达我们此刻想要从对方那里得到的答案，就越能有效地推动冲突走向解决。

# ↩

Using Action Verbs

使用行动动词

In Chapter 6 , we touched upon the role of action language in forming NVC requests. In situations of conflict, it is especially important to focus on what we do want rather than what we do not want. Talking about what one doesn’t want can easily create confusion and resistance among conflicting parties.

在第六章中，我们探讨了行动语言在非暴力沟通（NVC）请求中的作用。在冲突情境中，尤其重要的是要关注我们想要什么，而不是我们不想要什么。谈论自己不想要什么很容易在冲突各方之间造成困惑和抵触情绪。

Action language requires the use of action verbs, while also avoiding language that obscures, or language that can readily be inferred as an attack. I’d like to illustrate this with a situation where a woman expressed a need for understanding that wasn’t being met in her primary relationship. After her partner was able to accurately hear and reflect back the need for understanding, I turned to the woman and said, “Okay, let’s get down to strategies. What do you want from your partner in order to meet your need for understanding?” She faced her partner and said, “I’d like you to listen to me when I talk to you.” “I do listen to you when you talk!,” the partner retorted. It’s not unusual, if someone tells us they’d like us to listen when they are talking, for us to hear accusations and thus feel some resentment.

行动语言需要使用行动动词，同时也要避免使用含糊不清或容易被解读为攻击性的语言。我想用一个例子来说明这一点：一位女士表达了她对伴侣理解的需求，而这种需求在她的主要关系中没有得到满足。在她的伴侣能够准确地理解并回应她的需求之后，我转向这位女士说：“好了，我们来谈谈策略。你希望你的伴侣怎样做才能满足你对理解的需求？”她面对着她的伴侣说：“我希望你在我说话的时候认真听。”“你说话的时候我一直在听！”她的伴侣反驳道。如果有人告诉我们他们希望我们在他们说话的时候认真听，我们听到的往往是指责，因此感到有些不满，这并不奇怪。

Action language requires the use of action verbs.

行动语言需要使用行动动词。

They went back and forth, with the partner repeating, “I do listen,” and the woman countering, “No, you don’t.” They told me they’d had this “conversation” for twelve years, a situation that is typical in conflicts when parties use vague words like “listen” to express strategies. I suggest instead the use of action verbs to capture something that we can see or hear happening—something that can be recorded with a video camera. “Listening” occurs inside a person’s head; another person cannot see whether it is happening or not. One way to determine that someone is actually listening is to have that person reflect back what had been said: we ask the person to take an action that we ourselves can see or hear. If the other party can tell us what was just said, we know that person heard and was indeed listening to us.

他们来回争论，对方反复说着“我确实在听”，而对方则反驳道“不，你根本没听”。他们告诉我，他们已经这样“对话”了十二年，这种情况在冲突中很常见，因为双方都喜欢用“听”这类模糊的词语来表达策略。我建议他们改用行动动词，来描述我们能看到或听到的事情——比如可以用摄像机记录下来的事情。“听”发生在人的内心；别人无法看到它是否真的发生了。判断一个人是否真的在听的一种方法是让他复述刚才说过的话：我们要求他做出一个我们自己能看到或听到的行动。如果对方能够复述刚才说过的话，我们就知道他听到了，而且确实在听我们说话。

In another conflict between a husband and wife, the wife wanted to know that her husband respected her choices. Once she expressed her need successfully, her next step was to get clear on her strategy for meeting that need and to make a request of the husband. She told him, “I want you to give me the freedom to grow and be myself.” “I do,” he replied, and just as with the other couple, this was followed by a fruitless volley of “Yes, I do,” and “No, you don’t.”

在另一起夫妻冲突中，妻子希望丈夫尊重她的选择。她成功表达了自己的需求后，下一步是明确满足这一需求的策略，并向丈夫提出请求。她对丈夫说：“我希望你给我自由，让我成长，让我做我自己。” “我愿意，”他回答道。但就像另一对夫妻一样，接下来又是一连串徒劳的“是的，我愿意”和“不，你不愿意”的争论。

Non-action language, such as “Give me the freedom to grow” often exacerbates conflict. In this instance, the husband heard himself being judged as domineering. I pointed out to the wife that it wasn’t clear to her husband what she wanted: “Please tell him exactly what you’d like him to do to meet your need to have your choices respected.”

诸如“给我成长的自由”之类的空泛语言往往会加剧冲突。在这个例子中，丈夫觉得自己被评判为专横跋扈。我向妻子指出，她的丈夫并不清楚她想要什么：“请你明确地告诉他，你希望他怎么做才能满足你希望自己的选择得到尊重的需求。”

“I want you to let me—,” she began. I interrupted that “let” was too vague: “What do you really mean when you say you want somebody to ‘let’ you?”

“我希望你让我——”她刚开口，我就打断她，说“让我”这个词太笼统了：“你说你想让别人‘让我’你，你到底是什么意思？”

After reflecting for a few seconds, she arrived at an important understanding. She acknowledged that what she really meant when she said things like “I want you to let me be” and “I want you to give me the freedom to grow” is for her husband to tell her that no matter what she did, it was okay.

沉思片刻后，她恍然大悟。她意识到，当她说出“我希望你让我做自己”和“我希望你给我成长的自由”之类的话时，她真正的意思是希望丈夫告诉她，无论她做什么，都没关系。

When she got clear as to what she was actually requesting—for him to tell her something —she recognized that what she wanted did not leave him much freedom to be himself and to have his choices respected. And maintaining respect is a key element in successful conflict resolution.

当她明确自己真正想要的是什么——让他告诉她一些事情——之后，她意识到自己想要的这种做法并没有给他留下多少做自己的自由，也没有让他的选择得到尊重。而维护尊重是成功解决冲突的关键要素。

Maintaining respect is a key element in successful conflict resolution.

保持尊重是成功解决冲突的关键要素。

# ↩

Translating “No”

翻译“不”

When we express a request, it’s very important to be respectful of the other person’s reaction, whether or not they agree to our request. Many mediations I have witnessed consist of waiting for people to wear down to the point where they’ll accept any compromise. This is very different from a resolution in which everyone’s needs are met and nobody experiences loss.

当我们提出请求时，尊重对方的反应至关重要，无论他们是否同意我们的请求。我见过很多调解过程，都是等待双方忍无可忍，最终接受任何妥协方案。这与各方需求都得到满足、无人蒙受损失的解决方案截然不同。

In Chapter 8 , we discovered the importance of not hearing “no” as rejection. Listening carefully to the message behind the “no” helps us understand the other person’s needs: When they say “no,” they’re saying they have a need that keeps them from saying “yes” to what we are asking. If we can hear the need behind a “no,” we can continue the conflict resolution process—maintaining our focus on finding a way to meet everybody’s needs—even if the other party says “no” to the particular strategy we presented them.

在第八章中，我们了解到不要把“不”理解为拒绝。仔细聆听“不”背后的信息，有助于我们理解对方的需求：当他们说“不”时，他们是在表达自己的某种需求，这种需求让他们无法答应我们的请求。如果我们能够理解“不”背后的需求，即使对方对我们提出的特定策略说“不”，我们仍然可以继续推进冲突解决进程——始终专注于找到满足所有人需求的方法。

# ↩

NVC and the Mediator Role

非暴力沟通与调解员角色

Although in this chapter I have offered examples from mediations I’ve facilitated between conflicting parties, the focus so far has been on how to apply these skills when resolving conflicts between ourselves and another person. There are, however, a few things to keep in mind at those times when we want to use our NVC tools to help two other parties reach a resolution and we take on the role of mediator.

尽管本章我列举了一些我曾协助调解冲突双方的案例，但目前为止，重点在于如何运用这些技巧来解决我们自身与他人之间的冲突。然而，当我们想要运用非暴力沟通技巧帮助双方达成和解，并扮演调解人的角色时，有几点需要注意。

# ↩

Your Role, and Trust in the Process

您在过程中的角色和信任

When entering a conflict process as mediator, a good place to start might be to assure the people in conflict that we are not there to take sides, but to support them in hearing each other, and to help guide them to a solution that meets everyone’s needs. Depending on the circumstances, we may also want to convey our confidence that, if the parties follow the steps of NVC, both of their needs will be met in the end.

作为调解员介入冲突时，一个好的开端是向冲突各方保证，我们并非偏袒任何一方，而是支持他们倾听彼此，并引导他们找到一个满足各方需求的解决方案。根据具体情况，我们还可以表达我们的信心：如果各方遵循非暴力沟通的步骤，最终双方的需求都将得到满足。

# ↩

Remember: It’s Not About Us

记住：这与我们无关。

At the beginning of the chapter, I emphasized that the objective is not to get the other person to do what we want them to do. This also applies to mediating someone else’s conflict. Though we may have our own wishes for how the conflict is resolved—especially if the conflict is between family, friends, or co-workers—we need to remember that we are not here to accomplish our own goals. The mediator’s role is to create an environment in which the parties can connect, express their needs, understand each other’s needs, and arrive at strategies to meet those needs.

本章开头我强调，我们的目标并非强迫对方按照我们的意愿行事。这一点同样适用于调解他人的冲突。尽管我们可能对冲突的解决方式抱有自己的期望——尤其是在家人、朋友或同事之间——但我们必须记住，我们并非为了实现自身目标而来。调解员的角色是创造一个环境，让各方能够建立联系、表达自身需求、理解彼此的需求，并最终找到满足这些需求的策略。

The objective is not to get the parties to do what we want them to do.

我们的目标不是让各方按照我们的意愿行事。

# ↩

Emergency First-Aid Empathy

紧急急救同理心

As mediator, I stress my intention for both parties to be fully and accurately understood. Despite that, as soon as I express empathy toward one side, it is not unusual for the other side to immediately accuse me of favoritism. At this time, what’s called for is emergency first-aid empathy. This might sound like “So you’re really annoyed, and you need some assurance that you’re going to get your side on the table?”

作为调解人，我强调我的意图是让双方都得到充分、准确的理解。尽管如此，一旦我对一方表示同情，另一方往往会立即指责我偏袒。此时，最需要的是紧急的“急救式”同情。这听起来可能像是：“所以你真的很生气，需要我保证你的诉求会被摆到台面上来吗？”

Once the empathy has been expressed, I remind them that everyone will have the opportunity to be heard, and their turn will be next. It is then helpful to confirm they are in agreement with waiting by asking, for example, “Are you feeling reassured about that, or would you like more reassurance that your opportunity to be heard will come soon?”

表达完同理心后，我会提醒他们每个人都有机会发言，下一个就是他们。然后，我会询问他们是否同意等待，例如：“您对此感到放心吗？或者您是否希望我进一步保证您很快就能发言？”以此来确认他们是否同意等待。

We may need to do this repeatedly to keep the mediation on track.

为了确保调解顺利进行，我们可能需要反复这样做。

# ↩

Keep Track: Follow the Bouncing Ball

追踪：跟随弹跳球

When we are mediating, we have to “keep score” by paying careful attention to what has been said, making sure both parties have the opportunity to express their needs, listen to the other person’s needs, and make requests. We also need to “follow the bouncing ball”: being conscious of where one party left off so we can return to what that party said after the other party has been heard.

在调解过程中，我们需要“记录发言”，认真倾听双方的发言，确保双方都有机会表达自己的需求，倾听对方的需求，并提出自己的要求。我们还需要“跟进发言的进展”：时刻留意一方发言的结束位置，以便在另一方发言结束后，能够及时回到之前发言的内容。

This can be challenging, especially when things get heated. In such situations, I often find it helpful to use a white board or flip chart to capture the essence of what was spoken by the last speaker who had opportunity to express a feeling or need.

这可能颇具挑战性，尤其是在气氛紧张的时候。在这种情况下，我通常会使用白板或挂图来记录最后一位发言者表达感受或需求时的要点。

This form of visual tracking can also serve to reassure both parties that their needs will be addressed because so often before we have a chance to fully draw out one party’s needs, the other will be jumping ahead to express themselves. Taking the time to note those needs in a way that is visible to everyone present can help the listener feel comfortable that their own needs will also be addressed. In this way, everyone can more easily offer their full attention to what is being expressed in the current moment.

这种视觉追踪方式也能让双方都安心，确保他们的需求得到满足。因为很多时候，在我们有机会充分了解一方的需求之前，另一方就会抢先表达自己的想法。花时间以所有人都能看到的方式记录这些需求，可以帮助倾听者感到安心，相信自己的需求也会得到满足。这样一来，每个人都能更容易地将全部注意力集中在当下正在表达的内容上。

# ↩

Keep the Conversation in the Present

让对话保持在当下

Another important quality to bring to mediation is awareness of the moment: who needs what right now? What are their present requests? Maintaining this awareness requires a lot of practice in being present in the moment, which is something most of us have never been taught to do.

冥想中另一个重要的品质是对当下的觉察：谁现在需要什么？他们目前的需求是什么？保持这种觉察需要大量的练习才能真正活在当下，而这正是我们大多数人从未被教导过的。

As we move through the mediation process, it is likely that we will hear a lot of discussion about what happened in the past and what people want to happen differently in the future. However, conflict resolution can only happen right now, so now is where we need to focus.

在调解过程中，我们可能会听到很多关于过去发生的事情以及人们希望未来如何改变的讨论。然而，冲突的解决只能在当下进行，所以我们现在需要关注的是当下。

# ↩

Keep Things Moving

保持运转

Another mediation task is to keep the conversation from getting bogged down; this can happen very easily, as people often think that if they just tell that same story one more time, they will finally be understood and the other person will do what they want.

调解的另一项任务是防止谈话陷入僵局；这种情况很容易发生，因为人们常常认为，如果他们再把同样的故事讲一遍，他们最终就会被理解，对方也会按照他们的意愿行事。

To keep things moving, the mediator needs to ask effective questions, and when necessary, maintain or even speed up the pace. Once, when I was scheduled to lead a workshop in a small town, the event organizer asked if I would help him with a personal dispute related to the division of family property. I agreed to mediate, aware there was only a three-hour window in between workshops to do so.

为了推动调解进程，调解员需要提出有效的问题，并在必要时保持甚至加快节奏。有一次，我受邀在一个小镇主持一个研讨会，活动组织者问我是否愿意帮他处理一起与家庭财产分割有关的私人纠纷。我同意了，尽管我知道研讨会之间只有三个小时的空档时间。

The family dispute centered on a man who owned a large farm and was about to retire. His two sons were at war over how the property was to be divided. They hadn’t spoken in eight years even though they lived close to each other at the same end of the farm. I met the brothers, their wives, and their sister, all of whom were involved in this set of complicated legal matters and eight years of pain.

这场家庭纠纷的起因是一位即将退休的大农场主。他的两个儿子为了财产分割问题争执不休。尽管他们住在农场同一侧，彼此距离很近，却已经八年没有说过话了。我见到了这对兄弟、他们的妻子和妹妹，所有人都卷入了这桩错综复杂的法律纠纷，承受了八年的痛苦。

In order to get things moving—and to stay on schedule—I had to speed up the mediation process. To keep them from spending time telling the same stories over and over, I asked one of the brothers if I could play his role; then I would switch and play the part of the other brother.

为了推动事情进展并按计划进行，我不得不加快调解进程。为了避免他们反复讲述同样的故事，我问其中一位兄弟是否可以扮演他的角色；然后我再交换角色，扮演另一位兄弟。

Use role-play to speed up the mediation process.

运用角色扮演来加快调解过程。

As I was going through my role-play, I joked about wanting to see if I was playing the part right by asking if I could check in with my “director.” Looking over at the brother whose part I had been playing, I saw something I wasn’t prepared for: he had tears in his eyes. I guessed that he was experiencing deep empathy, both with himself from my playing his role, as well as for his brother’s pain, which he had not seen until then. The next day, the father approached me, also with tearful eyes, to say that the night before the whole family had gone out to dinner for the first time in eight years. Though the conflict had persisted for years, with lawyers on both sides working unsuccessfully to come to agreement, it became simple to resolve once the brothers heard each other’s pain and needs as revealed through the role-playing. If I had waited for both of them to tell their stories, the resolution would have taken much longer.

在角色扮演的过程中，我开玩笑说想看看自己演得对不对，于是问“导演”能不能给我点意见。我瞥了一眼扮演我哥哥的那位，却看到了意想不到的一幕：他眼里噙着泪水。我猜想，他当时既感同身受，既体会到我扮演他角色时自己内心的感受，也体会到他哥哥的痛苦——他之前从未见过哥哥的痛苦。第二天，父亲也含着泪走过来告诉我，前一天晚上，全家人八年来第一次一起出去吃饭。虽然这场冲突持续多年，双方律师也都试图调解却始终无果，但当兄弟俩通过角色扮演了解了彼此的痛苦和需求后，问题就迎刃而解了。如果我等到他们各自讲述自己的故事，解决问题恐怕要花更长的时间。

When relying on this method, I periodically turn to the person whose role I’m playing, addressing them as “my director” to see how I am doing. For a while I thought I had acting talent because of how often I find them crying and saying, “That’s exactly what I’ve been trying to say!” However, when I started training others in role-playing, I now know that any of us can do it as long as we are in touch with our own needs. No matter what else is going on, we all have the same needs. Needs are universal.

在使用这种方法时，我会时不时地转向我扮演的角色，称呼他们为“我的导演”，询问我的表演如何。有一段时间，我以为自己很有表演天赋，因为我经常看到他们哭着说：“这正是我一直想表达的！” 然而，当我开始训练其他人进行角色扮演时，我意识到，只要我们了解自己的需求，任何人都可以做到。无论发生什么，我们都有相同的需求。需求是普遍存在的。

I sometimes work with people who have been raped or tortured and where the perpetrator is absent, I would assume their role.

我有时会与遭受强奸或酷刑的人一起工作，如果施暴者不在场，我会承担起他们的责任。

Oftentimes the victim is surprised to hear me in the role-play saying the same thing they had heard from their perpetrator, and press me with the question, “But how did you know?” I believe the answer to that question is that I know because I am that person. And so are we all. As we apply a literacy of feelings and needs, we are not thinking about the issues, but simply putting ourselves in the other person’s shoes, trying to be that person. “Getting the part right” is not in our thoughts, although from time to time we check in with the “director” because we don’t always get it right. Nobody gets it right all the time, and that’s fine. If we’re off the mark, the person whom we are playing will let us know one way or another. We are thus offered another opportunity to make a closer guess.

很多时候，受害者听到我在角色扮演中说出他们从施暴者那里听到的同样的话时，都会感到惊讶，并追问我：“你怎么知道的？” 我相信答案是，我知道，因为我就是那个人。我们所有人都是如此。当我们运用对情感和需求的理解力时，我们并非在思考具体的问题，而是设身处地地站在对方的角度，努力成为那个人。“完美演绎”并非我们的目标，尽管我们偶尔会向“导演”确认，因为我们并非总能做到完美。没有人能永远做到完美，这很正常。如果我们偏离了主题，我们扮演的人会以某种方式让我们知道。这样，我们就有了再次尝试的机会，可以做出更准确的判断。

Role-play is simply putting ourselves in the other person’s shoes.

角色扮演就是把自己置于对方的位置上。

# ↩

Interrupting

打断

Sometimes mediations get heated, with people shouting at or talking over one another. To keep the process on track under such circumstances, we need to get comfortable with interrupting.
