Once when I was mediating in Israel, and having a difficult time because my translator was too polite, I finally taught him to be nasty: “Shut them up!,” I instructed. “Tell them to wait until we at least get the translation out before they go back to screaming at each other.” So when both sides are screaming or talking at the same time, I insert myself: “Excuse me, excuse me, excuse me!” I repeat this as loudly and as often as necessary until I regain their attention.

有时调解会变得激烈，人们互相叫喊或打断对方说话。为了在这种情况下保持调解进程顺利进行，我们需要习惯于打断对方。有一次我在以色列调解时，我的翻译过于客气，导致调解工作进展不顺。最后，我教他如何“粗鲁”一点：“让他们闭嘴！”我指示道，“告诉他们至少等到我们把翻译出来之后再继续互相叫喊。”所以，当双方同时叫喊或说话时，我会插话：“打扰一下，打扰一下，打扰一下！”我会反复大声地说，直到重新引起他们的注意。

When we are grabbing their attention, we have to be quick. If the person reacts with anger when we interrupt, we can sense that they are in too much pain to hear us. This is the time for emergency first-aid empathy. Here is what it might sound like, using an example from a business meeting.

当我们试图引起对方的注意时，必须迅速行动。如果我们打断对方后，对方表现出愤怒，这可能意味着他们正承受着巨大的痛苦，根本听不到我们说话。这时，我们需要运用紧急的同理心来表达我们的同情。下面举一个商务会议的例子，说明这种同理心的运用方式。

Speaker:
扬声器： 		This happens all the time! They’ve already called three meetings, and each time there is some new rationale as to why it can’t be done. Last time they even signed an agreement! Now another promise and it will be just that: another promise! There’s little point in working with people who …
这种事屡见不鲜！他们已经开了三次会，每次都有新的理由推脱。上次他们甚至还签了协议！现在又是一个空头支票，也只会是空头支票！跟这种人合作毫无意义……
Mediator:
调解员： 		Excuse me, excuse me, EXCUSE ME! Could you tell me back what the other person said?
打扰一下，打扰一下，打扰一下！你能告诉我对方说了什么吗？
Speaker:
扬声器： 		(realizing he had not listened to what had been said) No!
（意识到自己没有听进去别人说的话）不！
Mediator:
调解员： 		So you’re feeling so full of distrust right now and really need some trust that people will do what they say?
所以你现在感到非常不信任别人，真的很需要信任别人会说到做到？
Speaker:
扬声器： 		Well, of course but …
当然，但是……
Mediator:
调解员： 		So could you tell me what you heard them say? Let me repeat it for you. I hear the other side saying they have a real need for integrity. Could you just say it back so I’m sure we all understand each other?
所以，你能告诉我你听到他们说了什么吗？我再重复一遍。我听到对方说他们非常需要诚信。你能再说一遍吗？这样我们才能确保彼此都听懂。
Speaker:
扬声器： 		(silence)
（沉默）
Mediator:
调解员： 		No? Then let me say it again. And we say it again.
不？那我再说一遍。我们再说一遍。

We might view our role as that of a translator—translating each party’s message so as to be understood by the other. I ask them to get used to my interrupting for the sake of resolving the conflict. When I do interrupt, I also check that the speaker feels that I’m translating them accurately. I translate many messages even if I am only guessing, but the speaker is always the final authority on the accuracy of my translation.

我们可以把自己看作是翻译者——翻译每一方的信息，以便对方能够理解。我请他们习惯我为了解决冲突而打断他们。当我打断时，我也会确认说话者是否觉得我的翻译准确。即使我只是猜测，我也会翻译很多信息，但说话者始终是我翻译准确性的最终权威。

It’s important to remember that the purpose of interrupting and grabbing people’s attention back in this way is to restore the process of making observations, identifying and expressing feelings, connecting feelings with needs, and making doable requests using clear, concrete, positive action language.

重要的是要记住，以这种方式打断并重新吸引人们的注意力，是为了恢复观察、识别和表达感受、将感受与需求联系起来以及使用清晰、具体、积极的行动语言提出可行请求的过程。

The purpose of interrupting is to restore the process.

中断的目的是为了恢复进程。

# ↩

When People Say “No” to Meeting Face to Face

当人们对面对面会面说“不”时

I am optimistic about what can happen when we bring people together to express their needs and requests. However, one of the biggest problems I’ve encountered is simply getting access to both parties. Because it occasionally takes time for a party to become clear about its own needs, mediators require adequate access in order for both parties to express, and then receive each other’s needs. Oftentimes, what we hear from someone in conflict is: “No, there’s no use talking—they won’t listen. I’ve tried to talk and it doesn’t work.”

我对促成各方沟通、表达需求和诉求的结果持乐观态度。然而，我遇到的最大难题之一就是如何接触到双方。因为有时一方需要时间才能清晰地表达自己的需求，所以调解员需要充分的沟通渠道，才能让双方表达并理解彼此的需求。我们经常听到冲突中的一方说：“不，沟通没用——他们根本不听。我试过了，但没用。”

To solve this problem I’ve sought strategies to resolve conflicts where people in conflict are unwilling to meet. One method that shows promising results relies on the use of an audio recorder. I work with each party separately while playing the role of the other side. If there are two people in our own lives who are in too much pain to be willing to meet, this would be an option for us to consider.

为了解决这个问题，我一直在寻找能够化解冲突双方不愿见面的策略。其中一种效果显著的方法是使用录音设备。我会分别与双方沟通，同时扮演对方的角色。如果我们生活中也有两个人因为痛苦而不愿见面，这或许是一个值得考虑的选择。

As an example, a woman was suffering heavily from a conflict with her husband, particularly from the way he was directing anger toward her. First, I listened in a way that supported her to clearly express her needs and to experience being received with respectful understanding. Then, I took on the role of her husband, and asked her to listen to me as I expressed what I guessed to be the husband’s needs.

举例来说，一位女士正饱受与丈夫冲突的折磨，尤其难以忍受丈夫对她发泄怒气。首先，我倾听她的诉说，支持她清晰地表达自己的需求，并让她感受到被尊重和理解。然后，我扮演她丈夫的角色，请她听我解释我推测的丈夫的需求。

The needs of the conflicting parties having been clearly conveyed in this role-play, I asked the woman to share the recording with her husband for his reaction.

在这次角色扮演中，冲突各方的需求都得到了清晰的表达，于是我请这位女士将录音分享给她的丈夫，看看他的反应。

Because I had, in this case, been accurate in guessing the husband’s needs, he experienced huge relief when listening to the recording. With the increased trust that came from hearing himself understood, he later agreed to come in so we could work together until the two of them found ways of meeting their needs in mutually respectful ways.

因为我这次准确地猜到了丈夫的需求，所以他在听完录音后如释重负。听到自己被理解，他更加信任我，后来同意过来，我们一起努力，直到他们找到彼此尊重、满足需求的方法。

When the hardest thing about resolving a conflict is getting the parties together in the same room, the use of recorded role-plays may be the answer.

当解决冲突最困难的地方在于让各方坐在一起时，录制角色扮演视频或许能解决问题。

# ↩

Informal Mediation: Sticking Our Nose in Other People’s Business

非正式调解：干涉他人事务

Informal mediation is a polite way to refer to mediating in situations where we’ve not been invited to do so. In so many words, we’re sticking our nose in other people’s business.

非正式调解是一种委婉的说法，指的是在未经邀请的情况下进行调解。说白了，就是我们多管闲事。

I was shopping in a grocery store one day when I saw a woman strike her toddler. She was about to do it again when I jumped in. She didn’t ask, “Marshall, would you mediate between us?” Another time I was walking in the streets of Paris; a woman was walking alongside me when a rather inebriated man ran up from behind, turned her around, and slapped her in the face. As there wasn’t time for me to talk with this man, I resorted to the protective use of force by restraining him just as he was about to strike her again. I inserted myself between the two, and stuck my nose in their business. On another occasion, during a business meeting, I watched two factions in a repetitious exchange, arguing back and forth over an age-old issue and again I stuck my nose in between them.

有一天我在超市购物，看到一个女人打她的小孩。她正要再打一次，我赶紧上前制止。她并没有问我：“马歇尔，你能来调解一下吗？”还有一次，我在巴黎街头散步，一个女人走在我旁边，一个醉醺醺的男人从后面冲过来，把她转过来，扇了她一巴掌。我没时间跟那个男人说话，只好采取保护性武力，在他再次要打那个女人之前制止了他。我挡在两人中间，插手了他们的事。还有一次，在一次商务会议上，我看到两派人就一个老生常谈的问题争论不休，我又一次插手了。

When we witness behaviors that raise concern in us—unless it is a situation that calls for the protective use of force as described in Chapter 12 —the first thing we do is to empathize with the needs of the person who is behaving in the way we dislike. In the first situation, if we wanted to see more violence directed at the toddler, we could, instead of offering empathy to the mother, say something to imply that she was wrong to hit the child. Such a response on our part would only escalate the situation.

当我们目睹令我们担忧的行为时——除非是第十二章所述的需要使用武力保护的情况——我们首先应该做的是理解并同情做出我们不喜欢的行为的人的需求。在第一个例子中，如果我们想看到对幼儿施加更多暴力，我们不应该对母亲表示同情，而是会说些暗示她打孩子是错误的话语。我们这样的反应只会使情况升级。

We need to be well practiced at hearing the need in any message.

我们需要熟练地辨别任何信息中的需求。

In order to be truly helpful to people in whose business we are sticking our nose we need to have developed an extensive literacy regarding needs, and be well practiced at hearing the need in any message, including the need underneath the act of slapping another person. And we need to be practiced in verbal empathy such that the people sense that we are connected with their need.

为了真正帮助我们插手他人事务的人，我们需要对各种需求有深入的了解，并熟练地倾听任何信息背后的需求，包括打人行为背后隐藏的需求。此外，我们还需要练习语言上的同理心，让人们感受到我们与他们的需求息息相关。

We need to remember, when we choose to stick our nose in someone’s business, it’s not enough to simply support someone to get in touch with his or her own needs. We aim to practice all the other steps covered in this chapter. For example, after empathizing, we may tell the toddler’s mother that we care about safety and have a need to protect people, and then request her willingness to try another strategy to meet her need with her child.

我们需要记住，当我们选择介入他人事务时，仅仅帮助对方了解自身需求是不够的。我们的目标是实践本章中提到的所有其他步骤。例如，在表达同理心之后，我们可以告诉幼儿的母亲，我们关心孩子的安全，并且有责任保护他人，然后询问她是否愿意尝试其他方法来满足她对孩子的需求。

We refrain, however, from mentioning our own needs regarding the person’s behavior until it is clear to them that we understand and care about his or her needs. Otherwise people will not care about our needs nor will they see that their needs and ours are one and the same. As expressed so beautifully by Alice Walker in The Color Purple: “One day when I was sitting quiet and feeling like a motherless child, which I was, it come to me: that feeling of being part of everything, not separate at all. I knew that if I cut a tree, my arm would bleed.”

然而，在对方确信我们理解并关心他们的需求之前，我们不会提及我们自身对对方行为的需求。否则，人们不会关心我们的需求，也不会意识到他们的需求与我们的需求其实是一致的。正如爱丽丝·沃克在《紫色》中优美地描述的那样：“有一天，我静静地坐着，感觉自己像个失去母亲的孩子——而我的确如此——这时我突然明白了：我感觉自己是万物的一部分，而不是与万物分离。我知道，如果我砍倒一棵树，我的手臂就会流血。”

Unless we make sure that both sides are aware of their own as well as each other’s needs, it will be hard for us to succeed when we stick our nose in other people’s business. We are likely to get caught up in scarcity thinking—seeing only the importance of our own needs being met. When scarcity thinking then gets mixed with right-and-wrong thinking, any of us can become militant and violent, and blinded to even the most obvious solutions. At that point, the conflict seems unresolvable—and it will be if we don’t connect with the other person by first offering empathy without focusing on our own needs.

除非我们确保双方都清楚彼此的需求，否则当我们插手他人事务时，很难取得成功。我们很可能陷入匮乏思维——只看到满足自身需求的重要性。当匮乏思维与非黑即白的思维混杂在一起时，我们任何人都可能变得好斗甚至暴力，对最显而易见的解决方案视而不见。那时，冲突似乎无法解决——如果我们不先表达同理心，而不是只关注自身需求，那么冲突就真的无法解决。

# ↩

Summary

概括

The use of NVC to resolve conflict differs from traditional mediation methods; instead of deliberating over issues, strategies, and means of compromise, we concentrate foremost on identifying the needs of both parties, and only then seek strategies to fulfill those needs.

非暴力沟通解决冲突的方式与传统的调解方法不同；我们首先关注的是找出双方的需求，而不是讨论问题、策略和妥协手段，然后再寻求满足这些需求的策略。

We start by forging a human connection between the parties in conflict. Then we ensure that both parties have the opportunity to fully express their needs, that they carefully listen to the other person’s needs, and that once the needs have been heard, they clearly express doable action steps to meet those needs. We avoid judging or analyzing the conflict and instead remain focused on needs.

我们首先在冲突双方之间建立人与人之间的联系。然后，我们确保双方都有机会充分表达自己的需求，认真倾听对方的需求，并在需求被了解后，清晰地提出切实可行的行动步骤来满足这些需求。我们避免评判或分析冲突，而是始终专注于需求本身。

When one party is in too much pain to hear the needs of the other, we extend empathy, taking as long as necessary to ensure that the person knows their pain is heard. We do not hear “no” as a rejection but rather as an expression of the need that is keeping the person from saying “yes.” Only after all needs have been mutually heard, do we progress to the solutions stage: making doable requests using positive, action language.

当一方因痛苦难耐而无法倾听另一方的需求时，我们会给予对方充分的理解和同情，不厌其烦地倾听，确保对方感受到我们的理解。我们不会将“不”视为拒绝，而是将其理解为对方无法说“是”的原因。只有在双方都充分理解彼此的需求之后，我们才会进入解决方案阶段：用积极、行动导向的语言提出切实可行的请求。

When we assume the role of mediating a conflict between two other parties, the same principles apply. In addition, we keep careful track of progress, extend empathy where needed, keep the conversation focused on the present, moving it forward, and interrupting where necessary to return to the process.

当我们扮演调解双方冲突的角色时，同样的原则也适用。此外，我们还要密切关注进展，在必要时表达同理心，确保对话聚焦于当下，推动事态发展，并在必要时及时打断，使对话回到正轨。

With these tools and understanding, we can practice and help others resolve even long-standing conflicts to their mutual satisfaction.

借助这些工具和知识，我们可以练习并帮助他人解决长期存在的冲突，从而达到双方都满意的结果。

# ↩

12

The Protective Use of Force

保护性武力使用

When the Use of Force Is Unavoidable

当使用武力不可避免时

W hen two disputing parties have each had an opportunity to fully express what they are observing, feeling, needing, and requesting—and each has empathized with the other—a resolution can usually be reached that meets the needs of both sides. At the very least, the two can agree, in goodwill, to disagree.

当争端双方都有机会充分表达自己的观察、感受、需求和请求，并且彼此都理解对方的立场后，通常可以达成一个满足双方需求的解决方案。至少，双方可以本着善意，同意彼此保留意见。

In some situations, however, the opportunity for such dialogue may not exist, and the use of force may be necessary to protect life or individual rights. For instance, the other party may be unwilling to communicate, or imminent danger may not allow time for communication. In these situations, we may need to resort to force. If we do, NVC requires us to differentiate between the protective and the punitive uses of force.

然而，在某些情况下，对话的机会可能并不存在，为了保护生命或个人权利，使用武力或许是必要的。例如，对方可能不愿沟通，或者迫在眉睫的危险不允许我们进行沟通。在这些情况下，我们可能需要诉诸武力。如果确实如此，非暴力沟通要求我们区分保护性武力和惩罚性武力。

# ↩

The Thinking Behind the Use of Force

使用武力的思考

The intention behind the protective use of force is to prevent injury or injustice. The intention behind the punitive use of force is to cause individuals to suffer for their perceived misdeeds. When we grab a child who is running into the street to prevent the child from being injured, we are applying protective force. The punitive use of force, on the other hand, might involve physical or psychological attack, such as spanking the child or saying, “How could you be so stupid! You should be ashamed of yourself!”

保护性武力使用的目的是防止伤害或不公正行为。惩罚性武力使用的目的是让个人为其被认为的过错付出代价。当我们抓住一个跑到街上的孩子以防止他受伤时，我们是在运用保护性武力。另一方面，惩罚性武力使用可能涉及身体或心理上的攻击，例如打孩子屁股或说：“你怎么这么蠢！你应该感到羞耻！”

When we exercise the protective use of force, we are focusing on the life or rights we want to protect, without passing judgment on either the person or the behavior. We are not blaming or condemning the child who rushes into the street; our thinking is solely directed toward protecting the child from danger. (For application of this kind of force in social and political conflicts, see Robert Irwin’s book, Building a Peace System.) The assumption behind the protective use of force is that people behave in ways injurious to themselves and others due to some form of ignorance. The corrective process is therefore one of education, not punishment. Ignorance includes (1) a lack of awareness of the consequences of our actions, (2) an inability to see how our needs may be met without injury to others, (3) the belief that we have the right to punish or hurt others because they “deserve” it, and (4) delusional thinking that involves, for example, hearing a voice that instructs us to kill someone.

当我们行使保护性武力时，我们关注的是我们想要保护的生命或权利，而不是对当事人或行为本身做出评判。我们不会责备或谴责冲到街上的孩子；我们的想法完全集中于保护孩子免受危险。（关于此类武力在社会和政治冲突中的应用，请参阅罗伯特·欧文的著作《构建和平体系》。）保护性武力的前提假设是，人们之所以会做出伤害自己和他人的行为，是出于某种形式的无知。因此，纠正过程是教育，而非惩罚。无知包括：（1）缺乏对自身行为后果的认识；（2）无法理解如何在不伤害他人的情况下满足自身需求；（3）认为我们有权惩罚或伤害他人，因为他们“罪有应得”；以及（4）妄想思维，例如听到一个声音指示我们杀人。

The intention behind the protective use of force is only to protect, not to punish, blame, or condemn.

使用武力进行保护的目的仅仅是为了保护，而不是为了惩罚、责备或谴责。

Punitive action, on the other hand, is based on the assumption that people commit offenses because they are bad or evil, and to correct the situation, they need to be made to repent. Their “correction” is undertaken through punitive action designed to make them (1) suffer enough to see the error of their ways, (2) repent, and (3) change. In practice, however, punitive action, rather than evoking repentance and learning, is just as likely to generate resentment and hostility and to reinforce resistance to the very behavior we are seeking.

另一方面，惩罚性措施基于这样的假设：人们犯罪是因为他们本性邪恶，为了纠正这种情况，需要让他们忏悔。这种“纠正”是通过惩罚性措施来实现的，旨在让他们（1）遭受足够的痛苦以认识到自己的错误，（2）忏悔，以及（3）改变。然而，在实践中，惩罚性措施非但不会引起忏悔和学习，反而更有可能引发怨恨和敌意，并加剧人们对我们所寻求的行为的抵触情绪。

# ↩

Types of Punitive Force

惩罚性武力的类型

Physical punishment, such as spanking, is one punitive use of force. I have found the subject of corporal punishment to provoke strong sentiments among parents. Some adamantly defend the practice, referring to the Bible: “Spare the rod, spoil the child. It’s because parents don’t spank that delinquency is now rampant.” They are persuaded that spanking our children shows that we love them by setting clear boundaries. Other parents are equally insistent that spanking is unloving and ineffective because it teaches children that, when all else fails, we can always resort to physical violence.

体罚，例如打屁股，是一种惩罚性的暴力行为。我发现体罚这个话题在父母中引发了强烈的反响。一些父母坚决捍卫这种做法，并引用《圣经》：“棍棒底下出孝子。正是因为父母不打孩子，现在青少年犯罪才如此猖獗。”他们认为，打孩子能通过设定明确的界限来表达爱意。而另一些父母则同样坚持认为，打孩子既不爱孩子，也无效，因为它会让孩子觉得，当其他方法都无效时，我们还可以诉诸暴力。

My personal concern is that children’s fear of corporal punishment may obscure their awareness of the compassion that underlies parental demands. Parents often tell me that they “have to” use punitive force because they see no other way to influence their children to do “what’s good for them.” They support their opinion with anecdotes of children expressing appreciation for “seeing the light” after having been punished. Having raised four children, I empathize deeply with parents regarding the daily challenges they face in educating children and keeping them safe. This does not, however, lessen my concern about the use of physical punishment.

我个人担心的是，孩子们对体罚的恐惧可能会蒙蔽他们对父母要求背后所蕴含的关爱的感知。父母们经常告诉我，他们“不得不”使用惩罚手段，因为他们找不到其他方法来引导孩子去做“对他们有益的事”。他们还会举一些例子来佐证自己的观点，比如孩子在受到惩罚后“幡然醒悟”，并表达感激之情。作为四个孩子的养育者，我深切理解父母们在教育和保护孩子方面每天所面临的挑战。但这并不能减轻我对体罚的担忧。

Fear of corporal punishment obscures children’s awareness of the compassion underlying their parents’ demands.

对体罚的恐惧蒙蔽了孩子们的双眼，使他们无法意识到父母要求背后所蕴含的关爱。

First, I wonder whether people who proclaim the successes of such punishment are aware of the countless instances of children who turn against what might be good for them simply because they choose to fight, rather than succumb, to coercion. Second, the apparent success of corporal punishment in influencing a child doesn’t mean that other methods of influence wouldn’t have worked equally well. Finally, I share the concerns of many parents about the social consequences of using physical punishment. When parents opt to use force, we may win the battle of getting children to do what we want, but, in the process, are we not perpetuating a social norm that justifies violence as a means of resolving differences?

首先，我怀疑那些宣称体罚有效的人是否意识到，无数孩子仅仅因为选择反抗而非屈服于胁迫，就违背了原本可能对他们有益的原则。其次，体罚在影响孩子方面看似有效，并不意味着其他影响方式就一定无效。最后，我和许多家长一样，对体罚的社会后果感到担忧。当家长选择使用武力时，我们或许能够让孩子听话，但在这个过程中，我们是否也在助长一种将暴力作为解决分歧手段的社会规范呢？

In addition to the physical, other uses of force also qualify as punishment. One is the use of blame to discredit another person; for example, a parent may label a child as “wrong,” “selfish,” or “immature” when a child doesn’t behave in a certain way. Another form of punitive force is the withholding of some means of gratification, such as parents’ curtailing allowances or driving privileges. In this vein, the withdrawal of caring or respect is one of the most powerful threats of all.

除了体罚之外，其他形式的暴力也构成惩罚。其中之一是利用指责来贬低他人；例如，当孩子没有按照某种方式行事时，父母可能会给孩子贴上“错误”、“自私”或“不成熟”的标签。另一种惩罚性暴力形式是剥夺某些满足感，例如父母减少零用钱或驾驶特权。从这个意义上讲，剥夺关爱或尊重是最强大的威胁之一。

Punishment also includes judgmental labeling and the withholding of privileges.

惩罚还包括贴上带有评判性的标签和剥夺特权。

# ↩

The Costs of Punishment

惩罚的代价

When we submit to doing something solely for the purpose of avoiding punishment, our attention is distracted from the value of the action itself. Instead, we are focusing upon the consequences, on what might happen if we fail to take that action. If a worker’s performance is prompted by fear of punishment, the job gets done, but morale suffers; sooner or later, productivity will decrease. Self-esteem is also diminished when punitive force is used. If children brush their teeth because they fear shame and ridicule, their oral health may improve but their self-respect will develop cavities. Furthermore, as we all know, punishment is costly in terms of goodwill. The more we are seen as agents of punishment, the harder it is for others to respond compassionately to our needs.

当我们仅仅为了避免惩罚而去做某件事时，我们的注意力就会从行为本身的价值上转移开来。相反，我们会关注后果，关注如果我们不采取行动会发生什么。如果员工的绩效是出于对惩罚的恐惧，工作虽然能完成，但士气会受到打击；迟早，生产力会下降。使用惩罚手段也会损害自尊。如果孩子因为害怕羞辱和嘲笑而刷牙，他们的口腔健康或许会改善，但他们的自尊心却会受到损害。此外，我们都知道，惩罚会损害他人的善意。我们越是被视为惩罚的执行者，他人就越难对我们的需求给予同情和回应。

When we fear punishment, we focus on consequences, not on our own values.

当我们害怕惩罚时，我们关注的是后果，而不是我们自身的价值观。

Fear of punishment diminishes self-esteem and goodwill.

对惩罚的恐惧会降低自尊和善意。

I was visiting a friend, a school principal, at his office when he noticed through the window a big child hitting a smaller one. “Excuse me,” he said as he leapt up and rushed to the playground. Grabbing the larger child, he gave him a swat and scolded, “I’ll teach you not to hit smaller people!” When the principal returned inside, I remarked, “I don’t think you taught that child what you thought you were teaching him. I suspect what he learned instead was not to hit people smaller than he is when somebody bigger—like the principal—might be watching! If anything, it seems to me that you have reinforced the notion that the way to get what you want from somebody else is to hit them.”

我去拜访一位朋友，他是一位小学校长，当时正在他的办公室里。他透过窗户看到一个大孩子在打一个小孩子。“不好意思，”他一边说着，一边跳起来冲到操场上。他抓住那个大孩子，狠狠地打了他一下，训斥道：“我要教训你，让你知道不该打比自己小的人！”校长回到办公室后，我说道：“我觉得你教给那个孩子的东西和你以为的完全不一样。我怀疑他学到的却是，在像校长这样比自己大的人面前，不能打比自己小的人！在我看来，你反而强化了‘想要得到什么就打人’这种观念。”

In such situations, I recommend first empathizing with the child who is behaving violently. For example, if I saw a child hit someone after being called a name, I might empathize, “I’m sensing that you’re feeling angry because you’d like to be treated with more respect.” If I guessed correctly, and the child acknowledges this to be true, I would then continue by expressing my own feelings, needs, and requests in the situation without insinuating blame: “I’m feeling sad because I want us to find ways to get respect that don’t turn people into enemies. I’d like you to tell me if you’d be willing to explore with me some other ways to get the respect you’re wanting.”

在这种情况下，我建议首先要理解那个有暴力行为的孩子。例如，如果我看到一个孩子因为被辱骂而打人，我可能会这样说：“我感觉你生气是因为你想得到更多的尊重。”如果我的判断正确，孩子也承认这一点，那么我接下来会表达我自己的感受、需求和请求，但不会指责孩子：“我很难过，因为我希望我们能找到一些既能获得尊重又不会让别人反目成仇的方法。我想问问你是否愿意和我一起探讨一些其他获得你渴望的尊重的方法。”

# ↩

Two Questions That Reveal the Limitations of Punishment

揭示惩罚局限性的两个问题

Two questions help us see why we are unlikely to get what we want by using punishment to change people’s behavior. The first question is: What do I want this person to do that’s different from what he or she is currently doing? If we ask only this first question, punishment may seem effective, because the threat or exercise of punitive force may well influence someone’s behavior. However, with the second question, it becomes evident that punishment isn’t likely to work: What do I want this person’s reasons to be for doing what I’m asking?

有两个问题可以帮助我们理解为什么通过惩罚来改变人们的行为不太可能达到我们想要的效果。第一个问题是：我希望这个人做什么，才能与他/她目前的行为有所不同？如果我们只问第一个问题，惩罚似乎有效，因为惩罚的威胁或实施确实可能影响某人的行为。然而，第二个问题就清楚地表明惩罚不太可能奏效：我希望这个人做我要求的事情的理由是什么？

We seldom address the latter question, but when we do, we soon realize that punishment and reward interfere with people’s ability to do things motivated by the reasons we’d like them to have. I believe it is critical to be aware of the importance of people’s reasons for behaving as we request. For example, blaming or punishing would obviously not be effective strategies if we want children to clean their rooms out of either a desire for order or a desire to contribute to their parents’ enjoyment of order. Often children clean their rooms motivated by obedience to authority (“Because my Mom said so”), avoidance of punishment, or fear of upsetting or being rejected by parents. NVC, however, fosters a level of moral development based on autonomy and interdependence, whereby we acknowledge responsibility for our own actions and are aware that our own well-being and that of others are one and the same.

我们很少讨论后一个问题，但一旦讨论，我们很快就会意识到，惩罚和奖励会干扰人们出于我们希望他们拥有的理由而行事的能力。我认为，意识到人们按照我们的要求行事的理由至关重要。例如，如果我们希望孩子出于对秩序的渴望或为了让父母享受秩序而打扫房间，那么责备或惩罚显然不是有效的策略。孩子们打扫房间的动机通常是服从权威（“因为妈妈这么说”）、避免惩罚，或害怕惹父母生气或被父母拒绝。然而，非暴力沟通（NVC）培养了一种基于自主性和相互依存的道德发展水平，在这种水平上，我们承认自己对自身行为的责任，并意识到我们自身的福祉与他人的福祉是一体的。

Question 1: What do I want this person to do?

问题 1：我希望这个人做什么？

Question 2: What do I want this person’s reasons to be for doing it?

问题 2：我希望这个人这样做的理由是什么？

# ↩

The Protective Use of Force in Schools

学校中保护性使用武力

I’d like to describe how some students and I used protective force to bring order into a chaotic situation at an alternative school. This school was designed for students who had dropped out or been expelled from conventional classrooms. The administration and I hoped to demonstrate that a school based on the principles of NVC would be able to reach these students. My job was to train the faculty in NVC and serve as consultant over the year. With only four days to prepare the faculty, I was unable to sufficiently clarify the difference between NVC and permissiveness. As a result, some teachers were ignoring, rather than intervening in, situations of conflict and disturbing behavior. Besieged by increasing pandemonium, the administrators were nearly ready to shut down the school.

我想描述一下我和一些学生是如何在一所另类学校里运用保护性力量来维持秩序的。这所学校是为那些辍学或被传统课堂开除的学生设立的。我和校方都希望证明，一所基于非暴力沟通（NVC）原则的学校能够帮助到这些学生。我的工作是为教师提供非暴力沟通方面的培训，并在一年中担任顾问。由于只有四天的准备时间，我没能充分阐明非暴力沟通和放任自流之间的区别。结果，一些老师对冲突和扰乱秩序的行为选择视而不见，而不是进行干预。在日益混乱的局面下，校方几乎准备关闭这所学校。

When I requested to talk with the students who had contributed most to the turbulence, the principal selected eight boys, ages eleven to fourteen, to meet with me. The following are excerpts from the dialogue I had with the students.

当我要求与造成骚乱的主要学生谈话时，校长挑选了八名年龄在十一岁到十四岁之间的男生与我见面。以下是我与这些学生谈话的部分内容。

MBR:
MBR： 		(expressing my feeling and needs without asking probing questions) I’m very upset about the teachers’ reports that things are getting out of hand in many of the classes. I want very much for this school to be successful. I’m hopeful that you can help me understand what the problems are and what can be done about them.
（表达我的感受和需求，不追问细节）老师们反映很多班级的管理都失控了，我对此感到非常难过。我真心希望这所学校能够成功。我希望您能帮助我了解问题所在以及可以采取哪些措施。
Will:
将要： 		The teachers in this school—they fools, man!
这所学校的老师——他们都是傻瓜！
MBR:
MBR： 		Are you saying, Will, that you are disgusted with the teachers and you want them to change some things they do?
威尔，你是说你对老师们感到厌恶，希望他们改变一些做法吗？
Will:
将要： 		No, man, they is fools because they just stand around and don’t do nothin’.
不，伙计，他们才是傻瓜，因为他们只会站在那里什么也不做。
MBR:
MBR： 		You mean you’re disgusted because you want them to do more when problems happen. (This is a second attempt to receive the feelings and wants.)
你的意思是，你感到反感是因为你希望他们在出现问题时做得更多。（这是第二次尝试理解你的感受和需求。）
Will:
将要： 		That’s right, man. No matter what anybody do they just stand there smilin’ like fools.
没错，伙计。不管别人做什么，他们都像傻子一样站在那里傻笑。
MBR:
MBR： 		Would you be willing to give me an example of how the teachers do nothing?
您能否举例说明一下老师们是如何无所作为的？
Will:
将要： 		Easy. Just this morning a dude walks in wearin’ a bottle of Wild Turkey on his hip pocket plain as day. Everybody seen it; the teacher, she seen it but she’s lookin’ the other way.
简单。今天早上，有个家伙走进来，裤兜里明晃晃地别着一瓶野火鸡威士忌。人人都看到了；老师也看到了，但她却把目光移开了。
MBR:
MBR： 		It sounds to me, then, that you don’t have respect for the teachers when they stand around doing nothing. You’d like them to do something. (This is a continued attempt to fully understand.)
听起来，你似乎对那些袖手旁观的老师缺乏尊重，你希望他们能做点什么。（我仍在努力理解你的意思。）
Will:
将要： 		Yeah.
是的。
MBR:
MBR： 		I feel disappointed because I want them to be able to work things out with students, but it sounds like I wasn’t able to show them what I meant.
我感到很失望，因为我希望他们能够与学生一起解决问题，但听起来我没能让他们明白我的意思。

The discussion then turned to one particularly pressing problem: that of students who didn’t want to work disturbing those who did.

随后，讨论转向了一个特别紧迫的问题：不想学习的学生打扰了那些想学习的学生。

MBR:
MBR： 		I’m anxious to try to solve this problem because the teachers tell me it’s the one that bothers them the most. I would appreciate your sharing whatever ideas you have with me.
我很想解决这个问题，因为老师们告诉我这是他们最头疼的问题。如果您有什么想法，请与我分享，我将不胜感激。
Joe:
乔： 		The teacher got to get a rattan (a stick covered with leather that was carried by some principals in St. Louis to administer corporal punishment).
老师得到了一根藤条（一种用皮革包裹的棍子，圣路易斯的一些校长用它来实施体罚）。
MBR:
MBR： 		So you’re saying, Joe, that you want the teachers to hit students when they bother others.

Joe:

Joe:

如果这是唯一的办法，我会很沮丧。我讨厌这种解决问题的方式，我想学习其他方法。

（我确信自己理解了埃德的意思，也确信他知道我理解，所以我没有复述。）这就是我的意思。我想让你明白，我对这种解决问题的方式很不满。我太健忘了，总是忘了带根大棒，就算记得带，我也舍不得用它打人。

I said I thought the plan might work if we could show that the purpose was not to punish, but to provide a place to go for those who weren’t ready to study, and simultaneously a chance to study for those who wanted to study. I also suggested that a do-nothing room would be more likely to succeed if it was known to be a product of student brainstorming rather than staff decree.

我说，如果我们能证明这个计划的目的不是为了惩罚，而是为了给那些还没准备好学习的学生提供一个去处，同时也为那些想学习的学生提供学习的机会，那么这个计划或许可行。我还建议，如果让大家知道这个“无所事事的房间”是学生集思广益的成果，而不是教职工的命令，那么它成功的可能性会更大。

A do-nothing room was set up for students who were upset and didn’t feel like doing schoolwork or whose behavior kept others from learning. Sometimes students asked to go; sometimes teachers asked students to go. We placed the teacher who had best mastered NVC in the do-nothing room, where she had some very productive talks with the children who came in. This set-up was an immense success in restoring order to the school because the students who devised it made its purpose clear to their peers: to protect the rights of students who wanted to learn. We used the dialogue with the students to demonstrate to the teachers that there were other means of resolving conflicts besides withdrawal from the conflict or using punitive force.

我们设立了一个“无所事事室”，供那些情绪低落、不想做作业或行为妨碍他人学习的学生使用。有时学生会主动要求进入，有时则是老师要求学生离开。我们安排了一位精通非暴力沟通（NVC）的老师在“无所事事室”里，与进入的孩子们进行了一些非常有成效的谈话。这个安排在恢复学校秩序方面取得了巨大的成功，因为设计者们向同学们明确阐述了其目的：保护那些渴望学习的学生的权利。我们利用与学生的对话，向老师们展示了除了回避冲突或使用惩罚性手段之外，还有其他解决冲突的方法。

# ↩

Summary

概括

In situations where there is no opportunity for communication, such as in instances of imminent danger, we may need to resort to the protective use of force. The intention behind the protective use of force is to prevent injury or injustice, never to punish or to cause individuals to suffer, repent, or change. The punitive use of force tends to generate hostility and to reinforce resistance to the very behavior we are seeking. Punishment damages goodwill and self-esteem, and shifts our attention from the intrinsic value of an action to external consequences. Blaming and punishing fail to contribute to the motivations we would like to inspire in others.

在无法沟通的情况下，例如面临迫在眉睫的危险时，我们可能需要诉诸保护性武力。保护性武力的目的是防止伤害或不公正，绝非为了惩罚或使个人遭受痛苦、悔改或改变。惩罚性武力往往会引发敌意，并强化人们对我们所期望行为的抵制。惩罚会损害善意和自尊，并将我们的注意力从行为的内在价值转移到外部后果上。责备和惩罚无助于激发我们希望在他人身上看到的动机。

# ↩

13

Liberating Ourselves and Counseling Others

解放自己，并指导他人

Freeing Ourselves From Old Programming

摆脱旧程序

W e’ve all learned things that limit us as human beings, whether from well-intentioned parents, teachers, clergy, or others. Passed down through generations, even centuries, much of this destructive cultural learning is so ingrained in our lives that we are no longer conscious of it. In one of his routines, comedian Buddy Hackett, raised on his mother’s rich cooking, claimed that he never realized it was possible to leave the table without feeling heartburn until he was in the army. In the same way, pain engendered by damaging cultural conditioning is such an integral part of our lives that we can no longer distinguish its presence. It takes tremendous energy and awareness to recognize this destructive learning and to transform it into thoughts and behaviors that are of value and of service to life.

我们都曾学到一些限制我们自身发展的观念，这些观念可能来自好心的父母、老师、神职人员或其他人士。这些有害的文化习得代代相传，甚至延续数百年，早已根深蒂固地融入我们的生活，以至于我们习以为常，不再意识到它们的存在。喜剧演员巴迪·哈克特（Buddy Hackett）在他的一段表演中提到，他从小吃着母亲丰盛的菜肴长大，直到参军后才意识到，原来吃完饭后不感到胃灼热是可能的。同样，有害的文化熏陶所带来的痛苦也已成为我们生活不可分割的一部分，以至于我们无法察觉它的存在。我们需要付出巨大的努力和觉察力，才能认识到这些有害的习得，并将其转化为有益于生活、有价值的思想和行为。

This transformation requires a literacy of needs and the ability to get in touch with ourselves, both of which are difficult for people in our culture. Not only have we never been educated about our needs, we are often exposed to cultural training that actively blocks our consciousness of them. As mentioned earlier, we have inherited a language that served kings and powerful elites in domination societies. The masses, discouraged from developing awareness of their own needs, have instead been educated to be docile and subservient to authority. Our culture implies that needs are negative and destructive; the word needy applied to a person suggests inadequacy or immaturity. When people express their needs, they are often labeled selfish, and the use of the personal pronoun I is at times equated with selfishness or neediness.

这种转变需要我们具备需求认知能力和自我觉察能力，而这两点对于我们文化中的人们来说都十分困难。我们不仅从未接受过关于自身需求的教育，而且常常受到文化熏陶，这种文化熏陶会阻碍我们对自身需求的觉察。正如前文所述，我们继承了一种服务于统治社会中君主和权贵阶层的语言。民众被阻止发展对自身需求的认知，反而被教育要顺从权威。我们的文化暗示需求是消极的、具有破坏性的；用“需要”来形容一个人，意味着其能力不足或不成熟。当人们表达自身需求时，他们常常被贴上自私的标签，而使用人称代词“我”有时也被等同于自私或需要。

By encouraging us to separate observation and evaluation, to acknowledge the thoughts or needs shaping our feelings, and to express our requests in clear action language, NVC heightens our awareness of the cultural conditioning influencing us at any given moment. And drawing this conditioning into the light of consciousness is a key step in breaking its hold on us.

非暴力沟通鼓励我们区分观察和评价，觉察塑造我们感受的想法或需求，并用清晰的行动语言表达我们的诉求，从而提升我们对当下文化制约因素的觉察力。而将这种制约因素带入意识层面，是打破其束缚的关键一步。

We can liberate ourselves from cultural conditioning.

我们可以摆脱文化束缚。

# ↩

Resolving Internal Conflicts

解决内部冲突

We can apply NVC to resolve the internal conflicts that often result in depression. In his book The Revolution in Psychiatry, Ernest Becker attributes depression to “cognitively arrested alternatives.” This means that when we have a judgmental dialogue going on within, we become alienated from what we are needing and cannot then act to meet those needs. Depression is indicative of a state of alienation from our own needs.

我们可以运用非暴力沟通来解决那些常常导致抑郁的内在冲突。欧内斯特·贝克尔在其著作《精神病学的革命》中，将抑郁症归因于“认知停滞的替代方案”。这意味着，当我们内心进行评判性的对话时，我们会与自身的需求疏离，从而无法采取行动来满足这些需求。抑郁症正是这种与自身需求疏离状态的体现。

A woman studying NVC was suffering a profound bout of depression. She was asked to identify the voices within her when she felt the most depressed and to write them down in dialogue form as though they were speaking to each other. These were the first two lines of her dialogue:

一位正在学习非暴力沟通（NVC）的女士正遭受严重的抑郁症困扰。她被要求在感到最抑郁的时候，找出内心的声音，并以对话的形式写下来，就好像这些声音在彼此交谈一样。以下是她对话的前两行：

Voice 1 (“career woman”): I should do something more with my life. I’m wasting my education and talents.

声音1（“职业女性”）：我应该做些更有意义的事情。我浪费了我的教育和才能。

Voice 2 (“responsible mother”): You’re being unrealistic. You’re a mother of two children and can’t handle that responsibility, so how can you handle anything else?

声音 2（“负责任的母亲”）：你太不现实了。你都是两个孩子的母亲，连这个责任都承担不了，又怎么能承担得起其他事呢？

Notice how these inner messages are infested with judgmental terms and phrases such as should, wasting my education and talents, and can’t handle. Variations of this dialogue had been running in this woman’s head for months. She was asked to imagine the “career woman” voice taking an “NVC pill” in order to restate its message in the following form: “When a , I feel b , because I am needing c . Therefore I now would like d .”

注意这些内心独白是如何充斥着评判性的词语和短语，例如“应该”、“浪费我的教育和才能”以及“我应付不来”。这种对话的各种变体已经在这位女性的脑海中盘旋了数月。她被要求想象“职业女性”的声音服用了一颗“非暴力沟通药丸”，以便用以下形式重新表达它的信息：“当a发生时，我感到b，因为我需要c。因此，我现在想要d。”

She subsequently translated “I should do something with my life. I’m wasting my education and talents” into: “When I spend as much time at home with the children as I do without practicing my profession, I feel depressed and discouraged because I am needing the fulfillment I once had in my profession. Therefore, I now would like to find part-time work in my profession.”

她随后将“我应该做点有意义的事。我浪费了我的教育和才能”翻译成：“当我把大部分时间都花在家里陪孩子，而没有从事我的专业工作时，我感到沮丧和灰心，因为我需要以前在工作中获得的成就感。因此，我现在想找一份与我的专业相关的兼职工作。”

Then it was the turn of her “responsible mother” voice to undergo the same process of translation. These lines, “You’re being unrealistic. You’re a mother of two children and can’t handle that responsibility, so how can you handle anything else?” were transformed into: “When I imagine going to work, I feel scared because I’m needing reassurance that the children will be well taken care of. Therefore, I now would like to plan how to provide high-quality child care while I work and how to find sufficient time to be with the children when I am not tired.”

接下来，她“负责任的母亲”的语气也经历了同样的翻译过程。这几句“你太不切实际了。你都是两个孩子的母亲，连这点责任都承担不起，又怎么能承担得起其他事呢？”被转化成了：“一想到要去上班，我就感到害怕，因为我需要有人保证孩子们会得到妥善照顾。所以，我现在想好好计划一下，如何在工作的同时提供高质量的托儿服务，以及如何在不累的时候抽出足够的时间陪伴孩子。”

This woman felt great relief as soon as she translated her inner messages into NVC. She was able to get beneath the alienating messages she was repeating to herself and offer herself empathy. Although she still faced practical challenges, such as securing quality child care and her husband’s support, she was no longer subject to the judgmental internal dialogue that kept her from being aware of her own needs.

这位女士一旦将内心的声音转化为非暴力沟通（NVC），便感到如释重负。她能够看穿那些不断重复的、令自己感到疏离的声音，并学会关爱自己。尽管她仍然面临着一些实际挑战，例如如何找到合适的托儿服务和获得丈夫的支持，但她不再受制于那些评判性的内心对话，也不再因此而忽视自己的需求。

The ability to hear our own feelings and needs and empathize with them can free us from depression.

倾听自己的感受和需求，并与之共情，可以帮助我们摆脱抑郁。

# ↩

Caring for Our Inner Environment

关爱我们的内在环境

When we are entangled in critical, blaming, or angry thoughts, it is difficult to establish a healthy internal environment for ourselves. NVC helps us create a more peaceful state of mind by encouraging us to focus on what we are truly wanting rather than on what is wrong with others or ourselves.

当我们深陷批判、指责或愤怒的情绪中时，很难建立健康的内心环境。非暴力沟通（NVC）鼓励我们关注自己真正想要的是什么，而不是他人或自身的缺点，从而帮助我们营造更平和的心态。

A participant once reported a profound personal breakthrough during a three-day training. One of her goals for the workshop was to take better care of herself, but she woke at dawn the second morning with the worst headache in recent memory. “Normally, the first thing I’d do would be to analyze what I had done wrong. Did I eat the wrong food? Did I let myself get stressed-out? Did I do this; did I not do that? But, since I had been working on using NVC to take better care of myself, I asked instead, ‘What do I need to do for myself right now with this headache?’

一位学员曾分享过她在为期三天的培训中取得的深刻个人突破。她参加工作坊的目标之一是更好地照顾自己，但第二天清晨，她醒来时头痛欲裂，这是她记忆中最严重的一次。“通常情况下，我首先会分析自己做错了什么。我是不是吃错了东西？是不是压力太大了？是不是我做了什么错事，没做什么错事？但是，由于我一直在练习运用非暴力沟通来更好地照顾自己，所以我转而问自己：‘我现在头痛得厉害，我需要做什么？’”

Focus on what we want to do rather than what went wrong.

把注意力放在我们想做的事情上，而不是哪里出了问题。

“I sat up and did a lot of really slow neck rolls, then got up and walked around, and did other things to take care of myself right then instead of beating up on myself. My headache relaxed to the point where I was able to go through the day’s workshop. This was a major, major breakthrough for me. What I understood, when I empathized with the headache, was that I hadn’t given myself enough attention the day before, and the headache was a way to say to myself, ‘I need more attention.’ I ended up giving myself the attention I needed and was then able to make it through the workshop. I’ve had headaches all my life, and this was a very remarkable turning point for me.”

“我坐起来，做了很多缓慢的颈部旋转运动，然后起身走动，做些其他事情来照顾自己，而不是责备自己。我的头痛缓解到足以让我完成当天的研讨会。这对我来说是一个非常重大的突破。当我体会到头痛的感受时，我意识到前一天我没有给予自己足够的关注，头痛是在告诉自己：‘我需要更多关注。’最终，我给予了自己所需的关注，然后顺利完成了研讨会。我一生都饱受头痛的困扰，这对我来说是一个非常重要的转折点。”

At another workshop a participant asked how NVC might be used to free us from anger-provoking messages when we are driving on the freeway. This was a familiar topic for me! For years my work involved traveling by car across the country, and I was worn and frazzled by the violence-provoking messages racing through my brain. Everybody who wasn’t driving by my standards was an archenemy, a villain. Thoughts spewed through my head: “What the hell is the matter with that guy!? Doesn’t he even watch where he’s driving?” In that state of mind, all I wanted was to punish the other drivers, and since I couldn’t do that, the anger lodged in my body and exacted its toll.

在另一次工作坊上，一位学员问到，当我们驾车行驶在高速公路上时，如何运用非暴力沟通来摆脱那些激怒我们的信息。这对我来说是一个似曾相识的话题！多年来，我的工作需要我驾车穿越全国各地，脑海中不断涌现的暴力念头让我疲惫不堪、心力交瘁。所有不按我标准开车的人，在我看来都是死敌，都是恶棍。各种念头在我脑海中翻腾：“那家伙到底怎么了？！他开车的时候难道都不看路吗？” 在这种状态下，我只想惩罚其他司机，但由于无法做到，愤怒便积压在我的身体里，最终让我精疲力竭。

Eventually I learned to translate my judgments into feelings and needs and to give myself empathy: “Boy, I am petrified when people drive like that; I really wish they would see the danger in what they are doing!” Whew! I was amazed how I could create a less stressful situation for myself by simply becoming aware of what I was feeling and needing rather than blaming others.

最终，我学会了将我的评判转化为感受和需求，并学会体谅自己：“天哪，看到别人那样开车我真是吓坏了；我真希望他们能意识到自己行为的危险性！” 呼！我惊讶地发现，仅仅通过觉察自己的感受和需求，而不是责怪他人，就能为自己创造一个压力更小的环境。

Defuse stress by hearing our own feelings and needs.

倾听自己的感受和需求，从而缓解压力。

Later I decided to practice empathy toward other drivers and was rewarded with a gratifying first experience. I was stuck behind a car going far below the speed limit and slowing down at every intersection. Fuming and grumbling, “That’s no way to drive,” I noticed the stress I was causing myself and shifted my thinking instead to what the other driver might be feeling and needing. I sensed that the person was lost, feeling confused, and wishing for some patience from those of us following. When the road widened enough for me to pass, I saw that the driver was a woman who looked to be in her eighties with an expression of terror on her face. I was pleased that my attempt at empathy had kept me from honking the horn or engaging in my customary tactics of displaying displeasure toward people whose driving bothered me.

后来，我决定尝试对其他司机设身处地地感受，并得到了令人欣慰的初次体验。当时我被一辆车挡住了去路，它开得远远低于限速，而且每个路口都减速。我气得直跺脚，嘟囔着：“这根本不是开车的方式！”但我意识到自己给自己造成了很大的压力，于是把注意力转移到了对方司机的感受和需求上。我感觉她迷路了，感到困惑，希望我们这些后面的司机能多一些耐心。当道路变得足够宽阔，我可以超车时，我看到司机是一位看起来八十多岁的老太太，脸上带着惊恐的表情。我很高兴自己尝试设身处地地感受，这让我没有像往常那样按喇叭或用其他方式表达对那些开车方式让我感到不舒服的人的不满。

Defuse stress by empathizing with others.

通过体谅他人来缓解压力。

# ↩

Replacing Diagnosis With NVC

以非暴力沟通取代诊断

Many years ago, after having just invested nine years of my life in the training and diplomas necessary to qualify as a psychotherapist, I came across a dialogue between the Israeli philosopher Martin Buber and the American psychologist Carl Rogers in which Buber questions whether anyone can do psychotherapy in the role of a psychotherapist. Buber was visiting the United States at the time and had been invited, along with Carl Rogers, to a discussion at a mental hospital in front of a group of mental health professionals.

多年前，在我花费九年时间接受培训并获得心理治疗师资格所需的文凭之后，我偶然读到以色列哲学家马丁·布伯和美国心理学家卡尔·罗杰斯的一段对话。在对话中，布伯质疑任何人都可以扮演心理治疗师的角色。当时布伯正在美国访问，他和罗杰斯应邀在一家精神病院与一群精神健康专业人士进行了一场讨论。

In this dialogue Buber posits that human growth occurs through a meeting between two individuals who express themselves vulnerably and authentically in what he termed an “I-Thou” relationship. He did not believe that this type of authenticity was likely to exist when people meet in the roles of psychotherapist and client. Rogers agreed that authenticity was a prerequisite to growth. He maintained, however, that enlightened psychotherapists could choose to transcend their own role and encounter their clients authentically.

在这段对话中，布伯提出，人类的成长源于两个个体之间坦诚而脆弱的相遇，他称之为“我-你”关系。他认为，当人们以心理治疗师和来访者的身份相遇时，这种真诚不太可能存在。罗杰斯也认同真诚是成长的先决条件。但他同时指出，有远见的心理治疗师可以选择超越自身角色，以真诚的态度与来访者相遇。

Buber was skeptical. He was of the opinion that even if psychotherapists were committed and able to relate to their clients in an authentic fashion, such encounters would be impossible as long as clients continued to view themselves as clients and their psychotherapists as psychotherapists. He observed how the very process of making appointments to see someone at their office, and paying fees to be “fixed,” dimmed the likelihood of an authentic relationship developing between two persons.

布伯对此持怀疑态度。他认为，即使心理治疗师尽职尽责，能够以真诚的方式与来访者建立联系，只要来访者仍然将自己视为来访者，将心理治疗师视为心理治疗师，这种真诚的交流就不可能实现。他观察到，预约到诊所就诊并支付费用的过程本身，就降低了两个人之间建立真诚关系的可能性。

This dialogue clarified my own long-standing ambivalence toward clinical detachment—a sacrosanct rule in the psychoanalytic psychotherapy I was taught. To bring one’s own feelings and needs into the psychotherapy was typically viewed as a sign of pathology on the part of the therapist. Competent psychotherapists were to stay out of the therapy process and to function as a mirror onto which clients projected their transferences, which were then worked through with the psychotherapist’s help. I understood the theory behind keeping the psychotherapist’s inner process out of psychotherapy and guarding against the danger of addressing internal conflicts at the client’s expense. However, I had always been uncomfortable maintaining the requisite emotional distance, and furthermore believed in the advantages of bringing myself into the process.

这段对话让我明白了自己长期以来对临床疏离的矛盾心理——这在我所学的精神分析心理治疗中是一条神圣不可侵犯的规则。将自身的情感和需求带入心理治疗通常被视为治疗师自身存在问题的表现。合格的心理治疗师应该置身于治疗过程之外，扮演一面镜子的角色，让来访者将他们的移情投射到自己身上，然后在治疗师的帮助下处理这些移情。我理解将心理治疗师的内心活动排除在治疗之外，避免因处理自身内部冲突而损害来访者利益的理论依据。然而，我一直难以保持必要的心理距离，而且我始终相信将自己融入治疗过程的益处。

I thus began to experiment by replacing clinical language with the language of NVC. Instead of interpreting what my clients were saying in line with the personality theories I had studied, I made myself present to their words and listened empathically. Instead of diagnosing them, I revealed what was going on within myself. At first, this was frightening. I worried about how colleagues would react to the authenticity with which I was entering into dialogue with clients. However, the results were so gratifying to both my clients and myself that I soon overcame any hesitation. Today, thirty-five years later, the concept of bringing oneself fully into the client-therapist relationship is no longer heretical, but when I began practicing this way, I was often invited to speak to groups of psychotherapists who would challenge me to demonstrate this new role.

于是，我开始尝试用非暴力沟通（NVC）的语言取代临床语言。我不再按照我所学的人格理论来解读来访者的话语，而是全然地关注他们的言语，并给予共情的倾听。我不再诊断他们，而是坦诚地揭示自己的内心世界。起初，这让我感到害怕。我担心同事们会如何看待我与来访者如此真诚的对话方式。然而，这种做法给来访者和我自己都带来了极大的满足感，我很快就克服了所有的顾虑。如今，三十五年过去了，将自己完全融入来访者-治疗师关系的理念已不再是异端邪说，但当我开始以这种方式实践时，我经常受邀向心理治疗师团体发表演讲，他们会挑战我，要求我展现这种新的角色。

I empathized with clients instead of interpreting them; I revealed myself instead of diagnosing them.

我与客户共情，而不是解读他们；我袒露心扉，而不是诊断他们。

Once I was asked, by a large gathering of mental health professionals at a state mental hospital, to show how NVC might serve in counseling distressed people. After my one-hour presentation, I was requested to interview a patient in order to produce an evaluation and recommendation for treatment. I talked with the twenty-nine-year-old mother of three children for about half an hour. After she left the room, the staff responsible for her care posed their questions. “Dr. Rosenberg,” her psychiatrist began, “please make a differential diagnosis. In your opinion, is this woman manifesting a schizophrenic reaction or is this a case of drug-induced psychosis?”

有一次，在一家州立精神病院，我应邀向一大群精神健康专业人士展示非暴力沟通（NVC）如何应用于心理咨询，帮助那些情绪低落的人。一个小时的演讲结束后，我被要求与一位患者面谈，以便进行评估并提出治疗建议。我与这位29岁、育有三个孩子的母亲交谈了大约半个小时。她离开房间后，负责她护理的医护人员提出了问题。“罗森伯格医生，”她的精神科医生开口问道，“请您进行鉴别诊断。您认为，这位女士是出现了精神分裂症反应，还是药物引起的精神病？”

I said that I was uncomfortable with such questions. Even when I worked in a mental hospital during my training, I was never sure how to fit people into the diagnostic classifications. Since then I had read research indicating a lack of agreement among psychiatrists and psychologists regarding these terms. The reports concluded that diagnoses of patients in mental hospitals depended more upon the school the psychiatrist had attended than the characteristics of the patients themselves.

我说过我对这类问题感到不自在。即使在我接受培训期间在精神病院工作时，我也始终不确定如何将病人归入相应的诊断分类。此后，我读到一些研究，表明精神科医生和心理学家对这些术语的理解存在分歧。这些报告的结论是，精神病院对病人的诊断更多地取决于精神科医生的毕业院校，而非病人自身的特征。

I would be reluctant, I continued, to apply these terms even if consistent usage did exist, because I failed to see how they benefited patients. In physical medicine, pinpointing the disease process that has created the illness often gives clear direction to its treatment, but I did not perceive this relationship in the field we call mental illness. In my experience of case conferences at hospitals, the staff would spend most of its time deliberating over a diagnosis. As the allotted hour threatened to run out, the psychiatrist in charge of the case might appeal to the others for help in setting up a treatment plan. Often this request would be ignored in favor of continued wrangling over the diagnosis.

我继续说道，即使这些术语确实被一致使用，我也不愿采用，因为我看不出它们对患者有何益处。在内科，明确导致疾病的病理过程通常能为治疗提供清晰的方向，但在我们称之为精神疾病的领域，我并没有看到这种关联。根据我在医院病例讨论会上的经验，医护人员会把大部分时间花在讨论诊断上。当分配的时间即将结束时，负责该病例的精神科医生可能会请求其他医生协助制定治疗方案。但通常情况下，这种请求会被忽略，大家还是会继续争论诊断结果。

I explained to the psychiatrist that NVC urges me to ask myself the following questions rather than think in terms of what is wrong with a patient: “What is this person feeling? What is she or he needing? How am I feeling in response to this person, and what needs of mine are behind my feelings? What action or decision would I request this person to take in the belief that it would enable them to live more happily?” Because our responses to these questions would reveal a lot about ourselves and our values, we would feel far more vulnerable than if we were to simply diagnose the other person.

我向精神科医生解释说，非暴力沟通（NVC）鼓励我问自己以下问题，而不是去思考病人哪里出了问题：“这个人感觉如何？他/她需要什么？我对这个人有何感受？我的感受背后又隐藏着怎样的需求？我会要求这个人采取什么行动或做出什么决定，才能让他/她过得更幸福？” 因为我们对这些问题的回答会揭示很多关于我们自身和价值观的信息，所以如果我们只是简单地诊断对方，我们会感到更加脆弱。

On another occasion, I was called to demonstrate how NVC could be taught to people diagnosed as chronic schizophrenics. With about eighty psychologists, psychiatrists, social workers, and nurses watching, fifteen patients who had been thus diagnosed were assembled on the stage for me. As I introduced myself and explained the purpose of NVC, one of the patients expressed a reaction that seemed irrelevant to what I was saying. Aware that he’d been diagnosed as a chronic schizophrenic, I succumbed to clinical thinking by assuming that my failure to understand him was due to his confusion. “You seem to have trouble following what I’m saying,” I remarked.

另一次，我受邀向被诊断为慢性精神分裂症的患者演示如何教授非暴力沟通（NVC）。当时大约有八十位心理学家、精神科医生、社工和护士在场观看，十五位被诊断为慢性精神分裂症的患者被安排在台上。当我自我介绍并解释非暴力沟通的目的时，其中一位患者的反应似乎与我所说的内容无关。我知道他被诊断为慢性精神分裂症，于是不由自主地陷入了临床思维，认为我听不懂他的话是因为他的意识混乱。“你似乎很难理解我的意思，”我说道。

At this, another patient interjected, “I understand what he’s saying,” and proceeded to explain the relevance of the first patient’s words in the context of my introduction. Recognizing that the man was not confused, but that I had simply not grasped the connection between our thoughts, I was dismayed by the ease with which I had attributed responsibility for the breakdown in communication to him. I would have liked to have owned my own feelings by saying, for example, “I’m confused. I’d like to see the connection between what I said and your response, but I don’t. Would you be willing to explain how your words relate to what I said?”

这时，另一位病人插话道：“我明白他的意思。”并开始解释第一位病人的话与我刚才的介绍有何关联。我意识到这位男士并非神志不清，而是我没能理解我们之间想法的联系，这让我很懊恼，因为我竟然如此轻易地就把沟通不畅的责任归咎于他。我本想坦诚地表达自己的感受，比如这样说：“我感到困惑。我想弄明白我说的话和你的回应之间有什么联系，但我没弄明白。您能否解释一下您的话和我说的话有什么关系？”

With the exception of this brief departure into clinical thinking, the session with the patients went successfully. The staff, impressed with the patients’ responses, wondered whether I considered them to be an unusually cooperative group of patients. I answered that when I avoided diagnosing people and instead stayed connected to the life going on in them and in myself, people usually responded positively.

除了短暂地转向临床思考之外，与患者的会谈进行得很顺利。工作人员对患者的反应印象深刻，他们问我是否认为他们是一群特别配合的患者。我回答说，当我避免诊断患者，而是关注他们以及我自己的生活状态时，人们通常会有积极的回应。

A staff member then requested a similar session be conducted, as a learning experience, with some of the psychologists and psychiatrists as participants. At this, the patients who had been on stage exchanged seats with several volunteers in the audience. In working with the staff, I had a difficult time clarifying to one psychiatrist the difference between intellectual understanding and the empathy of NVC. Whenever someone in the group expressed feelings, he would offer his understanding of the psychological dynamics behind their feelings rather than empathize with the feelings. When this happened for the third time, one of the patients in the audience burst out, “Can’t you see you’re doing it again? You’re interpreting what she’s saying rather than empathizing with her feelings!”

随后，一位工作人员要求举办一次类似的培训，作为一次学习体验，并邀请一些心理学家和精神科医生参与。培训中，之前在台上的患者与几位观众席上的志愿者交换了座位。在与工作人员沟通的过程中，我很难向一位精神科医生解释非暴力沟通中理性理解与共情之间的区别。每当小组中有人表达感受时，他总是试图从心理层面分析这些感受背后的原因，而不是真正地去理解和体会他们的感受。当这种情况第三次发生时，一位观众席上的患者终于忍不住喊道：“你难道看不出来你又在重复同样的错误吗？你是在解读她的话，而不是去体会她的感受！”

By adopting the skills and consciousness of NVC, we can counsel others in encounters that are genuine, open, and mutual, rather than resort to professional relationships characterized by emotional distance, diagnosis, and hierarchy.

通过运用非暴力沟通的技巧和意识，我们可以在真诚、开放和相互的交流中为他人提供咨询，而不是诉诸于以情感疏离、诊断和等级制度为特征的专业关系。

Summary

概括

NVC enhances inner communication by helping us translate negative internal messages into feelings and needs. Our ability to distinguish our own feelings and needs and to empathize with them can free us from depression. By showing us how to focus on what we truly want rather than on what is wrong with others or ourselves, NVC gives us the tools and understanding to create a more peaceful state of mind. Professionals in counseling and psychotherapy may also use NVC to engender mutual and authentic relationships with their clients.

非暴力沟通（NVC）通过帮助我们将负面的内在信息转化为感受和需求，从而增强内在沟通。我们区分自身感受和需求并与之共情的能力，可以帮助我们摆脱抑郁。非暴力沟通引导我们关注自己真正想要的，而不是关注他人或自身的不足之处，从而赋予我们创造更平和心境的工具和理解。咨询和心理治疗领域的专业人士也可以运用非暴力沟通来建立与客户之间真诚互信的关系。

NVC in Action

非暴力沟通实践

Dealing With Resentment and Self-Judgment

如何应对怨恨和自我评判

A student of Nonviolent Communication shares the following story.

一位学习非暴力沟通的学生分享了以下故事。

I had just returned from my first residential training in NVC. A friend whom I hadn’t seen for two years was waiting for me at home. I first met Iris, who had been a school librarian for twenty-five years, during an intense two-week heartwork and wilderness journey that culminated in a three-day solo fast in the Rockies. After she listened to my enthusiastic description of NVC, Iris revealed that she was still hurting from what one of the wilderness leaders in Colorado had said to her six years before. I had a clear memory of that person: wild-woman Leav, her palms, gouged with rope cuts, holding steady a belayed body dangling against the mountain face; she read animal droppings, howled in the dark, danced her joy, cried her truth, and mooned our bus as we waved good-bye for the last time. What Iris had heard Leav say during one of the personal feedback sessions was this:

我刚结束第一次非暴力沟通（NVC）的住宿式培训回来。一位两年未见的朋友在家等着我。我第一次见到艾瑞斯是在一次为期两周的密集式心灵疗愈和荒野之旅中，她当了二十五年的学校图书管理员，那次旅程以在落基山脉为期三天的独自禁食告终。听完我热情洋溢地介绍非暴力沟通后，艾瑞斯告诉我，六年前在科罗拉多州，一位荒野导师对她说的话仍然让她感到痛苦。我对那个人记忆犹新：野性十足的莉芙，手掌被绳索勒得伤痕累累，稳稳地托着一个悬挂在山壁上的、系着安全绳的人；她会解读动物粪便，在黑暗中嚎叫，载歌载舞，倾诉衷肠，甚至在我们最后一次挥手告别时，还对着我们的巴士露出了屁股。艾瑞斯在一次个人反馈环节中听到莉芙说的是：

“Iris, I can’t stand people like you, always and everywhere being so damn nice and sweet, constantly the meek little librarian that you are. Why don’t you just drop it and get on with it?”

“艾瑞斯，我真受不了你这种人，总是那么和善温柔，永远都像个唯唯诺诺的小图书管理员。你为什么不干脆别再这样了，赶紧做你的事呢？”

For six years Iris had been listening to Leav’s voice in her head, and for six years she’d been answering Leav in her head. We were both eager to explore how a consciousness of NVC could have affected the situation. I role-played Leav and repeated her statement to Iris.

六年来，艾瑞斯一直在脑海中聆听莉芙的声音，也一直在脑海中回应莉芙。我们都渴望探究，如果能意识到非暴力沟通的重要性，情况会如何改变。我扮演莉芙，并向艾瑞斯重复了她的话。

Iris:
鸢尾花： 		(forgetting about NVC and hearing criticism and put-down) You have no right to say that to me. You don’t know who I am, or what kind of librarian I am! I take my profession seriously, and for your information, I consider myself to be an educator, just like any teacher …
（抛开非暴力沟通，直接面对批评和贬低）你没资格这样对我。你根本不了解我，也不知道我是什么类型的图书管理员！我认真对待我的职业，而且告诉你，我把自己视为一名教育者，就像其他老师一样……
Me:
我： 		(with NVC consciousness, listening empathically, as if I were Leav) It sounds to me like you’re angry because you want me to know and recognize who you really are before criticizing you. Is that so?
（运用非暴力沟通技巧，设身处地地倾听，就像我是Leav一样）听起来你生气是因为你希望我在批评你之前了解并认可你真实的为人。是这样吗？
Iris:
鸢尾花： 		That’s right! You have simply no idea how much it took for me to even sign up for this trek. Look! Here I am: I finished, didn’t I? I took on all the challenges these fourteen days and overcame them all!
没错！你根本无法想象我报名参加这次徒步旅行有多么不容易。瞧！我做到了，对吧？这十四天里，我接受了所有挑战，并且全部克服了！
Me:
我： 		Am I hearing that you feel hurt and would have liked some recognition and appreciation for all your courage and hard work?
我感觉你很受伤，希望你的勇气和努力能得到认可和赞赏吗？

A few more exchanges followed, whereupon Iris showed a shift; these shifts, when a person feels “heard” to his or her satisfaction, can often be observed bodily. For instance, a person may relax and take a deeper breath. This often indicates that the person has received adequate empathy and is now able to shift attention to something other than the pain they have been expressing. Sometimes they are ready to hear another person’s feelings and needs. Or sometimes another round of empathy is needed to attend to another area of pain. In this situation with Iris, I could see that another piece needed attention before she would be able to hear Leav. This is because Iris had had six years of opportunities to put herself down for not having produced an honorable comeback on the spot. After the subtle shift, she immediately went on:

接下来又进行了几次交流，这时艾瑞斯的情绪发生了转变；当一个人感到自己被充分“倾听”时，这种转变通常可以从身体上观察到。例如，一个人可能会放松下来，深呼吸。这通常表明这个人已经获得了足够的共情，现在可以将注意力从自己一直在表达的痛苦转移到其他事情上。有时，他们准备好倾听他人的感受和需求。有时，他们需要另一轮的共情来关注其他方面的痛苦。就艾瑞斯的情况而言，我可以看出，在她能够倾听利夫之前，还有其他方面需要关注。这是因为在过去的六年里，艾瑞斯有很多机会因为没能当场做出体面的回应而自责。在这种微妙的转变之后，她立刻继续说道：

Iris:
鸢尾花： 		Darn, I should have said all this stuff to her six years ago!
唉，我真应该六年前就把这些话告诉她！
Me:
我： 		(as myself, an empathic friend) You’re frustrated because you wish you could have articulated yourself better at the time?
（以我这个善解人意的朋友的身份）你感到沮丧是因为你希望当时自己能更好地表达自己的想法吗？
Iris:
鸢尾花： 		I feel like such an idiot! I knew I wasn’t a “meek little librarian,” but why didn’t I say that to her?
我觉得自己真是个白痴！我知道自己不是“温顺的小图书管理员”，但我为什么没跟她说呢？
Me:
我： 		So you wish you had been enough in touch with yourself to say that?
所以你希望自己当初能更了解自己，从而说出那样的话？
Iris:
鸢尾花： 		Yes. And I’m also mad at myself! I wish I hadn’t let her push me around.
是的。我也很生自己的气！我真希望当初没让她摆布我。
Me:
我： 		You’d like to have been more assertive than you were?
你希望自己当时能更自信一些吗？
Iris:
鸢尾花： 		Exactly. I need to remember I have a right to stand up for who I am.
没错。我需要记住，我有权捍卫自己的身份。

Iris was quiet for a few seconds. She expressed readiness to practice NVC and hear what Leav said to her in a different way.

艾瑞斯沉默了几秒钟。她表示愿意练习非暴力沟通，并以不同的方式倾听利夫对她说的话。

Me:
我： 		(as Leav) Iris, I can’t stand people like you, always so nice and sweet, being forever the meek little librarian. Why don’t you just drop it and get on with it?
（扮演利夫）艾瑞斯，我受不了你这种人，总是那么和善温柔，永远扮演着温顺的小图书管理员。你为什么不干脆别再纠结了，赶紧去做你的事呢？
Iris:
鸢尾花： 		(listening for Leav’s feelings, needs, and requests) Oh, Leav, it sounds to me like you’re really frustrated … frustrated because … because I …
（倾听莉芙的感受、需求和请求）哦，莉芙，听起来你真的很沮丧……沮丧是因为……因为我……

Here Iris catches herself at a common mistake. By using the word I, she attributes Leav’s feeling to Iris herself, rather than to some desire on Leav’s own part that generates the feeling. That is, not “You’re frustrated because I am a certain way,” but “You’re frustrated because you wanted something different from me.”

在这里，艾瑞丝意识到自己犯了一个常见的错误。她用了“我”这个词，把莉芙的感受归咎于自己，而不是莉芙自身某种产生这种感受的欲望。也就是说，不是“你感到沮丧是因为我是这样的”，而是“你感到沮丧是因为你想要的是我不同的东西”。

Iris:
鸢尾花： 		(trying again) Okay, Leav, it sounds like you’re really frustrated because you are wanting … um … you’re wanting …
（再次尝试）好的，莉芙，听起来你真的很沮丧，因为你想要……嗯……你想要……

As I tried in my role-play to earnestly identify with Leav, I felt a sudden flash of awareness of what I (as Leav) was yearning for:

当我在角色扮演中努力真诚地认同利夫这个角色时，我突然意识到我（作为利夫）渴望的是什么：

Me:
我： 		(as Leav) Connection! … That’s what I am wanting! I want to feel connected … with you, Iris! And I am so frustrated with all the sweetness and niceness that stand in the way that I just want to tear it all down so I can truly touch you!
（扮演利夫）连接！……这就是我想要的！我想感受到与你的连接……艾瑞斯！所有那些阻碍我们的甜蜜和美好都让我感到无比沮丧，我只想把它们全部摧毁，这样我才能真正触碰到你！

We both sat a bit stunned after this outburst, and then Iris said, “If I had known that’s what she had wanted, if she could have told me that it was genuine connection with me she was after … Gosh, I mean, that feels almost loving.” While she never did find the real Leav to verify the insight, after this practice session in NVC, Iris achieved an internal resolution about this nagging conflict and found it easier to hear with a new awareness when people around her said things to her that she might previously have interpreted as “put-downs.”

这次爆发之后，我们俩都有些懵，然后艾瑞斯说：“如果我早知道她想要的是这样，如果她能告诉我她真正渴望的是我和我之间的真诚联结……天哪，我的意思是，这感觉简直太美好了。”虽然她最终没能找到真正的莉芙来验证这个领悟，但在这次非暴力沟通练习之后，艾瑞斯内心深处对这个挥之不去的冲突有了更深的理解，也更容易以一种全新的觉察去倾听身边人对她说的那些她以前可能解读为“贬低”的话。
